title: Naseer Ahmed and others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves three men, Naseer Ahmed, Rehmat Ullah, and Muhammad Younas, who were convicted of murdering an 18-19 year old plumber named Mustafa. The victim went missing after telling a friend he was heading to a bazaar, and days later his strangled body was found dumped in a field, with one eye removed. There was no eyewitness account of the killing.

The prosecution's case rested on circumstantial evidence: the accused disclosed to police that they had lured the victim to a house planning to commit an unnatural sexual offence with him. When he resisted and threatened to call the police, they strangled him with a handkerchief, put his body in a sack, and dumped it. These disclosures led police to recover the victim's motorcycle, mobile phone, and other items like the handcart, sack, and handkerchief used in the crime. A handkerchief was also found tied around the victim's neck, matching medical evidence.

The court held that because these disclosures revealed facts previously unknown to anyone, and were followed by actual recovery of evidence, they were voluntary and legally admissible under Article 40 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat law. The court also ruled that the complainant's absence from trial didn't hurt the prosecution's case since he wasn't a witness to the actual crime.

Finding the circumstantial evidence credible and consistent, the Balochistan High Court dismissed all three appeals, upholding the convictions and life sentences.

title: Abbas Raza and others V. The State through Director General and others,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court and concerns pre-arrest bail applications filed by several government officials, including education department officers and accounts staff, who were accused by the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) of involvement in bogus recruitment of teachers, causing a loss of over 15 million rupees to the government.

The petitioners argued that NAB had already filed earlier references against them and others over the same set of bogus recruitment allegations, and that this new reference (No. 4 of 2017) was essentially a repeat case meant to pressurize and harass them, since the courts had already granted bail to most accused in those earlier, related references. They also pointed out that they had cooperated with the investigation.

The court noted that NAB had identified 125 bogus teacher appointments overall, but instead of filing one consolidated reference, it split the allegations into three separate references over time, covering overlapping facts and accused persons. The petitioners had already asked the trial court to consolidate all the references, and that request was still pending. The High Court found this piecemeal filing by NAB suspicious, suggesting mala fide intent, and concluded that whether the references truly involved separate offences or the same conduct required further evidence and inquiry by the trial court.

Because of this uncertainty and the appearance of bad faith in splitting the case, the High Court granted pre-arrest bail to the petitioners, treating the matter as one requiring further inquiry rather than immediate arrest.

title: Muhammad Arif V. Muhammad Ashraf and another,
explainer:
This case involved cross-complaints arising from a violent clash between two families in Quetta. The complainant, a doctor, alleged that named accused persons, including Muhammad Ashraf, attacked his home and that Ashraf shot him during the incident. In response, one of the accused had filed a separate FIR against the complainant and his brothers, alleging that they had assaulted the accused's side, injuring people on that end too.

The trial court had granted bail to Muhammad Ashraf, and the complainant asked the High Court to cancel that bail, arguing Ashraf was specifically named as the shooter and shouldn't have been released. The complainant also objected that the trial court's bail order had gone further than necessary, suggesting the case actually fit a less serious offence than attempted murder, which could unfairly weaken the prosecution's case at trial.

The Balochistan High Court refused to cancel the bail, agreeing with the trial court that since both sides had filed FIRs and both had visible injuries, the matter required further inquiry at trial rather than resolution at the bail stage. The court also noted there was no evidence Ashraf had misused his bail, such as skipping hearings or threatening witnesses, which are the usual grounds for cancellation.

However, the High Court agreed that the trial court's remarks favoring the lesser charge were premature and could prejudice the prosecution, so it ordered those specific observations struck from the record while keeping the bail intact. This shows courts must be careful not to prejudge a case while deciding bail.

title: Tareen alias Bado and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a death sentence handed down by a Sessions Court in Killa Saifullah, Balochistan. The accused, Tareen alias Bado, had been convicted of murder under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced to death, along with a separate conviction for causing injury. The case arose after a police patrol heard gunshots, rushed to the scene, and found the accused firing a weapon. One man was killed on the spot and another was seriously injured. The accused was caught red-handed with a pistol, and two spent bullet casings recovered from the scene matched the weapon according to forensic analysis.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence, including testimony from nine witnesses (police officials and relatives of the victims), medical reports confirming the cause of death and injury, and the forensic ballistics report. The court found the prosecution's case fully proven, rejecting defense arguments that the witnesses were biased or "interested." It held that police witnesses and relatives of victims can still be reliable if their testimony is consistent and not shown to be malicious.

However, the court noted the prosecution failed to prove any motive, and that the accused was elderly (72 years old). Given these circumstances, the court upheld the conviction but reduced the death sentence to life imprisonment. This case illustrates how courts weigh witness credibility, forensic evidence, and mitigating personal circumstances when deciding whether the death penalty is appropriate.

title: Lasbella Industrial Estate Development Authority through Managing Director V. Gul Hassan Bhootani and others,
explainer:

LIEDA claimed it had lawfully purchased the land and had it registered in its name through a mutation entry, but alleged that the land was later fraudulently transferred to another party through collusion involving a revenue official, and then passed through further transfers to other respondents.

LIEDA sued for a declaration that it was the rightful owner and sought cancellation of the disputed revenue entries. Both the trial court and the first appellate court dismissed its case, prompting LIEDA to file this revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found serious flaws in how the lower courts handled the case. It noted that the appellate court had not properly framed points for determination as required under the Civil Procedure Code, had not discussed the witnesses' testimony, and had issued a judgment that gave no real reasoning. The trial court, too, had failed to properly consider the evidence and documents on record, and had not given the parties a fair opportunity to present their case.

Because of these failures, the High Court set aside both lower court judgments and sent the case back to the trial court, directing it to give all parties a full and fair hearing and decide the matter afresh. The case highlights the importance of courts properly reasoning their decisions and ensuring the right to a fair trial before deciding property disputes.

title: Mir Fateh Muhammad and 5 others V. Muhammad Alam and another,
explainer:
This case was about a legal dispute over the proper venue for resolving environmental complaints. A landowner, Muhammad Alam, sued the operators of Crash Plants (stone and sand excavation equipment) in a civil court, claiming their operations polluted the area, damaged his orchards, and lowered the underground water level near his agricultural land. The trial court dismissed his suit, but an appellate court reversed that decision and ruled in his favor. The defendants then challenged this in the Balochistan High Court.

The core legal question was whether an ordinary civil court had the authority to decide an environmental dispute at all, given that Pakistan has a special law, the Environmental Protection Act, which creates its own dedicated forum, the Environmental Protection Tribunal, to handle such matters.

The High Court ruled that since the complaint was fundamentally about environmental harm, it fell under the special jurisdiction of the Environmental Protection Tribunal, not the regular civil courts. Because a specialized forum existed for this type of grievance, the civil court had no authority to entertain the suit in the first place. The High Court found that the appellate court's decision favoring the landowner was based on misreading the evidence, so it set aside that ruling and restored the trial court's dismissal. The landowner was told he could still pursue his complaint before the correct tribunal. This case is important because it clarifies that specialized environmental disputes must go through the dedicated tribunal system rather than ordinary civil courts.

title: The Base Commander Pakistan Air Force, P.A.F. Base, Quetta V. Provincial Government throuth Member Board of Revenue Balochistan and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Quetta between residents of villages belonging to the Bazai tribe and two government parties: the Pakistan Air Force Base Commander and the Balochistan provincial government. The villagers claimed longstanding ancestral rights over unsettled land adjoining their settled properties, citing custom and historical practice from before Partition. They sued for declaration of ownership and a permanent injunction, alleging that the PAF Base was pressuring them to vacate the land, claiming it as a firing range.

The trial court initially dismissed the villagers' suit, but on appeal it was decreed in their favor. However, when the appellate court sent notice to the PAF Base to inform them of the appeal, the notice was returned unserved because the process server was not allowed onto the base premises. Instead of trying another way to deliver the notice, the appellate court simply proceeded without the Air Force's participation and ruled against it.

The Balochistan High Court found this improper. It held that a party cannot be condemned without being given a fair chance to be heard, a principle rooted in due process (audi alteram partem, protected under Article 10-A of the Constitution). Since only one unsuccessful attempt at service was made, the Air Force's right to be heard was violated.

The Court set aside the appellate court's judgment and sent the case back for a fresh hearing where all parties, including the PAF Base, must be properly heard before a decision is made. The revision petitions were allowed.

title: The Collector Customs, through Additional Collector Model Customs Collectorate, Quetta and others V. Abdul Zahir and others,
explainer:
This case involved a customs fraud investigation in Quetta. The Customs Department accused several exporters and their clearing agent of mis-declaring rice export shipments worth millions of dollars by tampering with official E-Forms (bank certification documents required for exports) and Goods Declarations, allegedly adding extra zeros to inflate declared export values and using forged or uncertified forms. This was said to have caused huge losses in foreign exchange, export surcharges, and withholding tax. The accused were tried in the Special Customs Court, which acquitted all of them. The Customs Department then appealed these acquittals to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the acquittals and dismissed the department's appeals. It found that the prosecution's entire case depended on the allegedly forged Goods Declarations and E-Forms, but these key documents were never actually produced as evidence during the trial. The investigating officer even admitted that customs authorities were responsible for keeping such original records safely. Without producing the very documents needed to prove forgery, the prosecution's case remained unproven. The court also noted the FIR was lodged four years after the alleged offence, with no adequate explanation for the delay.

The judgment reinforces an important principle: once someone is acquitted, that acquittal carries a strong presumption of innocence that appellate courts should not disturb unless the decision was clearly unreasonable or against the evidence. It also highlights that prosecutions must actually produce their core evidence in court, not merely allege it.

title: Haday Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a bail application in a murder case pending before the Balochistan High Court, Sibi Bench. The applicant, Haday Khan, was accused, along with several others, of murdering a man named Rindo in 1996 over an old family enmity, as alleged in the FIR. After investigation, a formal charge (challan) was filed in the trial court, and the trial had already begun. Khan had earlier been denied bail by the Additional Sessions Judge and then approached the High Court.

His lawyer argued that Khan was innocent, that he had no specific role assigned to him in the murder, that no witness had directly linked him to the killing, that his long absence (absconsion) from the case for years was not deliberate, and that since investigation was already complete and he was in judicial custody, there was no need to keep him detained further. The state opposed bail, citing the seriousness of the murder charge.

The judge agreed that since Khan's guilt or innocence could only be properly determined once evidence was recorded at trial, and given the lack of clear evidence directly tying him to the shooting, this qualified as a case fitting the "further inquiry" bail standard. The court held that mere long absconsion could not be used to deny bail. As a result, the court granted Khan bail, subject to him providing a surety bond of Rs. 200,000. The court clarified its observations were tentative and would not affect the final outcome of the trial.

title: Haday Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns a bail application filed by Haday Khan, who was accused in a 1996 murder case registered under Sections 302/34 of the Pakistan Penal Code (murder committed with common intention). The FIR alleged that the accused, along with several others, had shot and killed a man named Rindo while he was sleeping at his home, with old enmity cited as the motive.

After investigation, the police had submitted the case for trial, and the applicant was in judicial custody while the trial proceeded. His earlier bail request had been rejected by the trial court. The court granted him bail on surety of Rs. 200,000, clarifying that these observations were tentative and would not affect the final outcome of the trial.

title: Bahlool Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a bail application filed by Bahlool Khan, who was accused of blackmailing a married woman named Hina Nadeem under Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016. According to the complaint, the accused had secretly taken objectionable pictures of the woman and then threatened to upload them online unless she paid him money. He was arrested during a police trap set up when the complainant, working with the Federal Investigation Agency, called him to collect payment. Two mobile phones were recovered from him, and messages on those phones supported the allegations. He had also allegedly confessed to the crime both during investigation and in a formal statement before a magistrate.

The accused's lawyer argued that he was innocent, that the confession was recorded too late to be reliable, and that the offense did not fall under the category of crimes for which bail is normally denied automatically. The court agreed that the offense technically did not fall into that automatic-denial category, but ruled that this alone does not entitle someone to bail as a right. The Balochistan High Court found that the evidence, including the messages and confessions, connected the accused to a serious and harmful crime against a woman's dignity and against society at large. Because of the serious nature of the offense and its potential to encourage similar misconduct by others, the court refused to grant bail, upholding the decisions of the lower courts.

title: Liaquat Ali V. Akhtar Hussain and 28 others,
explainer:
This case concerned a challenge to the results of the 2018 Provincial Assembly election for constituency PB-29, Quetta-VI in Balochistan. The losing candidate, Liaquat Ali, filed an election petition against the winner, Akhtar Hussain Langove, alleging that the returned candidate had conspired with polling officials and security personnel to rig the vote across 32 polling stations, including stuffing ballot boxes, casting bogus votes, and mishandling ballot boxes after polling closed. He asked the court to order a full recount, verify thumb impressions through NADRA, exclude fraudulent votes, or declare the election void and order re-polling.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It found that the petitioner's allegations were vague and general, lacking specifics such as the names of officials involved, particular polling stations, times, or persons responsible for the alleged rigging. Under the Elections Act 2017, a petitioner must provide full details of any claimed corrupt or illegal practice, and unsubstantiated general claims cannot meet this legal standard. The court also noted the large margin of victory (over 7,700 votes) and held that recounting or verification would only be justified if there was concrete, prima facie evidence of rigging—which was absent here.

The case highlights how strict the evidentiary burden is on candidates challenging election results in Pakistan; vague suspicions of fraud, without proof, are not enough to overturn an election outcome.

title: Khair Jan V. Abdul Qudoos Bizanjo and 22 others,
explainer:
I don't have the complete text to review, but based on what's provided, this case is about a losing candidate in Balochistan's 2018 provincial assembly election challenging the results.

Khair Jan contested the PB-44 Awaran-cum-Panjgur seat and lost to Abdul Qadoos Bizanjo, who received 8,055 votes against Khair Jan's 5,962. After the Election Commission declared Bizanjo the winner, Khair Jan filed an election petition alleging rigging, bogus voting, double-stamped ballots, and claims that polling staff arrived late at several polling stations, causing voters to leave before casting ballots. He asked the court to void the election, order thumb-impression verification through NADRA at numerous polling stations, and either declare fresh polling or declare himself the winner.

The court dismissed the petition. It held that the petitioner made only general, vague allegations of corrupt and illegal practices without naming specific officials or persons responsible, and without providing solid evidence to back the claims. Since Khair Jan failed to shift the burden of proof onto the respondent, and given the large vote margin between the two candidates, the court found no justification for ordering a recount or vote verification, and rejected the petition.

This case matters because it reinforces that election petitions require concrete, particularized evidence rather than sweeping allegations, protecting the integrity of election results from unsubstantiated challenges.

title: Ameer Bakhsh and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two brothers, Ameer Bakhsh and Wali Muhammad, who were convicted by a trial court in Nasirabad for the murder of a man named Band Ali and sentenced to life imprisonment. According to the prosecution, an argument broke out between the accused and the deceased outside his home, after which armed men, including the two appellants, allegedly opened fire, killing him.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found serious weaknesses in the prosecution's case. The key eyewitnesses, including the complainant, testified in court but failed to actually identify the appellants as the shooters, even though they had named them in the FIR. Because of this failure to identify them in court, all three witnesses were declared hostile. Additionally, no weapons were recovered from the appellants, no confession existed, and the witnesses never described what kind of firearms were used. The only remaining evidence was the medical report, which the court noted could confirm that a murder occurred but could not identify who committed it.

The court also pointed out that a co-accused in the same incident had already been acquitted by the same High Court in an earlier case, based on similar evidence.

Given the lack of reliable identification evidence, the High Court gave the appellants the benefit of the doubt, overturned their convictions, and ordered their release. The case highlights how convictions cannot stand when eyewitnesses fail to identify the accused and no other solid evidence links them to the crime.

title: Ikhtiar Khan V. Raies Raza Muhammad and 19 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over water rights. A man named Ikhtiar Khan filed a civil suit claiming he owned a water channel running through his properties and that certain neighbors (respondents) had illegally diverted this water toward their own land. During the trial, after most evidence had been recorded, including nine witnesses, Khan tried to amend his lawsuit to add a specific piece of land (identified by a khasra number, a land record reference) to the list of properties involved in the dispute.

The trial court rejected this request, noting that the proposed amendment did not establish any valid legal basis, that the land in question was jointly owned by several people who were not even part of the lawsuit, and that Khan had already been given multiple chances to complete his own testimony but kept delaying. The court felt he was trying to stall the case rather than genuinely correct an error. When Khan challenged this refusal, the District Judge upheld the trial court's decision, agreeing that allowing such a late-stage amendment would fundamentally change the nature of the case after evidence had already been presented.

Khan then approached the Balochistan High Court, but the High Court also dismissed his petition. It found no legal error, misreading of evidence, or irregularity in the lower courts' decisions. This case illustrates that courts are generally reluctant to allow amendments to a lawsuit that would alter its basic structure late in the proceedings, especially when such changes appear aimed at delaying justice rather than correcting genuine mistakes.

title: Abdul Khaliq V. Sardar Sanaullah Zehri and 12 others,
explainer:
This case involved a challenge to the results of the July 2018 general election for a Provincial Assembly seat, PB-38 Khuzdar-I, in Balochistan. The petitioner, Abdul Khaliq, had lost to Sardar Sanaullah Zehri by a narrow margin of just 18 votes. Khaliq filed an election petition alleging that the winning candidate had engaged in rigging and corrupt practices, working with polling staff at fifteen specific polling stations to allow bogus voting through impersonation, while denying his polling agents access to observe the process. He asked the court to examine the ballot records, verify voters' thumb impressions using NADRA technology, and either declare him the winner or order a re-poll.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It found that the petitioner had made only general, vague accusations without naming any specific officials involved in wrongdoing, and his witnesses failed to identify particular polling stations, times, or people connected to the alleged rigging. The court held that ordering verification of thumb impressions requires at least some preliminary evidence of rigging or invalid voting, and no such evidence existed here.

This case matters because it illustrates the high evidentiary bar election petitioners must meet in Pakistan—vague or unsubstantiated claims of electoral fraud, even in a closely contested race, are insufficient to overturn results or trigger forensic investigation of ballots.

title: Muhammad Alim V. the State,
explainer:
Muhammad Alim was convicted by a trial court for causing hurt (shajjah), mischief, and rioting offences after allegedly attacking the complainant's sons with knives and sticks during a road altercation, breaking vehicle glass in the process. His sentence was upheld with modifications on appeal, prompting him to file a criminal revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found serious problems with the prosecution's evidence. The complainant had not actually witnessed the attack and relied on hearsay from an unnamed caller, and he even got the date of the incident wrong. The two injured witnesses contradicted their earlier statements and admitted the incident happened near a Levies (paramilitary) checkpost, meaning a Levies employee, Muhammad Kareem, had likely seen the events firsthand. Yet the prosecution never produced this independent witness, and the investigating officer admitted that Kareem's recorded statement did not even place the accused at the scene. The accused also presented an alibi witness claiming he was elsewhere all day.

Applying the legal principle that withholding a key, independent witness allows the court to presume his testimony would have gone against the prosecution, the judge ruled the prosecution failed to prove Alim's presence and involvement. This case highlights how courts scrutinize contradictory testimony, hearsay, and the suppression of crucial witnesses, ultimately giving the accused the benefit of the doubt and acquitting him.

title: Abdul Ahad V. The State through Special Prosecutor ANF, Balochistan,
explainer:
This case involved Abdul Ahad, who was stopped at a checkpoint near Chaman-Quetta Road and found with 200 slabs of hashish, weighing 100 kilograms, hidden in the boot of the car he was driving. He was tried under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act and convicted by a trial court, receiving a life sentence and a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found serious problems with how the prosecution handled the evidence. Samples of the narcotics were sent for laboratory analysis, but the person who actually carried the samples to the forensic lab was never named as a witness or brought to court to testify about how the samples were handled. This raised doubts about whether the drugs tested were kept safe and were truly the same ones seized from the car.

Even more significantly, the court noted that ownership of the car itself was disputed. While the complainant claimed the appellant owned the vehicle at the time of arrest, the appellant later denied owning it, and the vehicle's registration documents were never properly investigated or seized by police. Since the entire case rested on the drugs being found in that car, this unresolved ownership question created reasonable doubt.

Because criminal defendants are entitled to the benefit of even the slightest doubt, the court ruled that the appellant could not fairly be held responsible for the recovery. The conviction and sentence were set aside, and Abdul Ahad was acquitted. The case highlights how procedural gaps in evidence handling can undermine even serious drug prosecutions.

title: Samiullah and others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Samiullah and Hussain, convicted by a Special Judge in Khuzdar under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, for possessing 40 kilograms of charas allegedly found hidden in secret cavities and a CNG cylinder of a car they were traveling in. They were sentenced to 25 years imprisonment each plus fines.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted both men. The key problem was a serious delay in sending drug samples for laboratory testing. Under the applicable rules, samples must be sent to the Chemical Examiner within 72 hours of seizure, but here they were sent 20 days later, with no explanation from the investigating officer for the delay. The court also noted that the official who transported the samples to the laboratory was never brought to testify about how the samples were handled and stored during those 20 days, meaning safe custody could not be proven. Additionally, the prosecution failed to prove that the appellants actually owned or possessed the vehicle where the drugs were found.

Because of these unexplained gaps and procedural violations, the court held that the case was riddled with doubt, and under the law an accused is entitled to the benefit of even the slightest doubt. This case highlights how strict compliance with evidence-handling procedures in narcotics cases is essential, and failure to follow them can result in acquittal even in cases involving serious allegations.

title: Syed Wali V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of murder for firing a gunshot that killed a person traveling in a wedding party convoy. The incident occurred when two vehicles were trying to overtake each other on a road near Noushki, Balochistan. During this encounter, the accused fired shots, and one bullet struck and killed a man named Satak. The trial court had convicted the appellant under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code, the provision for intentional murder, sentencing him to life imprisonment.

On appeal, the defense did not contest guilt but argued for a lesser sentence, claiming the shooting was aerial firing without intent to kill, and that the fatal shot may have hit the victim accidentally due to the vehicle crossing a speed-breaker.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence and found there was no prior enmity, dispute, or motive between the parties, the encounter arose spontaneously from a traffic dispute, and the accused did not fire repeatedly at the victims even though they were defenseless at his mercy. Based on this, the court concluded the necessary intent for murder was missing, and instead the case fit the lesser offense of qatl-bis-sabab (causing death without intent, through an unlawful act), punishable under Section 322 of the Penal Code.

The court therefore modified the conviction from murder to this lesser offense, replacing the life sentence with an order to pay diyat (blood money) as compensation. This case illustrates how courts distinguish between intentional murder and unintentional killing based on evidence of intent

title: Muhammad Saleem Malik V. Government of Pakistan through its Secretary Finance Division, Regulation Wing, Pakistan Islamabad and others,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court, involved a retired employee of Pakistan Telecommunication Company Limited (PTCL) who had served for over 32 years, originally joining the Telegraph and Telephone Department before it became a corporation and then a company. He had opted for a Voluntary Separation Scheme and later sought pension increases and allowances equal to those given to other government pensioners, arguing that several government and PTCL notifications discriminated against retired employees like him by not extending the same benefits.

The court examined relevant laws, including the Pakistan Telecommunication Corporation Act, 1991 and the Pakistan Telecommunication Re-Organization Act, 1996, which protect the terms and conditions of employees transferred from the old T&T Department. It also considered earlier Supreme Court rulings on similar pension disputes. However, the court found that the petitioner had not first approached the proper authority within PTCL to resolve his complaint, nor shown that any such authority had rejected his claim. Since he was no longer a civil servant and had an alternative, effective remedy available through the company's own redressal mechanism, the court held that filing a constitutional petition directly in the High Court was not appropriate.

As a result, the petition was dismissed. The judgment underscores that employees with service-related grievances against PTCL must first exhaust internal remedies before turning to the courts, even though their basic service terms remain legally protected.

title: Muhammad Saleem Malik V. Government of Pakistan through its Secretary Finance Division, Regulation Wing, Pakistan Islamabad and others,
explainer:
This case involved a former Pakistan Telegraph and Telephone (T&T) Department employee whose job was later transferred to Pakistan Telecommunication Corporation (PTC) and then to Pakistan Telecommunication Company Limited (PTCL). After opting for a Voluntary Separation Scheme and drawing pension, the petitioner asked the Balochistan High Court to declare several government and PTCL notifications discriminatory for not giving him the same pay raises, pension increases, and medical allowance benefits given to other government pensioners and in-service employees.

The petitioner argued that under the Pakistan Telecommunication Act, 1991 and the Pakistan Telecommunication (Re-organization) Act, 1996, his original service terms and conditions remained protected even after transfer, citing Supreme Court precedents supporting pension parity for transferred employees.

The Court reviewed the record and found that the petitioner had never actually approached the relevant competent authority within PTCL or the government to raise this specific grievance, nor did he produce any adverse order against him that could be challenged. The Court held that while his service terms remain protected by law, he was no longer a civil servant, and had an alternate, effective remedy available - namely, applying to the competent authority for redress before coming to court.

Because he skipped that step, the High Court ruled the petition was not properly before it and dismissed it, leaving the door open for him to pursue his claim through the proper administrative channel first.

title: Muhammad Azam and 4 others V. Nabi Bakhsh and another,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved a dispute over a piece of land between two families, both claiming to be its rightful owners and possessors. The complainant said he was the recorded owner of the land and that the petitioners had illegally entered it, started building a wall, and attacked him when he objected. He filed a complaint under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, and asked the trial court for interim relief to restore his possession. The trial court agreed and ordered the petitioners to hand over the land immediately.

The petitioners challenged this order, arguing the land was actually their ancestral property, that a mosque and houses already existed on it, that the complainant's ownership records were the result of fraud, and that a civil suit over the same land was already pending in another court. They also pointed out that a similar complaint filed earlier by the complainant's brother had been rejected.

The High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners, setting aside the trial court's order. It held that under Section 7 of the Illegal Dispossession Act, courts can only form a tentative opinion at this stage, not decide the case's merits. Since ownership and possession were seriously disputed and required evidence from both sides, the trial court had gone too far by effectively deciding the case outright. The court ordered both parties to maintain the status quo until the matter is properly resolved through trial.

title: Najeebullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves a bail application from Balochistan High Court in a murder case. Najeebullah was named in an FIR along with two other men for the killing of Muhammad Shah, who was allegedly attacked and shot while fitting sewerage pipes. The FIR accused two co-accused of actually firing the fatal shots, while Najeebullah was said to merely be present. He was empty-handed at the scene, and no act of violence, threat, or provocation was attributed to him in the original FIR. Later, through a supplementary statement, the complainant claimed Najeebullah had physically controlled or restrained the deceased during the attack, but failed to explain why this important detail was left out of the original complaint.

The court found this inconsistency significant, ruling that the delayed and unexplained addition of a specific role created reasonable doubt about Najeebullah's actual participation in the crime. Since he was unarmed and no clear role was assigned to him initially, the judge held that the case required further inquiry to determine whether he shared the common intention to commit murder or was merely present by chance. The court also noted that investigation was already complete and trial had begun, so keeping him in custody served no further purpose.

As a result, the judge granted Najeebullah bail. The case illustrates how Pakistani courts scrutinize FIRs for consistency and require clear evidence of intent or action before denying bail, especially when the prosecution's story shifts over time regarding an accused's role.

title: Ehsam-Ud-Din V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about an appeal against a criminal conviction. Ehsam-ud-Din was convicted by a trial court for causing a firearm injury (badi'ah) to a man named Syed Iqbal and was sentenced to one year's imprisonment plus a fine (Daman). He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The complainant alleged that after he objected to a stranger loitering near a street used by women, the accused came out, abused him, and shot him in the leg. However, the High Court found serious problems with the evidence. The complainant gave inconsistent accounts, first in his police complaint and then in court, adding new details that didn't appear earlier. He also tried to hide that the accused was actually his cousin, later admitting this under cross-examination, suggesting a possible family dispute motive. The only supposed eyewitness, a shopkeeper, hadn't actually seen the shooting himself and was only repeating what the complainant told him afterward. There was also a pre-existing land dispute between the parties, raising the possibility of false implication. Additionally, the weapon, spent bullet casings, and blood-stained soil were never recovered, and the medical report contradicted the complainant's claim by showing the injury was on the left thigh, not the right leg as stated.

Given these contradictions and doubts, the High Court ruled that the accused deserved the benefit of the doubt and overturned the conviction, acquitting him. The case highlights how inconsistent testimony and weak evidence can undermine a criminal conviction.

title: Wali Muhammad V. Returning Officer and 18 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a challenge to the results of a by-election held on 31 December 2018 in constituency PB-26 Quetta-III. The by-election became necessary after the originally declared winner was disqualified for being an Afghan national. In the fresh by-election, Qadir Ali secured the most votes and was declared the returned candidate. Wali Muhammad, who came second, filed an election petition alleging massive rigging, including bogus votes cast in the names of dead people and persons living abroad.

Before examining the rigging allegations, the Election Tribunal at the Balochistan High Court had to decide a preliminary objection raised by the winning candidate: that the petition itself was legally defective and should be thrown out. The court found several serious problems - the petition was filed after the 45-day deadline required by law, with no application asking the court to excuse the delay; it had not been properly verified on oath; and copies of the petition and its supporting documents had not been sent to the other contesting candidates as required.

title: Abdul Rashid and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a murder conviction. The prosecution alleged that the accused, along with his sons, shot and killed the complainant's father following prior phone threats. The trial court had convicted the accused, and he appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found serious problems with the prosecution's evidence. The claims about threatening phone calls came from interested witnesses (relatives of the deceased) who could not confirm exact timing, and police never obtained call records or verified whose phone number was used. No FIR was even filed about these alleged threats. As for direct eyewitness testimony, the deceased's son claimed to have watched the shooting but his account was illogical - he said he ran home to get a weapon instead of trying to help his dying father, and other witnesses' statements did not support his presence at the scene. A confession recorded under Section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code was also found unreliable, since the accused had been held illegally for an extra day before confessing, with no explanation from police. Medical evidence only confirmed how the victim died, not who did it.

The court ruled that mere family relationship doesn't automatically disqualify a witness, but such testimony must survive cross-examination intact. Since it didn't, and multiple doubts existed, the court applied the principle that any single reasonable doubt must benefit the accused. The conviction was overturned and the accused acquitted, highlighting how weak, uncorroborated evidence and questionable confessions cannot sustain a murder conviction.

title: Umer Din V. Mairaj-Ud-Din & another,
explainer:

The High Court, hearing the father's revision petition, agreed with the lower courts. It found no sufficient cause had been shown for the delay, and no legal error or jurisdictional defect in the appellate court's decision. The revision was dismissed, meaning the ex-parte decree in the son's favor stands. The case highlights how strictly Pakistani courts enforce appeal deadlines, even in family property disputes, unless a genuinely credible excuse for delay is provided.

title: Naib Subedar Nasabuddin, Frontier Corps (South) and others V. Ali Nawaz and others,
explainer:

He was charged with causing death by negligent driving and rash driving on a public road.

At trial, the accused was acquitted, and both the complainant and the state (through the Prosecutor General) appealed against the acquittal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the prosecution's evidence and found serious weaknesses. The complainant had not actually witnessed the incident himself and was relying on secondhand information. The two supposed eyewitnesses gave contradictory accounts and admitted their statements were recorded thirteen days after the incident, with no explanation for the delay. Given these gaps, the court held that reasonable doubt existed, which under the law entitles the accused to acquittal as a matter of right, not leniency. Since acquittals carry a strong presumption of innocence, courts should not interfere unless the decision was clearly unreasonable. The High Court therefore dismissed both appeals, upholding the acquittal.

title: Muhammad Azam and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a murder trial in Balochistan. A man reported that his brother had gone missing while grazing goats in 2014. Two years later, he claimed that through informal tribal channels of communication, he learned that certain men had murdered his brother and buried the body secretly. Based on this, an FIR was filed and one accused, Muhammad Azam, was arrested, tried, and convicted by the trial court for murder, receiving a life sentence.

On appeal, the High Court closely examined the evidence and found serious problems. The complainant himself had not witnessed the crime, and his account was based on hearsay. He never reported his brother missing to police. The two so-called eyewitnesses could not even remember when the crime occurred, stayed silent for two years despite being relatives of the complainant, and gave accounts that contradicted the medical evidence about how the victim died. No DNA testing was done to confirm the exhumed body was actually the missing brother. The accused was named only after a two-year delay, raising suspicion of false implication.

Because of these serious doubts, the High Court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. It set aside the conviction and acquitted the appellant, also dismissing the complainant's separate request to increase the sentence to death. The judgment reinforces the principle that any reasonable doubt in a criminal case must benefit the accused, not the prosecution.

title: Naseer Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Naseer Khan, who was convicted of murdering Abdul Majeed in 2008. During the trial, the victim's family agreed to a compromise, forgiving him under Pakistan's qisas and diyat law, which normally allows murder cases to be settled between the accused and the victim's heirs, leading to acquittal.

However, the trial court, while accepting the compromise, did not acquit him outright. Instead, it convicted him under Section 311 of the Pakistan Penal Code, which allows punishment (ta'zir) even after a compromise if the crime is considered "fasad-fil-arz," meaning it disturbed public order or made the offender a danger to society. The court sentenced him to 14 years in prison.

Naseer Khan appealed this conviction. The Balochistan High Court examined his history and found he was not an isolated offender: after the original murder, he had gone on to kill another man, murdered his own father and brother, attempted to murder another brother, and also committed robbery. His conduct during trial was described as harsh and defiant.

Given this pattern of repeated violent crimes, the High Court ruled he was a genuine threat to society and upheld the trial court's decision, dismissing his appeal. The case illustrates how courts can still punish dangerous offenders even when victims' families forgive them, ensuring that private compromises in murder cases do not let habitual criminals escape all punishment.

title: Deen Muhammad V. Labour Appellate Tribunal Balochistan, Quetta and others,
explainer:
This case is about a factory worker, Deen Muhammad, who was dismissed from his job as a helper after being accused of misconduct. The company issued him a charge sheet, held an inquiry where he admitted his guilt, and then dismissed him. The worker later sent a legal notice (called a grievance notice) through his lawyer, challenging his removal, and eventually got a labour court to order his reinstatement with back pay. However, the employer appealed, and the Labour Appellate Tribunal overturned that decision. The worker then challenged the Tribunal's decision in the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It found that under the law governing labour disputes in Balochistan, a worker must personally serve a grievance notice on the employer before going to court, not through a lawyer. More importantly, the court found that the grievance notice the worker had sent was not even about his dismissal - it was about an earlier suspension order. There was no evidence he had ever formally raised a grievance specifically about being fired. Since a valid grievance notice is the essential first step required before a worker can seek relief in these cases, its absence meant his entire case had no legal foundation.

This ruling matters because it shows how strictly courts enforce procedural requirements in labour disputes - even a worker with a seemingly valid complaint can lose the case entirely if the correct legal notice was not properly issued at the right time and against the right decision.

title: Jameel Ahmed Dashti V. Abdul Rasheed and 13 others,
explainer:
This case involves an election petition filed under Pakistan's Elections Act, 2017, before the Balochistan High Court, challenging the result of a by-election for a Provincial Assembly seat (PB-47 Kech-III) held in December 2018. The petitioner, Jameel Ahmed Dashti, lost to respondent Abdul Rasheed by 1,330 votes. He alleged that Abdul Rasheed had won through rigging and corrupt practices, possibly with the collusion of election officials, and also claimed the winning candidate had concealed assets in his nomination papers, making him dishonest and constitutionally unfit to hold office. The petitioner sought recounting, verification of thumb impressions through NADRA, and a declaration that he himself was the rightful winner.

The court dismissed the petition. It found the petition procedurally flawed because unnecessary government officials had been added as respondents without the tribunal's permission, when only contesting candidates should normally be named. More importantly, on the merits, the court found the allegations of rigging and corrupt practices to be vague, general, and unsupported by concrete evidence. No polling staff were produced to prove wrongdoing, and there was no proof that any missing ballot materials resulted from collusion with the winning candidate. The court held that mere suspicion or carelessness by election staff isn't enough to void an election; the petitioner must prove specific allegations with names, dates, and evidence. This case reinforces the standard that overturning election results requires solid proof, not just claims of irregularity.

title: Zakia Begum and another V. Nasir-Ul-Islam Khan and others,
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over inheritance among the children of Abdul Salam Khan, who died in 1977 leaving substantial property and businesses in Quetta. His daughters (the appellants) claimed they were rightful co-owners of these properties as legal heirs but had been excluded. Their brothers (the respondents) relied on a Will and an agreement to claim ownership, and had already sold parts of the property to third parties who were unaware of any dispute.

The trial court dismissed the sisters' suit, but the Balochistan High Court overturned this decision on appeal. The High Court ruled that under Islamic law, a bequest (Will) in favor of an heir is not valid unless all other heirs consent to it after the testator's death, and even then, only the consenting heir's own share can be affected. Since the sisters never consented, the Will and the agreement used to transfer property were declared null and void, along with related revenue records and business transactions.

However, the Court protected innocent third-party buyers who had purchased property in good faith after checking official land records and had been paying and using it openly. Rather than reversing those sales, the Court ruled that the sisters should instead receive their proportionate share of the money paid for that property, valued as of the sale date.

This case reaffirms that under Quran and Sunnah, a Will cannot override the fixed inheritance shares of legal heirs without their consent, while still protecting genuine, good-faith purchasers from losing property they legitimately bought.

title: Jumma Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court and involved a man convicted of murdering Shah Muhammad after an alleged dispute over a motorcycle. The prosecution's case relied mainly on two eyewitnesses, both brothers of the deceased, who said they were traveling together when the accused and an absconding co-accused opened fire, killing Shah Muhammad. Two bystanders were also injured in the shooting.

The trial court had convicted the appellant, Juma Khan, sentencing him to life imprisonment. He appealed, while the complainant separately sought the death penalty instead.

The High Court found serious problems with the evidence. The two eyewitness brothers gave vague accounts, failing to explain the shooters' position, why only one brother was targeted while they were spared, or how they tried to protect themselves or the victim. The court found their presence and account "unnatural" and doubtful. Meanwhile, the two injured bystanders, who were independent witnesses, actually testified they had not seen the shooting or the accused at all, undermining rather than supporting the prosecution. Additionally, no weapon was recovered from the accused, and the accused's police statement added no new facts.

Concluding that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, the High Court acquitted Juma Khan, setting aside his conviction, and dismissed the complainant's request for a harsher sentence. The case reinforces the principle that any reasonable doubt in evidence must benefit the accused.

title: Abdul Manan V. Abdul Hadi and 7 others,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute in Quetta over land that had been the subject of multiple sales and agreements. The petitioner, a co-owner of the land, had filed a suit seeking declaration, partition, permanent injunction, and cancellation of certain sale agreements. While the case was ongoing, two other people applied to be added as defendants, claiming they had separately purchased part of the property, taken possession, built structures on it, and even resold some units to others. The court allowed them to be added to the case.

After learning these new facts, the original plaintiff asked the trial court for permission to amend his lawsuit to address these developments. The trial court refused. He then challenged that refusal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court ruled in his favor. It held that amending a plaint is a basic right of a plaintiff, so long as the amendment does not change the fundamental nature of the case and is needed to resolve the real dispute between the parties. Courts should be flexible and generous when considering such requests, since procedural technicalities should not block justice. The High Court found that refusing the amendment would defeat the purpose of the lawsuit and lead to unnecessary additional litigation, causing no unfair harm to either side. It set aside the trial court's order and allowed the amendment.

The case matters because it reinforces the principle that courts should prioritize resolving the true issues between parties over rigid procedural rules, especially when new relevant facts emerge during a lawsuit.

title: Dil Jan V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man named Dil Jan who was convicted of attempting to murder his wife, Mst. Haseeba, by stabbing her with a knife. A trial court in Panjgoor found him guilty under Section 324 of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced him to ten years in prison plus a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found serious problems with the evidence. The complainant, the injured woman's relative, gave contradictory accounts of what happened, and admitted the couple had never had complaints against each other and lived happily. A second witness told a completely different version of events and made improvements to his testimony that the court found dishonest. Most critically, the prosecution never produced the injured wife herself as a witness, claiming she died in an accident while being taken for treatment, but offered no evidence to prove this happened. The prosecution also failed to produce the couple's son, who had allegedly first informed the complainant of the attack and would have been a key witness.

The court held that when the prosecution withholds its most crucial witnesses without explanation, a legal presumption arises that their testimony would have hurt the prosecution's case. Since these two witnesses were central to the entire story, their absence made the whole case doubtful. The court ruled the accused deserved the benefit of the doubt and overturned the conviction, acquitting Dil Jan. This case illustrates how failing to produce key eyewitnesses can unravel a criminal prosecution.

title: Attaullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns Attaullah, who was convicted by a Sessions Court in Mastung for the murder of Kaleem Ullah under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced to life imprisonment along with a fine. He appealed this conviction before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found serious problems with the prosecution's evidence. The FIR was lodged four hours after the complainant learned of the incident, raising suspicion of deliberation and false implication. title: Abdul Wajid V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Abdul Wajid, who was convicted by a Special Judge in Lasbella for possessing and transporting 45 kilograms of charas found in his car during a Coast Guard checkpoint search. He was sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction due to serious flaws in how the evidence was handled. First, samples of the seized drugs were supposed to reach the Forensic Science Laboratory within 72 hours under the relevant rules, but they actually arrived eight days after seizure, with no explanation for the delay and no proof the samples were kept safely and untampered with in the meantime. Second, the person who carried the samples to the laboratory was never identified as a witness or brought to court to confirm the samples were handled properly along the way. Third, the laboratory report itself did not follow required legal form: it lacked the signatures of two authorized officers as mandated, and failed to describe what testing procedures were used to determine the substance was actually charas.

Because the prosecution could not prove the drug samples remained secure and unaltered from seizure to laboratory testing, and because the report itself was procedurally defective, the court held that guilt had not been proven beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed and the conviction set aside.

This case highlights how strict compliance with evidence-handling procedures in narcotics cases is essential, and any break in that chain of custody can undermine even serious criminal convictions.

title: Abdul Razzaq and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Abdul Razzaq and Abdul Manan, who were convicted by a Special Judge in Quetta under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947, for allegedly running an unauthorized hundi/hawala currency exchange business. The FIA had raided their shop based on a tip-off, recovering Pakistani and foreign currency along with notebooks and other items allegedly linked to illegal currency dealings. They were sentenced to time already served plus fines.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction. The court found that the law required a strict procedure before such raids and arrests could occur: a written complaint from a person authorized by the Federal Government or State Bank of Pakistan, supported by a sworn statement, must first be presented to a Magistrate, who then issues a search warrant. In this case, the FIA skipped this entire process—no warrant was obtained, no permission was sought from any Magistrate, and no independent witnesses or local police were involved in the raid.

The court held that when the law specifies a particular procedure, it must be followed exactly, and failure to do so invalidates the entire proceeding. Since the prosecution's case was built on an illegal raid and arrest, the conviction could not stand. The appeal was allowed and the men were acquitted.

This case matters because it reinforces that law enforcement agencies cannot bypass mandatory legal safeguards, even when investigating serious financial crimes, and that convictions based on procedurally flawed evidence cannot be sustained.

title: Akhter Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
Akhter Muhammad was convicted of murder by a trial court in Loralai and sentenced to life imprisonment plus compensation to the victim's family for allegedly shooting Kifayat Ullah while the victim was staying overnight at his house. On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the evidence closely and found it riddled with serious problems.

The complainant, the victim's mother, had not witnessed the killing herself and gave a confused account of the timeline that did not match the FIR's stated date. The other prosecution witnesses only learned of the death afterward and merely helped bury the body, making their evidence hearsay. The prosecution's supposed key eyewitness contradicted the FIR and other testimony on basic facts like the date of the incident. Additionally, the accused had been held illegally for over 21 days instead of the permitted 14, and his extra-judicial and judicial confessions came only after this prolonged unlawful detention, making them unreliable. The alleged murder weapon was never produced in court, and no forensic report confirmed it was even functional. The prosecution also failed to properly establish the death itself.

Given these contradictions, unexplained delays, and lack of credible corroborating evidence, the High Court ruled that the prosecution had not proven guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted the appellant, allowing his appeal. The case highlights how illegal detention, unreliable confessions, and weak forensic proof can undermine a murder conviction.

title: Abdul Qahar Khan Wadan V. Zamarak Khan Achakzai and 12 others,
explainer:
This case concerns an election petition filed by Abdul Qahar Khan Wadan, a losing candidate in the 2018 general elections for constituency PB-21 Killa Abdullah-I, challenging the victory of Zamarak Khan Achakzai, who had won by a significant margin of votes. Wadan asked the Balochistan High Court, acting as an election tribunal, to order recounting, verification of thumb impressions through NADRA, and either declare the result void or declare himself the winner.

Before deciding the substance of these claims, the court had to resolve a preliminary objection raised by the winning candidate: that the election petition itself was legally defective because it had been verified before a Notary Public instead of an Oath Commissioner, as required under Section 144(4) of the Elections Act, 2017.

The court held that the law requires election petitions to be verified in the same manner as civil pleadings under the Civil Procedure Code, meaning the oath must be administered by an authorized Oath Commissioner, not a Notary Public. Since Wadan's petition was verified before a Notary Public, who had no legal authority to administer such oaths after amendments to the Notaries Ordinance, the petition failed to meet mandatory legal requirements. The court rejected arguments that this objection came too late, emphasizing that ignorance of the law is no excuse and that legally prescribed procedures must be strictly followed. As a result, the election petition was dismissed as not maintainable, regardless of the evidence already gathered on the merits.

title: Hamayoun Saeed V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a criminal appeal before the Balochistan High Court concerning an accusation of kidnapping and wrongful confinement of a minor girl. The complainant reported that his 13/14-year-old sister went missing and was later found and told police that the appellant had confined her in a room and repeatedly committed zina (illicit intercourse) with her, while a co-accused kissed her. The trial court had convicted the appellant under section 365-B of the Pakistan Penal Code, sentencing him to life imprisonment, while acquitting the co-accused.

On appeal, the High Court closely examined the alleged victim's own testimony and found serious inconsistencies. She admitted she voluntarily accompanied the appellant out of fear rather than being forcibly abducted, stayed with him for over a month, was taken to a shared bathroom on the building's roof daily, and never tried to escape, call for help, or alert other residents in the building despite having opportunities to do so. The court held that such conduct was unnatural and inconsistent with a genuine abduction. Medical evidence confirmed she was no longer a virgin but did not prove the appellant specifically committed zina, and a forensic swab report was never even collected.

Concluding that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, the High Court accepted the appeal and overturned the conviction. title: Mir Lashkari Raisani V. Qasim Khan Soori and others,
explainer:
This case is about a challenge to the 2018 general election results for National Assembly seat NA-265 (Quetta-II) in Balochistan. The losing candidate, Mir Lashkari Raisani, filed an election petition against the winner, Qasim Khan Soori, alleging massive rigging, bogus voting, and violations of election law. He claimed that on polling day a bomb blast caused chaos, his polling agents were kept out of stations, required forms were not properly issued or signed, and there were major discrepancies between different vote-count forms. Verification of thumb impressions by NADRA showed many ballots involved invalid or incomplete identity cards, and a large percentage of votes could not even be verified, raising serious doubts about the result's integrity.

The Election Tribunal found strong evidence supporting the rigging allegations, noting that the returned candidate failed to rebut them with any real proof, and that the Returning Officer had unfairly rejected a request for recounting. The Tribunal concluded that the election had not been conducted freely, fairly, or transparently, as required by the Elections Act 2017, and that the scale of bogus votes and procedural violations affected the outcome.

As a result, the court set aside the notification declaring Soori the winner and ordered the Election Commission to hold a fresh election in the constituency. The case highlights how courts can void election results when there is credible evidence of rigging and failure to follow proper electoral procedures.

title: Muhammad Jaffar V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a death sentence handed down by a trial court in Kalat, Balochistan. The accused, Muhammad Jaffar, had been convicted of raping and murdering two women, Bibi Nazia and Bibi Asia, whose bodies were found under a bridge. He was sentenced to death on multiple counts under laws dealing with rape and murder, along with fines to be paid to the victims' families.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence, including medical reports confirming sexual assault and death by strangulation, forensic lab results showing human sperm on the victims' clothing, and the accused's own confession and disclosure statements. These statements, given voluntarily and without coercion, matched the medical evidence and explained in detail how the crime was planned and carried out along with absconding co-accused.

The court upheld Jaffar's conviction for both rape and murder, finding the prosecution's case solid. However, it reduced his death sentence to life imprisonment. The reason was that one of the deceased women had a prior consensual relationship with the accused, which the court considered a factor lessening the severity of punishment, even though it did not affect his guilt.

This case matters because it shows how courts weigh confessions, forensic evidence, and personal circumstances between accused and victim when deciding not just guilt, but the severity of punishment in serious criminal cases.

title: Azmatullah and others V. The University of Balochistan through Registrar and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the appointment of Lecturers in Zoology at the University of Balochistan. Several candidates, including the petitioners, applied for the post following a public advertisement in 2014. A screening test was conducted through the National Testing Service (NTS), in which the petitioners scored higher marks than the private respondents who were ultimately selected. The petitioners argued that since they scored higher in the NTS test, they should have been given the job, and that the subsequent interview process could not override the NTS merit list. They also claimed the Selection Board that interviewed candidates was improperly constituted, lacking certain required members.

The University and the selected candidates argued that the NTS test was only a screening mechanism to shortlist candidates for interview, and that final selection was based on overall performance in the interview, which is a recognized practice even in competitive exams like CSS and PCS. They maintained the Selection Board was properly constituted under the University of Balochistan Act, 1996, with the minimum required three members present, each of whom scored the candidates fairly.

The Balochistan High Court found no evidence of illegality or irregularity in the Selection Board's process. Since the board was properly constituted and followed lawful procedure, and the respondents were selected based on interview performance by a competent authority, the court dismissed the petitioners' case. The ruling clarifies that scoring highest in a screening test does not guarantee appointment if a properly conducted interview process determines the final selection.

title: Behram V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and another,
explainer:
Behram was detained under the Balochistan Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960 (MPO), a law originally promulgated during martial law in 1960 and later adopted by Balochistan. While in confinement, he filed a constitutional petition asking the Balochistan High Court to declare the entire Ordinance null and void, arguing it was created by a military dictator to suppress political dissent, that it violated fundamental rights guaranteed by the 1973 Constitution (including rights to life, liberty, dignity, and freedom of movement), that it clashed with international human rights standards, and that it was unnecessary since laws like the Anti-Terrorism Act already existed and had never been properly validated by the Constitution.

The court rejected these arguments. It explained that the MPO Ordinance was meant to let authorities detain, without a warrant, anyone credibly suspected of anti-State activity, for a period not exceeding three months, in order to maintain public peace. Crucially, the judges found that this Ordinance had been validated by the Constitution itself under Article 225, which continued pre-existing laws in force unless repealed or amended by the proper legislature. Since it had constitutional backing, the Ordinance could not be called ultra vires (beyond legal authority).

The court did note that citizens whose fundamental rights are actually violated can always approach courts for individual redress, but this does not make the law itself invalid. The petition was therefore dismissed, meaning the Ordinance remains valid law.

title: National Construction Limited, through Authorized Officer and others V. National Industrial Relations Commission and others,
explainer:
This case involved 43 petitions filed by National Construction Limited against decisions of the National Industrial Relations Commission (NIRC), which had ruled in favor of the company's former employees.

The employees had worked for the company on a construction project in Quetta. In 2015, they were told the company was facing financial difficulties due to disputes with clients and could no longer retain their services, though it promised to pay outstanding dues later. The employees challenged this, arguing they were effectively terminated without following proper legal procedures and were owed unpaid salaries and arrears, including for a period ending December 2014.

The company failed to properly contest the case before the NIRC Quetta Bench, was proceeded against ex-parte, and the employees' claims were allowed. When the company appealed to the NIRC's Full Bench, that appeal was also dismissed. The company then approached the Balochistan High Court, arguing it had not been given a fair hearing.

The High Court found that the company's appeal to the NIRC Full Bench had itself been filed 22 days beyond the legal deadline, without any credible explanation for the delay. The court held that the law of limitation protects those who are vigilant about their rights, not those who neglect them. Since the company had shown a consistent pattern of disinterest and delay at every stage, the court refused to interfere with the concurrent decisions of the two lower forums and dismissed all the petitions, reaffirming that courts cannot examine the merits of a case once it is barred by time.

title: Mst. Anita Anam and others V. General Public and others,
explainer:
This case involved two related succession disputes from Quetta. A daughter of a deceased government doctor claimed she was entitled to half of her father's pension, arguing she had not been informed about it and had been denied her share as a legal heir from his second marriage. In a separate but connected matter, other legal heirs sought to revoke a succession certificate earlier granted to the same daughter, alleging she had fraudulently obtained it without including them as heirs and by making false statements.

Both matters were appealed directly to the Balochistan High Court after being decided against the appellants by trial courts (a Judicial Magistrate acting as Civil Judge, and a Civil Judge). Before examining the merits, the High Court had to decide whether it was even the correct forum to hear these appeals.

The court held that under the Succession Act, 1925, appeals from orders passed by an inferior court (not a District Judge) must first go to the District Judge, not directly to the High Court. Only appeals from orders made by a District Judge go straight to the High Court. Since the orders being challenged here were passed by Civil Judges, not District Judges, the appeals were filed in the wrong forum.

As a result, the High Court did not decide the substantive pension and succession certificate disputes. It simply ordered that both appeals be returned to the appellants so they could refile them before the appropriate District Judge, clarifying the correct appellate route under the law.

title: The Collector of Customs, through Additional Collector of Customs and others V. Akhtar Hussain and others,
explainer:
This case involved six trucks seized by Pakistan Customs authorities, allegedly used to smuggle Iranian diesel across the border, along with one truck (LEZ-7771) confiscated separately for having a tampered chassis number. Customs officials claimed drivers fled when confronted, and armed men later tried to tow away one stalled truck during an exchange of gunfire, but the culprits also escaped. Customs seized about 123,000 liters of smuggled diesel and the vehicles, and an Adjudicating Officer confiscated the trucks and fined the registered owners Rs. 50,000 each.

The truck owners appealed, and the Customs Appellate Tribunal ruled in their favor, ordering the trucks released upon payment of a 20% redemption fine and reducing the personal penalty to Rs. 20,000. The Collector of Customs then challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the Tribunal's decision and dismissed the Customs Department's references. It found that while smuggling by drivers or cleaners may have occurred, the prosecution failed to prove that the truck owners themselves were involved in or even aware of the smuggling activity. Since there was no evidence linking the owners to the crime, the Court held that confiscating their property outright was not justified, and only penalizing them with a reduced fine plus redemption fee was fair. This case highlights an important principle: vehicle owners cannot be punished for crimes committed by drivers or employees without proof of their knowledge or involvement.

title: Muhammad Naeem Khan V. Government of Balochistan Through Secretary and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a retired government employee, Muhammad Naeem Khan, who worked at the Balochistan Coastal Development Authority as an Accounts Officer (BPS-18). He sought promotion and, after his retirement in August 2013, the Authority's Governing Body approved promoting him retroactively to Director Planning (BPS-19) and then upgraded that post to BPS-20, with effect from dates before his retirement. He was also given a six-month contract job after retiring, during which he was paid BPS-20 salary. However, when he later sought arrears of salary and pension based on this higher grade, the Finance Department rejected his claim, stating no policy allowed promotions after retirement or upgrading posts during a ban on such upgrades.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed his petition. It found that the Director General's order promoting him and upgrading his post appeared illegal and without lawful authority, since there was no policy permitting promotion two weeks after retirement, there was an existing ban on upgrading posts, and the proper procedure had not been followed by the Governing Body when granting the promotion.

This case matters because it clarifies that retrospective promotions and post upgrades granted after an employee's retirement, without following proper procedure or policy, cannot be used to claim higher pension or salary benefits, reinforcing the importance of due process in civil service promotions.
