title: Faqir Dad V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves a bail application before the Balochistan High Court by a man named Faqir Dad, who had been arrested in connection with a 2009 murder case registered under sections 302 and 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code (murder and common intention). He was seeking post-arrest bail after a trial court had already denied it.

Key facts: Faqir Dad was not named in the original police report (FIR). He was only implicated later, based on a supplementary statement given by the complainant nine days after the FIR was filed, raising the possibility that this statement was the product of deliberation rather than immediate, reliable identification. The only evidence against him was his own disclosure statement, which was not backed up by other evidence. Additionally, two co-accused in the same case had already been acquitted by the trial court. He had also been absconding for about ten years before his arrest.

The High Court granted him bail. It reasoned that where a case calls for "further inquiry" into guilt due to weak or uncorroborated evidence, bail should be granted as a right, not a favor. The court also held that the acquittal of co-accused in similar circumstances cannot be ignored when deciding bail, and that a long period of absconding does not automatically disqualify someone from bail if the case is otherwise fit for it. This judgment reinforces important bail principles: evidentiary weakness and co-accused acquittals matter, and absconding alone isn't an absolute bar to bail.

title: Taqveem Shah V. Government of Balochistan and 2 others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with a challenge to the government's decision to hire a retired civil servant, Abdul Wahid Kakar, on a two-year contract as Senior Coordination Officer for CPEC (China-Pakistan Economic Corridor) in the Chief Secretary's Office. The petitioner, Taqveem Shah, filed a constitutional petition seeking what is known as a writ of quo warranto, essentially asking the court to question the legal authority behind this appointment.

The central issue the court examined was whether Shah had the legal standing to bring this challenge at all. Under Pakistan's Constitution, only an "aggrieved person" can file such a petition. The court explained that to qualify as aggrieved, a person must show that some personal right or interest of theirs was directly affected by the decision being challenged, not just a general objection to how government business is conducted.

The court found that Shah failed to demonstrate any personal stake in the matter. He could not show that the appointment violated any right belonging to him or caused him any personal loss, disadvantage, or harm. Citing several precedents from Pakistani and Indian courts, the judges emphasized that constitutional courts exist to resolve real disputes affecting genuine rights, not to entertain challenges from parties with no direct connection to the issue.

Because Shah did not meet this threshold, the court dismissed his petition outright, without going into the merits of whether the appointment itself was proper. The case underscores the importance of legal standing as a gatekeeping requirement in public interest lit

title: Messrs Iqra Anwar-Ul-Quran Lil Itefal through Director V. Pakistan Broadcasting Corporation, Headquarter Islamabad through Station Director BPS, Quetta,
explainer:
This case is about a landlord-tenant dispute over four flats in Quetta rented to a religious teaching trust by the Pakistan Broadcasting Corporation (PBC). PBC filed for eviction, claiming it needed the flats back to house its own employees, and also alleged the tenant had defaulted on rent payments. The tenant contested this, denying the claims.

The trial court (Rent Controller) ruled in favor of PBC, ordering the tenant to vacate the flats and pay outstanding rent. The tenant appealed, but the Balochistan High Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the eviction. The tenant then went to the Supreme Court, which sent the case back to the High Court for a fresh, more detailed review of the evidence.

On reconsideration, the High Court again ruled against the tenant. It found that PBC's witnesses gave consistent testimony about needing the flats for staff accommodation, and the tenant failed to disprove this during cross-examination. The court held that when a landlord's sworn statement about genuine personal need matches the eviction application and survives cross-examination, that is enough to prove the need is real. The court also emphasized that under Pakistan's Constitution, property ownership rights are a protected fundamental right that takes precedence over a tenant's lesser right of occupancy, meaning a tenant cannot second-guess whether the landlord's need is sufficient.

This case matters because it clarifies how courts assess a landlord's "bona fide need" in eviction cases and reinforces that ownership rights generally

title: Bahadur Khan V. The Vice-Chancellor, Balochistan University of Medical And Health Sciences, Quetta,
explainer:
This case involved a student challenging the admission policy of Bolan Medical College, Quetta, run by the Balochistan University of Medical and Health Sciences. The petitioner had passed his matriculation exam in 2012 but then pursued Islamic religious education before completing his intermediate (F.Sc) exam in 2017, six years later. When he applied for an MBBS/BDS seat, the university deducted five marks per year for the six-year gap between his matriculation and intermediate qualifications, as required by the prospectus's merit formula. He argued this deduction was unfair and unconstitutional, and also complained that he was denied 20 bonus marks awarded to religious scholars or those with madrasa qualifications, even though marks were deducted for his religious studies gap.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It found that the petitioner had not submitted a certificate proving he was a Hafiz-e-Quran or met the specific madrasa qualification requirements needed to claim the 20 bonus marks, so he was not entitled to them. On the marks deduction issue, the court held that admission eligibility criteria are policy matters set by the college, and courts cannot act as an appellate body over such policy decisions unless they are shown to be unconstitutional, illegal, arbitrary, or made in bad faith. Since no such flaw was shown here, the court refused to interfere and dismissed the petition outright, reaffirming that courts generally defer to institutions on academic policy matters.

title: Azizullah V. The Inspector General of Police Balochistan, Central Police Office and 18 others,
explainer:
This case concerns Azizullah, who applied for the post of Inspector Police in the Home and Tribal Affairs Department after an advertisement was issued in 2019. He passed the written test and qualified, but during the physical measurement stage, he was declared unfit due to short height. Police Rules, 1934 require a minimum height of 5 feet 7 inches for recruits, and his measured height fell short of this requirement, first recorded at 5 feet 6 3/4 inches, and later, after an inquiry into his complaint, found to be even shorter at 5 feet 6 inches and 2 soot.

The petitioner argued he had separately been measured and found fit for the post of ASI, and challenged his rejection for the Inspector post. An inquiry was conducted, which found inconsistencies in how his height had been measured by different committees using different scales, and even recommended disciplinary action against officials who had wrongly recorded his height for the ASI post.

The Balochistan High Court held that meeting the minimum height requirement is a mandatory condition for appointment, and can only be relaxed with special sanction from the Deputy Inspector General of Police, which had not been granted in this case. Since the petitioner did not meet the height standard, the court dismissed his petition, while directing authorities to continue the recruitment process on merit. The case underscores that physical eligibility rules in police recruitment are strictly enforced unless properly relaxed by the competent authority.

title: Sheikh Abdul Aziz V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a pre-arrest bail application before the Balochistan High Court. The applicant, Sheikh Abdul Aziz, was accused in an FIR alleging that he and others, armed with a pistol, set fire to machinery belonging to a coal company using petrol. He faced charges including mischief by fire, criminal intimidation, and rioting.

The court noted several important facts: the FIR was lodged with an unexplained 20-hour delay even though the police station was only 3 kilometers from the crime scene; no specific individual role was attributed to the applicant, only a general collective one; and notably, the applicant himself had filed an earlier FIR against the coal company's laborers over an incident where machinery was damaged, mines were set on fire, and one person died with another injured. This made the case against the applicant look like a "counterblast" - a retaliatory complaint filed to undermine his original FIR.

The judge explained that pre-arrest bail is meant to protect people from false or malicious prosecution, and that courts can examine the merits of a case when deciding such applications. Given the delay in filing the FIR, lack of specific allegations against the applicant, and the suspicious timing suggesting retaliation, the court found sufficient grounds to grant pre-arrest bail. This case illustrates how courts scrutinize delayed FIRs and counter-complaints to guard against misuse of the criminal justice system for personal disputes.

title: Deputy Commissioner/Collector, Quetta V Sheikh Muhammad Islam and others,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over how much compensation the government owed for land it acquired to build a police station in Quetta. The Deputy Commissioner/Collector had originally set compensation at Rs. 690 per square foot for land belonging to Sheikh Muhammad Islam. However, Islam and his family had moved to Lahore in 2007 due to law and order problems, and he was not present when the compensation award was announced, nor was he ever properly notified as required by law. When he found out about the award, his representative filed a formal objection asking for a much higher rate of Rs. 20,000 per square foot.

A trial court (the Referee Court) heard evidence about the land's location—near a main road, opposite a hospital, within city limits—and raised the compensation significantly to Rs. 18,000 per square foot, plus additional costs. The government appealed, arguing the claim was filed too late and that the higher valuation was not properly justified.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the government's appeal. It clarified that the deadline for filing such objections depends on whether the landowner was present at the award announcement or properly notified—if neither happened, as in this case, the landowner has six months from the award date to object, not six weeks. Since Islam had not been present or notified, his objection was filed on time. The court also found the lower court had properly weighed evidence about the land's value and saw no error in its reasoning, so it upheld the enhanced compensation.

title: Abdul Malik V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a bail application by Abdul Malik, who was accused, along with several co-accused, of murdering two men (the complainant's uncles) in a firearm attack in Kalat district. The FIR named Malik among the accused, but only alleged that he provided cover for the main assailants who actually fired the shots. Malik had fled after the incident and was arrested much later, then denied bail by the trial court before approaching the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court noted that the FIR did not specify whether Malik was even armed at the scene, and that merely being present during a crime is not enough to establish guilt. Criminal responsibility for a group crime requires proof that the accused shared a common intention with the others or actively helped them. The court observed that if Malik was unarmed, he could not have meaningfully assisted the shooters, and may even have been at risk himself. While his absconding was seen as an attempt to avoid legal consequences, the court held that this alone should not block bail if there was a genuine case for further inquiry.

The court concluded that the exact role Malik played could only be determined once evidence was recorded at trial, and granted him bail. The judgment reaffirms the principle that vague allegations of "giving cover," without clear evidence of shared intent or active participation, may justify bail pending trial, and that observations in bail orders are tentative and do not affect the final outcome of the case.

title: Taj Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about Taj Muhammad, who was arrested in 2022 for allegedly possessing 2000 grams of charas (hashish), found in a bag on a motorcycle he was riding, which itself turned out to be stolen property from another case. He was charged under Section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and denied bail by a trial court. He then approached the Balochistan High Court seeking bail.

His lawyer argued that police investigation was already complete, so there was no need to keep him in custody for further questioning. He also argued that a 2022 amendment to the law, which introduced stricter provisions (Section 9(1)(3)(C)), should not apply to his case since he was arrested and charged before that amendment came into force.

The State opposed bail, arguing the recovery was properly proven against him.

The High Court agreed with the defence. It held that the 2022 amendment does not apply retrospectively, meaning it cannot take away rights an accused already had before the amendment. The court also noted that since the investigation was complete and the challan already submitted to the trial court, the accused was no longer needed for further probe. Importantly, the court found that whether the drugs were in his exclusive and conscious possession was still something to be proven at trial, not yet established. On these grounds, the court granted him bail, calling it a case fit for "further inquiry."

title: Ahmed Ali V. Ali Bakhsh and 21 others,
explainer:
This case is about a land dispute in Turbat, Balochistan. The petitioner, Ahmed Ali, claimed he owned certain land but said the respondents had fraudulently transferred it to themselves. The parties had allegedly signed two agreements regarding the property, but the respondents failed to honor their terms. During the case, defendant No. 1 denied that the signatures on these agreements were his. In response, the petitioner asked the trial court to send the signatures to a handwriting expert for verification. Both the trial court and the revisional court refused this request, so the petitioner challenged those refusals before the High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions and dismissed the petition. It explained that handwriting expert opinions are considered weak evidence under the law and cannot by themselves prove that a document is genuine. Since the two witnesses who had supposedly watched the agreements being signed refused to come to court and testify, the court reasoned that their absence suggested the agreements may never have been properly executed in their presence. The proper way to prove such agreements, the court said, was for the petitioner to produce the attesting witnesses, and only if they confirmed signing the documents would expert verification become useful. This ruling matters because it clarifies that parties cannot rely solely on expert examination of signatures to prove a disputed document; they must first present direct witness testimony as stronger evidence.

title: Abid V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a murder conviction from the Balochistan High Court's Turbat Bench. Abid was convicted by a trial court for killing Rahim Bakhsh with an axe following a dispute over firewood left behind at a vacated Army camp. The victim had confronted the accused for collecting the wood, leading to a fight in which Abid struck him fatally on the head. A co-accused, Javed, was acquitted.

The prosecution's case rested on the testimony of the deceased's brother (the complainant), a minor eyewitness (the deceased's young son, aged 12-13, who was present grazing cattle), and another witness who arrived shortly after hearing about the attack. The court found these witnesses' accounts consistent and mutually corroborating regarding the time, place, and manner of the killing. The child witness's testimony was found reliable because he answered questions clearly and consistently even under cross-examination, and his account was backed by other evidence including medical findings. The recovery of the axe used in the attack from Abid's possession further strengthened the case. The court also rejected the defense argument that the witnesses were unreliable simply because they were relatives of the victim, noting that related witnesses' testimony is trustworthy when it is truthful and not shown to be biased or influenced by enmity.

Finding no reasonable doubt about Abid's guilt, the High Court dismissed his appeal and upheld his conviction and life sentence, along with the compensation ordered for the victim's family.

title: Yar Muhammad alias V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Yar Muhammad, who was convicted under Pakistan's Anti-Terrorism Act for allegedly providing services to a banned organization (identified as DAESH) and for possessing money said to be meant for supporting the group's activists, along with a letter bearing the organization's markings. He appealed his conviction to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found serious flaws in how the case was investigated and prosecuted. The complainant's own testimony contradicted the prosecution's version during cross-examination, and no independent witnesses, such as the taxi driver present at the arrest, were included in the investigation despite the arrest happening in a populated area. Records meant to track custody of the seized evidence, particularly a police register documenting the handling of sealed evidence, were never produced in court. Most critically, the actual letter allegedly linking the accused to the banned organization was never produced as evidence at trial, even though it was central to the case.

The court also noted that the case began based on secret informant information that was never documented in writing, which raised fairness concerns, since written records help protect innocent people from false accusations.

Given these gaps, missing evidence, unreliable testimony, and poor investigative practices, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction was overturned and the appeal was allowed, highlighting the importance of solid, verifiable evidence, especially in serious terrorism-related cases where wrongful conviction risks are high.

title: Imran V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns Muhammad Imran, who was arrested after police in Quetta allegedly found him carrying 2000 grams of charas (cannabis) during a routine patrol on 10th January 2025. He was charged under Section 9(1)(3)(C) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, an offence that can carry up to fourteen years imprisonment plus a fine.

After his bail request was rejected by the trial court, Imran approached the Balochistan High Court seeking bail pending trial. His lawyer argued he was innocent, that the recovery wasn't properly linked to his conscious possession, and that the quantity was small enough that any eventual sentence would not fall under the law's stricter bail restrictions.

The State opposed this, arguing the large quantity recovered directly connected Imran to the crime and that the offence fell within the category of cases where bail is generally not granted except in special circumstances.

The High Court agreed with the prosecution's tentative assessment, noting that at the bail stage courts should not speculate about final sentencing or make detailed observations that might affect the actual trial. Citing Supreme Court precedent, the court held that such drug offences are serious crimes against society, and quantity alone doesn't automatically entitle an accused to bail. Since the case fell within the law's restrictive bail category, the court dismissed the bail application, leaving Imran's guilt or innocence to be decided during a full trial, which the court directed be completed promptly.

title: Sajjad Khan and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns two men, Sajjad Khan and another appellant, convicted under Pakistan's narcotics law for allegedly possessing six kilograms of crystal drugs found hidden in secret compartments of the vehicle they were driving. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court against their conviction.

The High Court overturned the conviction, finding the prosecution's case riddled with serious doubts. Witnesses gave contradictory accounts on basic facts, such as whether the drug packets were square or round shaped, where exactly the recovery took place, and where the drugs were found before police arrived. The vehicle's engine and chassis numbers on the recovery memo did not match the vehicle later produced in court, raising doubts about whether the same vehicle was even involved.

The court also found that the chain of custody for the seized drugs was compromised, since the police register recording custody was not properly maintained, lacked required signatures, and did not follow official rules. Additionally, the investigating officer's timeline for completing the recovery did not match when the drugs were handed over to the malkhana (evidence storage) in-charge, and there was no explanation of how the recovery was conducted at night without any lighting source. Finally, the chemical examiner's report was defective because it combined results for all twelve samples into one report instead of separate detailed reports, violating official rules.

Given these cumulative doubts, the court gave the accused the benefit of the doubt and acquitted them, reinforcing that narcotics convictions require solid, consistent evidence and proper legal procedure.

title: Liaqut Ali and another V. Dr. Sahibzada Saeed Ahmed and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over one acre of land in Lasbela district, Balochistan. The complainant, Dr. Sahibzada Saeed Ahmed, claimed he had purchased the land in 2002 but was illegally dispossessed by the appellants, Liaqat Ali and Noor Muhammad, who allegedly grabbed his land and built construction on it. A trial court convicted the appellants under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, sentencing them to seven years imprisonment, fines, compensation, and ordering the land returned to the complainant.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction. The court noted that the complainant had stayed silent for eleven years, from 2010 to 2021, without approaching any legal forum against these specific appellants, even though he had earlier filed a similar case and a civil suit against a different person over the same land. The court found this long delay, combined with the appellants' long-standing possession and the absence of any explanation of how the dispossession actually occurred, suggested this was a civil property dispute rather than a criminal case of land grabbing.

The court explained that the Illegal Dispossession Act exists specifically to target organized land grabbers and property mafias, not ordinary civil disputes between people claiming ownership or possession through competing claims. Since there was no evidence connecting the appellants to any land mafia, the court ruled the case did not fall under this law and allowed the appeal, meaning the appellants' conviction was set aside.

title: Abdul Baqi V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about the limits of a special legal power called "Ex-Officio Justice of Peace," usually held by a Sessions Judge. During investigation of a kidnapping case, a police (Levies) investigating officer recovered a stolen car. The car's owner later applied to the Sessions Judge, acting as Ex-Officio Justice of Peace, for release of the vehicle. While deciding that application, the judge went further and directed senior officials, the Commissioner and Deputy Commissioner, to register a criminal case (FIR) against the investigating officer himself, accusing him of misappropriation and criminal breach of trust.

The investigating officer challenged this order before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that no complaint had ever been filed against him and he was never given a chance to explain his position before such serious directions were issued.

The High Court agreed. It held that under the law, an Ex-Officio Justice of Peace can only issue directions when a written complaint is actually filed against a police or levies official for misconduct, negligence, or excess of duty. Since no such complaint existed here, and the officer was never given a hearing or inquiry, the judge had acted beyond his authority. The Court quashed the part of the order directing an FIR against the petitioner.

The judgment matters because it clarifies that this special judicial power cannot be used to initiate criminal proceedings against officials without a proper complaint and fair hearing, protecting officials from arbitrary action.

title: Kazim Ali V. Nadir Ali and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about an alteration of charges in a criminal case in Quetta, Balochistan. The complainant, Kazim Ali, alleged that he and his family members were attacked with a knife by the accused, Nadir Ali and his brother, causing various injuries. Police initially registered the case citing certain sections of the Pakistan Penal Code, and after investigation, the trial court framed charges under Section 337-F(iii) (causing a specific type of hurt) along with Section 34 (common intention).

The complainant wanted the charge changed to Section 324, which deals with attempted murder, arguing this better reflected the seriousness of the attack. The trial court rejected this request, finding that the medical evidence and case facts matched the hurt-related offense rather than attempted murder. It then transferred the case to a Magistrate's court, which has jurisdiction over such lesser offenses.

The complainant challenged this transfer through a criminal revision petition. The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition, agreeing with the trial court's assessment that the facts did not support an attempted murder charge. The Court also clarified that under Section 347 of the Criminal Procedure Code, a trial court can transfer a case to a court of appropriate jurisdiction (higher or lower) if it realizes partway through the trial that the case belongs there. It emphasized that when two courts share jurisdiction, cases should generally go to the lower court.

title: Naseebullah V. Naqeebullah and another,
explainer:
This case involved an application to cancel bail that had been granted to two men accused of murder. The applicant, Naseebullah, was the brother of the man who lodged the original complaint after an armed attack that killed a minor boy. The accused had been charged under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code covering murder, attempted murder, criminal intimidation, and related offences. A trial court had earlier granted them pre-arrest and post-arrest bail, and the complainant's side asked the Balochistan High Court to cancel that bail.

The applicant argued that the offence was extremely serious, that the FIR named the accused promptly, that eyewitness evidence was ignored, and that the trial court wrongly relied on an alibi defence that should not be considered at the bail stage, plus there was confusion over the date of the incident due to a clerical error.

The High Court rejected the cancellation request. It held that once bail is granted, only strong reasons like misuse of bail, threats to witnesses, or tampering with evidence justify cancelling it. The seriousness of the charge alone is not enough. The court also clarified that an alibi defence can legitimately be considered even at the bail stage, citing Supreme Court precedent. Since the accused were regularly appearing at trial and had provided sureties, there was no need to interfere with the bail order.

title: Abdul Sattar Lasi V. The State through DPG, NAB Balochistan and another,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted by an Accountability Court in 2001 for corruption, sentenced to prison and fined Rs. 250 million. His appeals were rejected by the High Court and Supreme Court, though the Supreme Court reduced his sentence from 12 to 10 years while upholding the fine. After the conviction became final, NAB sought to recover the fine by auctioning his property and seizing his bank account, filing an application under the National Accountability Ordinance along with provisions of the Penal Code and Criminal Procedure Code that allow recovery of unpaid fines.

The convict challenged the trial court's 2022 order permitting this recovery. Separately, NAB challenged a later 2023 order in which the trial court agreed to modify or recall its earlier recovery order after a third party claimed he had purchased the disputed property before the recovery proceedings began.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed both petitions together since they involved the same facts and legal questions. It found that the trial court had properly applied the law when it allowed NAB's recovery application, issuing a well-reasoned order free of legal errors. Finding no illegality or irregularity in the trial court's handling of the matter, the High Court declined to interfere and dismissed the constitutional petition.

This case matters because it confirms that once a fine imposed in an accountability case becomes final after appellate review, courts can enforce recovery through property auction and bank seizure, and such enforcement orders will not be lightly overturned.

title: Muhammad Irfan and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a dacoity (armed robbery) conviction from the Balochistan High Court. The appellant, Muhammad Irfan, along with another accused, had been convicted for robbing a college professor and his cousin of Rs. 30,00,000 (three million rupees) and a mobile phone at gunpoint near a bank in Quetta, after the victims had withdrawn the cash. The trial court had sentenced the appellant to seven years imprisonment plus a fine, while acquitting one co-accused.

The High Court examined the evidence in detail. Three eyewitnesses gave consistent accounts of the robbery, correctly describing the time, place, and manner of the crime, and they identified the appellant in court. The appellant had also made an extra-judicial confession describing how the gang planned and carried out the robbery, which led police to recover looted money and other details previously unknown to investigators. The court explained that such confessions can be the basis for conviction if proven to be true, voluntary, and free from coercion, especially when followed by actual recovery of evidence. Additionally, a properly conducted identification parade, supervised by a judicial magistrate, confirmed the witnesses had correctly picked out the appellant as one of the robbers.

Finding no flaws in this evidence and no successful challenge during cross-examination, the High Court upheld the conviction and dismissed the appeal, reinforcing how confessions, eyewitness testimony, and identification parades can combine to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt in robbery cases.

title: Syed Maqbool Ahmed V. Bibi Memoona and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a husband challenging family court rulings in a Khula (divorce) matter. His wife had filed a suit for dissolution of marriage, recovery of dowry articles, gold ornaments, and past maintenance. When the husband failed to respond to court summons, the Family Court decided the case against him without his participation, granting the wife's requests. He then appealed to the Additional District Judge, who modified the decision somewhat, but the husband remained unsatisfied and filed a constitutional petition directly with the Balochistan High Court, asking it to overturn both the trial court and appellate court decisions and send the case back for a fresh hearing.

The High Court refused to hear the case on its merits. It ruled that the Family Courts Act allows only one appeal from a family court decision, and once that appeal has been decided, the law does not permit challenging the appellate court's decision through a constitutional petition as an indirect second appeal. The court also noted that the husband's arguments involved factual disputes already examined by both lower courts, and the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction is not meant to re-examine facts or act as an additional appellate layer.

This decision reinforces that family court litigants have a limited right of appeal, and courts will not allow constitutional petitions to be used as a backdoor method for further appeals, protecting the finality of decisions in family law disputes.

title: Muhammad Rashid V. Bibi Fatima and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a custody dispute between a father and mother over their minor son. After the mother left the family home, the father sued for custody of the child in the family court, but that court dismissed his suit and awarded custody to the mother. The father appealed to the District Court, which also ruled against him. He then approached the Balochistan High Court under Article 199 of the Constitution, asking that the child be handed over to him.

The High Court dismissed the father's petition. It held that the paramount consideration in custody matters is the welfare of the child, not merely the biological relationship between parent and child. Since the child had lived with his mother since birth and had developed a strong bond with her, disturbing that arrangement could harm his upbringing. The court noted the mother had not remarried, was properly caring for the child, and that he was attending a good school. It also pointed out that the father, being a government servant often away from home, had no female family member available to care for the child. The court further clarified that while a mother's right to custody can end upon remarriage to someone unrelated to the child, this is not an absolute rule and welfare of the child remains decisive.

This judgment reinforces that Pakistani courts prioritize a child's actual wellbeing and stability over rigid parental rights when deciding custody matters.

title: Collector of Customs, through Additional Collector of Customs, MCC Gawadar, Custom, Gaddani V. Messrs Mehboob Steel Pipe Industry and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over customs duties and taxes on imported steel worth over 9.5 million rupees, imported by Messrs Mehboob Steel Pipe Industry under a manufacturing bond scheme. The company was required to either export or dispose of the goods and pay applicable duties within two years, but failed to do so, leading to violations of customs warehousing rules. The Collector of Customs ordered recovery of surcharge for the delay and payment of sales tax on wasted material. The company appealed, and the Customs Appellate Tribunal, through a single Member sitting alone, disposed of the appeal by sending the matter back to the Federal Board of Revenue for reconsideration and halting coercive action against the company.

The Collector of Customs challenged this before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that under the law, a single Member of the Appellate Tribunal only has authority to decide cases where the disputed amount is five million rupees or less. Since this case involved an amount exceeding that limit, the single Member had no legal power to decide it alone.

The High Court agreed. It held that this monetary limit is a mandatory legal condition, and any Tribunal decision made beyond it is invalid, void, and without legal effect. As a result, the Court set aside the Tribunal's earlier judgment and ruled in favor of the Customs authorities.

This case matters because it reinforces that tribunals must strictly follow jurisdictional limits set by law, and decisions made outside those limits, even in good faith, cannot stand.

title: Muhammad Irfan V. The State,
explainer:
This is a decision from the Balochistan High Court on a criminal revision petition challenging a theft conviction.

The petitioner, Muhammad Irfan, had been convicted under Section 380 of the Pakistan Penal Code for allegedly stealing a mobile phone from a shop and sentenced to two years' imprisonment plus a fine. Both the trial court and the appellate court had upheld this conviction, so he approached the High Court.

The complainant claimed his phone was stolen while his servant was praying in the shop, and that CCTV footage showed the theft. However, the High Court found the prosecution's case riddled with problems. Witnesses gave contradictory statements about basic facts, such as whether police visited the shop. The recovery witness admitted the person's face in the CCTV footage was not clearly identifiable. The supposed eyewitness had never mentioned watching the video in his earlier police statement and didn't even know when or where the accused was arrested. The investigation was also flawed: no forensic report was obtained on the CCTV footage or USB, no independent witnesses were involved despite the area being densely populated, and the DVR itself was never seized. Additionally, there was an unexplained 17-hour delay in filing the police report.

Given these serious contradictions, missing evidence, and investigative lapses, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It set aside the conviction and acquitted Irfan, reaffirming that even one significant doubt can entitle an accused to acquittal.

title: Saif-Ur-Rehman V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man, Saif-ur-Rehman, who was convicted by a trial court in Loralai and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a heavy fine and compensation, after being found guilty of sodomy (an offence under Section 377 of the Pakistan Penal Code) against a nine-year-old boy. He appealed this conviction to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court carefully reviewed the evidence, including testimony from nine prosecution witnesses, and found serious problems. Most witnesses had not actually seen the crime happen and their evidence was hearsay. The victim's own account of events contradicted statements given by his father and another witness about basic facts like where people were and what happened. Medical evidence also failed to support the allegation: while a doctor noted bleeding, no clear evidence of intercourse was recorded, a promised expert surgeon was never produced, and forensic DNA testing found no semen on the samples taken from the victim. Additionally, the FIR (police complaint) was lodged six hours after the incident despite the police station being only two kilometers away, and no explanation was given for this delay.

Given these contradictions, gaps in medical proof, and unexplained delay, the court held that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. It ruled that an accused must be given the benefit of doubt even if only one significant doubt exists. The court allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction, highlighting how inconsistent testimony and weak evidence can undermine even serious criminal charges.

title: Najeebullah V. Family Judge-II, Quetta and others,
explainer:
Najeebullah married a woman, with dower (mehr) initially fixed at Rs. 200,000 at the time of Nikah. Later, the couple executed a post-marital agreement in which the husband promised monthly maintenance, separate accommodation, and other financial commitments. The marriage later broke down amid allegations of maltreatment, and the wife sued in the Family Court for recovery of dower, gold, and maintenance. The Family Court ruled in her favor. The husband's appeal to the District Court was dismissed as time-barred, since he filed it about five months late without adequate justification. He then challenged both rulings before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed his petitions. It held that under Islamic law, dower is not fixed only at the time of marriage - it can be set, increased, or agreed upon before marriage, at marriage, or afterward through mutual consent. So the post-marital agreement enhancing financial obligations was valid, and the Family Court had proper jurisdiction to hear the dower claim arising from it. The Court also rejected the husband's argument that the agreement was forged, noting that Family Courts are not bound by strict evidentiary rules like the Qanun-e-Shahadat (which normally requires two witnesses to prove documents), because family law disputes call for a more flexible, conciliatory approach. Finally, the Court emphasized that limitation law protects the vigilant, not those who delay without justification, and upheld the dismissal of the husband's time-barred appeal.

title: Molvi Najeebullah and others V. Khan Gul and others,
explainer:
This case is about a long-running dispute over shops attached to a mosque in Quetta. The mosque's Mutawalli (caretaker) had been trying, over multiple rounds of litigation spanning more than two decades, to evict tenants occupying shops on the mosque's premises so the mosque could be reconstructed and expanded to accommodate its growing number of worshippers. The tenants had also allegedly stopped paying rent. This time, the Rent Controller dismissed the eviction applications outright under a procedural rule (Order VII Rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code), ruling the case not maintainable without even hearing evidence.

The mosque caretaker appealed to the Balochistan High Court. The Court held that the Rent Controller was wrong to dismiss the case so summarily. It found that there was no proof the mosque had been officially registered with or taken over by the Auqaf (religious endowments) department, so claims that only that department could handle the matter were baseless. The Court also clarified that while civil procedure rules don't strictly apply to rent proceedings, fairness principles still require that parties get a chance to present evidence, especially on complex mixed questions like whether the applicant had legal standing to sue.

The High Court set aside the dismissal and sent the case back for a proper hearing with evidence. This matters because it reinforces that special tribunals like Rent Controllers cannot shortcut fair trial procedures just because technical procedural codes don't strictly bind them.

title: Muhammad Khan alias Akhtar Muhammad V. The State,

Police said they found him counting large amounts of Pakistani currency, and the search also turned up several bank account records, 26 cheque books, and ATM cards. He was accused of being an active facilitator of the banned organization Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan, allegedly collecting donations and extortion money, including funds routed through Afghanistan.

During his trial in the Anti-Terrorism Court, Khan applied for early acquittal under section 265-K of the Criminal Procedure Code, arguing that he had already been acquitted in a separate, similar case registered in Kohat. The trial court rejected this application, and Khan challenged that rejection before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the trial court's decision. It found that the Kohat case involved different facts, a bomb blast and a single bank transaction, while the Chaman case involved large cash recovery, extensive banking records, and evidence of fund transfers from Afghanistan. The court ruled that these were separate matters, so acquittal in one could not automatically justify acquittal in the other. It also held that early acquittal powers should not normally be used when there is a real possibility of conviction based on available evidence, and that guilt or innocence should be determined only after a full trial with witness testimony. The petition was dismissed as not maintainable.

title: Bakhtawar V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a bail application filed by a woman named Bakhtawar, who was arrested after police allegedly recovered about 2040 grams of charas (a narcotic substance) from her possession in Quetta. The police claimed they had received prior secret information that she was accompanying a man named Ashiq, from whom narcotics had already been recovered that day, and that they then searched and arrested her.

The Balochistan High Court granted her bail, finding that the case fell into the category of "further inquiry," meaning there were unresolved doubts that needed to be examined at trial before guilt could be established. The key issue was that despite having advance information about the raid, the police failed to video record the search and recovery process, even though modern devices like phone cameras are legally permitted as evidence under Article 164 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984. The court relied on Supreme Court precedents emphasizing the importance of recording such recoveries to ensure transparency and reliability.

The court also noted that whether the contraband was in her exclusive and conscious possession still needed to be proven through full trial evidence. Since such doubts existed, the court held that bail should be granted as a matter of right. Importantly, the court clarified that its observations were tentative and would not affect how the trial court eventually decides the actual merits of the case.

title: Abdul Hayee V. Muhammad Yousaf and 3 others,
explainer:
This is a summary of a Balochistan High Court decision on a property dispute. The petitioner had bought 10 acres of land through a registered sale deed but only received 6 acres, so he filed a civil suit for declaration, specific performance, correction of land records, and an injunction against the sellers.

The trial court dismissed his entire suit because his lawyer failed to appear on a particular date. The petitioner later got the suit restored, but the opposing side challenged this restoration in a revision petition, which succeeded in cancelling the restoration order. The petitioner then approached the High Court.

The key issue was that the date on which the suit was dismissed had not actually been fixed for a full hearing of the case. It was only scheduled for arguments on a temporary, interim application seeking an injunction. The High Court held that dismissing an entire suit for non-appearance on such an interlocutory date exceeds the court's jurisdiction, since a hearing in the legal sense means examination of evidence or the main questions in the case, not consideration of temporary applications.

Because the original dismissal order was passed without jurisdiction, it was declared void, meaning it had no legal effect. The court also ruled that time limits for seeking restoration do not apply to void orders. As a result, the High Court set aside the revisional court's order and restored the petitioner's suit, allowing the property dispute to proceed to a proper hearing.

title: Muhammad Sadiq V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a bail application filed by Muhammad Sadiq, who along with a co-accused was arrested for allegedly transporting a huge quantity of narcotics, about 28 kg and 921 grams of ice/sheesha, in a vehicle stopped at a checkpoint in Mastung. He was charged under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. His trial court had already refused him bail, so he approached the Balochistan High Court seeking post-arrest bail.

His lawyer argued he was innocent, falsely implicated, that police witness statements contradicted each other, and that the arrest violated procedural safeguards since no private witness was involved. The prosecution countered that the recovered quantity was extremely large, no enmity or false implication was alleged against the police, ownership of the vehicle carrying the drugs was undisputed, and a co-accused's bail had already been rejected by the same court.

The High Court refused bail. It held that given the huge quantity of narcotics recovered, the offence fell within the prohibited category under Section 497 of the Criminal Procedure Code and also attracted the special bar on bail under Section 51 of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act. The court also noted that since the trial was at an advanced stage, granting bail at that point could prejudice either side's case. This case matters because it reinforces how courts treat bail strictly in large-scale narcotics cases and emphasizes that bail should not be granted once a trial nears conclusion.

title: Hidayatullah alias Dili Jan and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns two men, Hidayatullah alias Dili Jan and a co-accused, who were arrested by CTD police in Naseerabad after allegedly being found carrying bags containing explosive materials, detonators, and wires while walking near Landhi Gandawah road. Police claimed the men confessed to belonging to a banned organization (BLA) and intended to carry out a bombing in Dera Murad Jamali. They were charged under the Explosive Substances Act and the Anti-Terrorism Act, and a trial court had refused them bail.

The Balochistan High Court granted the accused bail. It found that the men had made no such disclosure to police witnesses or during investigation linking them to any banned organization, and nothing on record proved this connection, meaning the requirements for treating the case as an act of terrorism under Section 7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act were not met. The prosecution also failed to show any prior criminal history for the accused. Notably, one accused had reportedly been abducted two months earlier, a fact recorded in police daybooks (roznamcha), which investigators ignored. Additionally, police violated Section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code by failing to involve independent local witnesses during the search and recovery, despite having ample time to do so.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that bail decisions and terrorism charges must be backed by solid evidence and proper procedure, not just police allegations, and that mandatory safeguards like independent witnesses cannot be bypassed even in serious explosives cases.

title: Inayat Ullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves a bail application filed by Inayat Ullah, who was accused in a shooting incident in Dera Murad Jamali, Balochistan. According to the FIR, the applicant and several co-accused allegedly opened indiscriminate gunfire on a shop, killing two people and critically injuring two others, including a passerby. The applicant was specifically accused of firing shots that contributed to the deaths.

The applicant sought post-arrest bail, arguing he was innocent, falsely implicated, that no weapon was recovered from him, and that witness statements were recorded 25 days after the incident without explanation, and that investigation was complete so his continued detention was unnecessary.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the bail application. It held that the delay in recording witness statements could not by itself justify bail, especially since the murder charge under section 302 of the Pakistan Penal Code is a non-bailable offence. The court emphasized that at the bail stage, only a tentative assessment of the evidence is permissible, not a deep evaluation of its merits. Based on this tentative assessment, the court found that the FIR and witness statements prima facie connected the applicant to a serious, non-bailable crime involving firing that led to loss of life.

This case illustrates how Pakistani courts handle bail requests in murder cases, showing that courts require substantial justification before releasing someone accused of a serious, non-bailable offence like murder, and that procedural delays alone are usually insufficient grounds for bail.

title: Janan Khan Achakzai V. The State Bank of Pakistan Banking Services Corporation (Bank) through Deputy Director of Adjudication Foreign Exchange and 2 others,
explainer:
The case involved an exporter of rice from Pakistan to Iran who had signed export declarations (E-Forms) promising to bring back the full sale proceeds through banks within six months of shipment, as required by law. The State Bank of Pakistan filed twelve complaints against him for failing to repatriate this money on time, which is a violation under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947. The exporter claimed the delay wasn't his fault since Iranian buyers had issued bad cheques, and he had hired a lawyer in Iran to recover the money and had managed to recover some funds. He argued he shouldn't be penalized since the failure to pay wasn't within his control, and that the way the adjudicating officer was handling the case violated his right to a fair trial.

The State Bank countered that this was a factual dispute unsuitable for direct constitutional court intervention, and that eight of the twelve cases were still pending before the proper adjudicating officer, with a right of appeal available if the petitioner disagreed with any decision.

The High Court agreed with the State Bank's position. Since no final orders had yet been passed against the petitioner and the dispute involved factual questions about whether his failure to repatriate funds was excusable, the court held this wasn't something it could resolve directly. Instead, it directed the petitioner to present his evidence and documents to the adjudicating officer, who could properly weigh the facts and decide accordingly, with an appeal available afterward if needed. The petition was disposed of on this basis.

title: Rehmatullah and others V. Naseer Ahmed and others,
explainer:
Rehmatullah and others, claiming to be the heirs of one Abu Bakar, filed a civil suit against Naseer Ahmed and others, saying they owned and possessed a piece of agricultural land in Mastung and that the respondents were illegally interfering with it. The respondents countered that their ancestors had been given part of this land long ago as tenant cultivators, that they had been paying land dues, and that their occupancy rights were protected under a tenancy law. They also relied on a decision by a locally appointed arbitrator who had ruled in their favour.

The trial court dismissed the petitioners' suit, and the first appellate court partly sided with the petitioners, declaring them owners but still recognizing the respondents as possessors. The petitioners challenged this outcome before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found serious flaws in how the lower courts handled the case. The trial court had ignored the petitioners' oral and documentary evidence, wrongly given weight to a private arbitration decision that had no legal standing as proof, and failed to consider an official revenue report. It also failed to properly decide each legal issue as required by law. The appellate court simply agreed with the trial court instead of independently reviewing the evidence, which is not proper appellate practice.

The High Court accepted the revision petition, set aside the lower decisions, and sent the case back to the trial court to frame additional issues and decide the matter properly on merits. This case underscores that courts must independently evaluate evidence and give reasoned decisions on every issue raised.

title: Chairman National Accountability Bureau through Prosecutor General Accountability, NAB V. Abdul Nabi Jattak and another,
explainer:
This case involved the Chairman of the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) challenging the acquittal of Abdul Nabi Jattak, a government official, and another accused, Abdul Ghani. Jattak had worked in Balochistan's Local Government Department for decades, rising to Town Planner. NAB accused him of accumulating property and bank assets far beyond what his salary could explain, and alleged that Abdul Ghani held some of this property on his behalf as a front man (benamidar). A trial court had already acquitted both men, finding the prosecution's evidence insufficient, so NAB appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence, including testimony from tenants, revenue officials, and the accused's brother, and found that the properties in question actually belonged to Jattak's father and were ancestral family assets, not illegally acquired wealth. The prosecution could not prove the properties were bought using illicit income or that Jattak had misused his official position to acquire them.

The High Court upheld the acquittal, explaining that when reviewing an acquittal (as opposed to a conviction), courts only intervene if there was a serious error or misreading of evidence causing injustice. Since the trial court's decision was well-reasoned and not flawed, the High Court dismissed NAB's appeal.

This case matters because it shows the higher burden prosecutors face in overturning acquittals in corruption cases, and reinforces that mere suspicion of unexplained wealth isn't enough without solid proof linking assets to abuse of public

title: Muhammd Azeem V. The State,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court, Sibi Bench, deciding an appeal by Muhammad Azeem, who was convicted of murdering his wife, Mst. Noor Jahan, and sentenced to life imprisonment plus compensation under the Pakistan Penal Code.

According to the prosecution, on 8 July 2018 Azeem arrived at his wife's family home, quarreled with her over having only one son, and shot her multiple times with a pistol before fleeing on his motorcycle. He evaded arrest for nearly two years before being caught in March 2020. At trial, two eyewitnesses (the victim's brother and uncle) testified they directly saw him shoot her, and medical evidence confirmed she died from multiple gunshot wounds. The murder weapon was never recovered.

Since the death occurred inside the couple's own home, the burden shifted to Azeem to explain how his wife died unnaturally, and he failed to offer any explanation or proof of false implication.

explainer:

He was sentenced to one and a half years in prison plus a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence, particularly the testimony of the Head Moharror (record keeper), a key prosecution witness responsible for handling the seized drugs. This witness admitted that the samples sent for laboratory analysis were dispatched through a "special messenger," and also revealed that his official statement to police was recorded 23 days after the incident, rather than promptly. The court found this delay troubling because it created uncertainty about whether the drug samples were properly secured and handled from the time of seizure until they reached the laboratory for testing.

Citing a Supreme Court precedent, the judges emphasized that a compromised chain of custody makes laboratory reports unreliable for securing a conviction. The court also reiterated the constitutional principle that personal liberty is precious and should only be denied for compelling reasons.

title: Niaz Muhammad and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved a brother who was kidnapped for ransom and later murdered. The main accused, Niaz Muhammad, was convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court and sentenced to death along with life imprisonment. A co-accused had been acquitted at trial, and the State appealed that acquittal separately.

The evidence showed that the victim's dismembered body, cut into 39 pieces, was found buried in a sewage pit at a farmhouse. DNA testing matched the remains to the victim using samples from his parents, and forensic evidence including a bloodstained weapon, cap, and sandals further linked the accused to the crime. Ransom money was traced through creditors who received debt repayments, and cash was recovered from the accused. The Balochistan High Court found this circumstantial evidence overwhelming and upheld the murder conviction, dismissing the appeal.

However, the court ruled that the death sentence under the anti-terrorism law was wrongly applied, since this was an ordinary kidnapping-for-ransom case, not an act meant to spread terror in society, so that specific charge was set aside while the murder conviction stood.

Regarding the previously acquitted man, the court found he had helped dispose of the body, took a share of the ransom, and hid the crime from police. The court overturned his acquittal and convicted him instead of a lesser offense of concealing the crime, sentencing him to seven years in prison.

This judgment matters because it clarifies the distinction between ordinary kidnapping-for-ransom murders and actual terror

title: Inayatullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by Inayatullah, who had been convicted by a trial court for possession of narcotics under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. Police claimed they recovered 4000 grams of charas (hashish) hidden in a bag on his motorcycle after acting on a tip-off. He was sentenced to four years imprisonment and a fine.

On appeal, Inayatullah's lawyer argued there were contradictions in police testimony, no independent witnesses from the local community were involved, and the drug samples may have been kept unsafely or sent for lab testing after unexplained delay. He also presented two defense witnesses claiming he was arrested along with several other people at a gathering, not alone on a motorcycle as police claimed.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It found the police witnesses' testimony consistent and credible even under cross-examination, and noted that police officers are considered just as reliable as private citizens when giving evidence. The court also found the defense witnesses' story weak, since they never reported any wrongdoing by police to community elders or filed any formal complaint, and showed no evidence of police malice against the appellant.

The court ruled that the prosecution had proven its case beyond reasonable doubt through consistent testimony, proper handling and testing of the drug samples, and lab confirmation. The appeal was dismissed and the conviction upheld. The case illustrates how Pakistani courts evaluate narcotics evidence and weigh police testimony against defense claims of false implication.

title: Jamal Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Jamal Ahmed, who was caught driving a vehicle in Turbat, Balochistan, carrying 1000 kilograms of charas (hashish) hidden under a tarpaulin. He was charged under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and the trial court convicted him, sentencing him to death along with a heavy fine.

On appeal to the Balochistan High Court, his lawyer argued that the prosecution failed to properly prove safe custody of the drugs from seizure to laboratory testing, that there were delays in recording certain witness statements, and that all prosecution witnesses were police officials rather than independent civilians, which he claimed weakened the case.

The High Court rejected these arguments. It found that the chain of custody was properly documented: the drugs were seized, representative samples were separated and sealed, kept securely, and sent to the chemical examiner without any gaps in the process. The court also reaffirmed established legal principle that police witnesses are just as credible as any other witnesses and their testimony cannot be dismissed simply because they belong to the police.

However, the court took into account that Jamal Ahmed had no prior criminal record and was a first-time offender. Treating this as a mitigating factor, the court upheld his conviction but reduced his sentence from death to life imprisonment.

title: Abdul Basit and others V. The State,
explainer:
This is a Balochistan High Court decision from the Turbat Bench deciding two criminal appeals and a murder reference together. The case arose from a night-time robbery in which armed men broke into a complainant's house, shot dead his cousin, wounded her four-year-old daughter, and stole a laptop, mobile phone, and watch. The trial court had convicted Abdul Basit and Altaf Raja for murder and robbery-related offences (sentencing Basit to death and Raja to life imprisonment), while acquitting two co-accused. Both convicted men appealed, and the murder reference asked the High Court to confirm or reject the death sentence.

The High Court examined the evidence, including eyewitness accounts from the complainant, a neighbor, and others who chased and caught one of the accused with a pistol near the crime scene, as well as recovery of the murder weapon, a Kalashnikov, whose empties matched forensic reports. The judges found the witnesses credible, consistent, and free of any motive to falsely implicate the accused.

Importantly, the court upheld the conviction of one accused for murder even though he had not personally fired the fatal shots, ruling that he shared a common intention with the shooter during the robbery and was therefore vicariously liable under the law. The court dismissed both appeals, confirming the convictions and sentences, reinforcing that participants in a joint criminal plan can be held equally responsible for a killing committed by one of them.

title: Sajid Ali V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves an appeal by Sajid Ali against his conviction for murdering Waqar, the brother of the complainant. The Balochistan High Court heard the appeal after the trial court had convicted Sajid Ali under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced him to life imprisonment plus a fine to be paid to the deceased's heirs.

The background is that after the killing, an FIR was initially filed against unknown persons. Later that same day, the complainant recorded a supplementary statement naming Sajid Ali as the killer, based on information from an eyewitness who had seen the accused firing a pistol at the deceased near date palm trees.

The High Court examined the evidence, including the eyewitness account, medical evidence confirming a firearm wound, and physical evidence such as a spent bullet casing, bloodstained soil, and the deceased's clothes. Crucially, the murder weapon itself was recovered based on information provided by the accused, from a location unknown to others, and forensic testing confirmed the recovered casing had been fired from that weapon.

Weighing this evidence together, the court found it consistent, credible, and sufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The eyewitness was found trustworthy with no motive to falsely implicate the accused. As a result, the court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction and sentence, reinforcing how eyewitness testimony combined with forensic and physical evidence can solidify a murder conviction.

title: The Secretary Communication and Works, Government of Balochistan, Quetta and another V. Mirwais Khan and 6 others,
explainer:
This case arose from a land acquisition dispute in Quetta. The Balochistan government acquired private land near Sariab Phatak to build a flyover, and set compensation rates for different categories of land. The landowners felt the compensation offered for their land (in Ward No.8) was far below market value, and after their complaints went unanswered, they filed a legal reference under the Land Acquisition Act challenging the award. The trial court agreed with the landowners and increased the compensation rate from Rs.4,200 to Rs.5,000 per square foot, plus a 15 percent compulsory acquisition charge.

The government then tried to appeal this decision to the Balochistan High Court, but filed the appeal five months and six days late. The only excuse offered was that the relevant law department had been slow in granting the necessary approvals to file the appeal.

The High Court dismissed the government's appeal, refusing to excuse the delay. It held that once the deadline for appeal passes, the other party gains valuable legal rights, and these rights cannot be taken away unless the party seeking delay condonation provides a very strong, convincing, and day-by-day explanation for the delay. Bureaucratic slowness in obtaining internal approvals was not considered a sufficient reason.

This case matters because it reinforces the strict application of limitation laws even against government bodies, emphasizing that administrative inefficiency is not an acceptable excuse for missing legal deadlines, and that landowners' rights to fair compensation, once judicially decided, deserve protection from delayed challenges.

title: Bibi Sakina and another V. Zakir Hussain alias Shah Wali and 3 others,
explainer:
This case was about the murder of Syed Karim, who was shot and killed on 20 September 2016 in Quetta while driving home. The complainant, a relative who witnessed the shooting, initially filed a police report naming unknown attackers, without describing them. Sixty-two days later, he filed a supplementary statement naming the respondents as the killers. A trial court acquitted the three accused men, and the complainant's family appealed that acquittal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the acquittal. It found that the 62-day delay in naming the accused seriously undermined the reliability of the supplementary statement, since such a long gap raised the possibility of consultation or fabrication, especially since the original FIR named no one and gave no description of the attackers. Another key witness only came forward 26 days after the incident with no explanation for the delay, making her testimony inadmissible. Since no description of the attackers existed in the original report, the court found there was no valid basis for later identifying the accused.

The court also reaffirmed important legal principles: appeals against acquittals are treated as extraordinary remedies, since wrongly convicting an innocent person is considered far worse than letting a guilty person go free. Once acquitted, an accused enjoys a "double presumption of innocence," which can only be overturned for compelling reasons. Any reasonable doubt must benefit the accused. Based on these principles, the appeal was dismissed and the acquittals stood.

title: Muhammad Tahir etc V. Rasheed Khan and others,
explainer:
This case involved five connected appeals concerning eviction applications filed by Muhammad Tahir and others against tenants occupying a property in Quetta. The appellants claimed they had purchased the property from the legal heirs of the original owner, had it mutated in their name, and were thus entitled to collect rent as the new landlords. They alleged the tenants stopped paying an agreed increased rent and sought their eviction under the West Pakistan Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, 1959.

The tenants disputed being in a landlord-tenant relationship with the appellants, pointed out that the property had passed through several other buyers, noted there were disputed "red entries" in the official land records, and highlighted that a separate succession case was still pending in civil court. They also denied ever agreeing to pay increased rent.

The trial court (Rent Controller) dismissed the eviction applications, and the Balochistan High Court upheld that decision. The High Court emphasized that merely owning property or having mutation entries in one's name does not automatically prove someone is a "landlord" for rent law purposes. The appellants failed to produce any rent receipts, could not specify details of alleged rent payments, and there was no written tenancy agreement. Since the essential relationship between landlord and tenant was never proven, the eviction claims could not succeed.

This ruling reinforces an important principle in rental law: ownership of property and the legal status of "landlord" are distinct, and eviction requires solid proof of an actual tenancy relationship, not just paperwork showing property ownership.

title: Waqas Masih alias Sanwal V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a murder conviction. The accused, Waqas Masih alias Sanwal, was charged with killing the son of the complainant by throwing acid on him, causing severe burns to his face, chest, and legs. The victim survived for about five months before dying from his injuries. The trial court had convicted the appellant under provisions dealing with qatl-i-amd (intentional murder) and causing hurt with a corrosive substance, and he appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The court examined medical evidence confirming the acid burns and unnatural death, along with forensic reports confirming acid traces on the recovered bottle and the victim's clothes. Crucially, before he died, the victim gave a statement to the investigating officer naming the appellant as his attacker. The court treated this as a valid dying declaration, holding that such statements carry strong evidentiary weight since a dying person is unlikely to lie. The appellant's mother, though not produced as a witness, had earlier told police she saw her son and the victim quarrelling with an acid bottle in her son's hand; the court found her absence understandable given family loyalty and did not weaken the prosecution's case. The defence version, presented through a defence witness, contradicted the medical and other evidence and was rejected.

The High Court upheld the conviction, dismissing the appeal, emphasizing the strength of dying declarations and corroborating medical and forensic evidence in acid-attack murder cases.

title: Nasrullah alias Momin and another V. The State,

This case involved Nasrullah, who was accused of killing a man named Rafiullah during an alleged robbery in Chaman, Balochistan, and stealing his mobile phone. title: Abdul Rehman and 3 others V. Messrs Progressive Minerals through Najeeba and others,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running property dispute over 50 acres of mining land near Ziarat, Quetta. Progressive Minerals (the decree holders) had earlier won a court decree declaring them the lawful owners of the land, with a ruling that the other side (Abdul Rehman and others) had no right to interfere with or encroach on it. That decree was upheld through multiple levels of courts. When the winning party tried to enforce the decree, they found the losing party had dumped construction material on the land and were occupying it, so they filed an execution application asking the court to remove the encroachment and restore their possession.

The losing party objected, arguing the decree was only for "injunction" (an order not to interfere) and not for possession, so it could not be enforced this way. They also raised a partnership deed and a separate, previously undisclosed ex-parte judgment they claimed supported their rights.

The High Court dismissed their revision petition. It held that when someone holding an injunction decree is dispossessed or their land is encroached upon by the losing party, they can ask the same executing court to restore possession and remove the encroachment, rather than filing a fresh lawsuit. An injunction decree, the court said, carries full legal force like any other decree. The court also noted the losing party had suspiciously concealed the existence of their ex-parte judgment throughout the litigation. This ruling clarifies that execution courts have real power to enforce injunction decrees practically, not just on paper.

title: Saqib Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a tragic road accident in which four people died when a trailer carrying a container collided with vehicles on the RCD Road, crushing a Mehran car and killing everyone inside. The trailer driver, Saqib Muhammad, was tried and convicted by a Sessions Court in Hub for causing death by rash and negligent driving, along with related offenses of dangerous driving and causing property damage. He was sentenced to prison and ordered to pay substantial compensation (diyat) to the families of the four deceased.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined whether the prosecution had actually proven that the accused drove rashly and negligently. The court found serious gaps in the evidence: no eyewitness testimony was recorded describing how the accident actually happened, the cleaners of both the trailer and truck (who may have witnessed the crash) were never questioned, and neither vehicle was examined by a Motor Vehicle Examiner to check speed or brake conditions that could establish fault. The court held that simply asserting the accident was caused by rash and negligent driving, without concrete evidence, was insufficient to sustain a conviction for such a serious charge.

As a result, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted the appellant. This case highlights an important legal principle: criminal convictions, especially those carrying severe penalties, require solid, independent evidence rather than assumptions, and prosecutors must thoroughly investigate accidents using available technical and eyewitness evidence before guilt can be established.

title: Bibi Zainab and others V. Haji Muhammad Hassan and others,
explainer:
This case is about a 2008 murder in Nushki, Balochistan, in which a man named Khuda-e-Dad was killed during a violent clash. His widow, along with other injured persons, later entered into a compromise with the accused, pardoning them and giving up their rights to prosecution and compensation (Qisas and Diyat). Based on this compromise, the trial court acquitted the accused in 2009.

More than ten years later, children of the deceased, claiming to be his legal heirs and stating they were minors at the time and unaware of the compromise, asked the trial court to reopen the case. They argued their mother, an illiterate widow, had not properly represented them, and their names were never disclosed during the compromise proceedings. The trial court rejected their request, and they then approached the Balochistan High Court seeking to have the acquittal order quashed and the case reopened.

The High Court noted that although there were gaps in the record about why the children weren't named in the compromise, it could not use its special powers (under Section 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code) to reopen a decade-old case and revisit it on merits. Instead, the court said the petitioners' proper remedy was to file an appeal against the acquittal under Section 417 of the Cr.P.C. As a result, the petition was dismissed. This case highlights the limits of High Court powers to overturn old compromise-based acquittals and points affected parties toward the correct legal appeal process.
