title: Aminullah V. Khalil Ur Rehman and another,
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over property auctioned to recover a money decree. Aminullah had won a money decree against Khalil Ur Rehman, and when Rehman failed to pay, the execution court had his property attached and put up for auction. Aminullah participated and was declared the highest bidder, and the property was transferred into his name. Later, an executing court ordered Rehman to hand over possession, but a revisional court set aside the entire auction and transfer, prompting Aminullah to challenge that decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the procedural rules governing court auctions under the Civil Procedure Code, which require the executing court to have the property properly valued, set a reserve price, allow parties time to inspect it, and include these details in the public auction notice. None of this had been done. The court also found that since Aminullah, the decree-holder, wanted to bid in the auction himself, he needed prior court permission to do so, which he never obtained. Additionally, evidence showed that Rehman had actually paid the full decretal amount during the case. Because of these serious procedural violations and the proof of payment, the court held that the auction was illegal and that the revisional court was right to cancel it.

The petition was dismissed, meaning the property transfer to Aminullah was not restored. The case reinforces that strict compliance with auction procedures is mandatory, and decree-holders cannot bypass these safeguards even to recover their own dues.

title: Ikram-Ul-Haq and others V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary, Quetta and others,
explainer:
This case is about a family's fight to get a domicile certificate for the city of Quetta. The father, petitioner No.1, originally held a domicile certificate from Dera Ghazi Khan issued in 1994, but had it cancelled at his own request in 2025. He and his family, including his children who were born and raised in Quetta after he moved there in 2003, sought domicile and permanent resident certificates for Quetta, which his daughter needed for higher education. Authorities rejected the application, and the family challenged this decision in the Balochistan High Court, arguing it violated their constitutional rights to equality, fair treatment, freedom of movement, and access to education.

The Court dismissed the petition. It explained that domicile is a distinct legal concept, separate from mere residence or nationality, requiring both actual residence and a genuine intention to permanently settle in a place. Under the Pakistan Citizenship Act and Rules, applicants must prove continuous residence, typically ten years, backed by solid evidence like property ownership or long-term rental agreements. The Court found the family had not properly documented this, noting suspicious circumstances such as a thirteen-year delay in registering the daughter's birth certificate. It also held that administrative guidelines requiring such proof do not violate fundamental rights, since they serve legitimate purposes of verification and public order. This case matters because it clarifies the strict evidentiary standards courts expect for domicile claims, even for long-term residents.

title: Dr. Sara Jaffer V. Zarak Khan and another,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court, concerned a dispute over a government-allotted residential quarter in Quetta. The respondent's late father, and later his mother, had lawfully occupied the quarter as government employees, and it was eventually allotted to the respondent himself in 2019. The petitioner challenged that allotment in court, which directed the housing authority to reconsider the matter after hearing both sides. The authority then cancelled the respondent's allotment and gave the quarter to the petitioner instead, without properly hearing the respondent. The respondent sued, seeking to have the petitioner's allotment declared illegal and to stop his own eviction, and asked for an interim injunction to maintain the status quo while the case was pending. The trial court refused the injunction, but the appellate court reversed this and ordered status quo in the respondent's favour. The petitioner then challenged that appellate order before the High Court.

The High Court examined procedural requirements under the Civil Procedure Code, particularly the rule requiring a party appealing an interim order to formally notify the opposing side before filing the appeal. It held that this notice requirement is mandatory, and an appeal filed without complying with it is not valid, though a fresh appeal can still be filed later if limitation permits. title: Jan Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Jan Muhammad and Raz Muhammad, accused of robbing two people at gunpoint in Quetta and then opening fire on police who arrived at the scene. Police shot back, wounding and arresting both accused. They were charged under Pakistan Penal Code sections dealing with attempted murder, robbery, and obstructing public servants.

The accused had already been refused bail twice by the trial court. They then applied to the Balochistan High Court for bail solely on medical grounds, arguing they had suffered serious firearm injuries requiring ongoing treatment that the jail could not adequately provide.

Medical reports confirmed one man had surgery for a firearm-related abdominal injury (laparotomy) and the other had fractures in his arm and leg bones from gunshot wounds. Although a police surgeon described their condition as "stable," the injuries were on vital parts of the body, and the men had already been under treatment for more than a month and a half without full recovery.

The High Court granted bail, reasoning that the purpose of a criminal trial is to bring the accused to face justice, not to punish an undertrial prisoner through inadequate medical care while awaiting trial. The judge stressed that this bail decision was only a tentative assessment and would not affect the actual merits of the case at trial. This shows courts can grant bail on humanitarian medical grounds even in serious criminal cases.

title: Syed Shakeel Ahmed V. Raj Kumar,
explainer:
This case involved a government official, an Inspector at the Evacuee Trust Property Board in Quetta, who sued another man for 10 million rupees in damages, claiming defamation. The plaintiff alleged that during a meeting on minority rights, the defendant falsely accused him of illegally occupying and selling a school property for personal gain, in front of other officials, damaging his 35-year unblemished service record and reputation.

The trial court, without holding a full trial or recording evidence, dismissed the case early based only on legal issues, apparently deciding that the suit was not maintainable under certain government service rules and procedural provisions.

The Balochistan High Court overturned this dismissal. It explained that questions of defamation involve both law and facts, so they cannot simply be decided as a preliminary legal issue without evidence. Courts can only reject a plaint outright, without evidence, if it is clear from the plaint itself that the case is legally barred - not when the matter requires weighing facts, like whether statements were defamatory or made in good faith. Since this case required factual examination, the trial court acted improperly in dismissing it prematurely.

The High Court therefore set aside the trial court's dismissal and sent the case back for a full decision on its merits, meaning evidence will now need to be recorded and considered. This case matters because it reinforces the principle that courts cannot dismiss factually complex claims, such as defamation suits, without a proper trial.

title: Zubair Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a bail application by Zubair Ahmed, who was accused in a serious criminal case involving multiple murders, attempted murder, kidnapping, and robbery. According to the prosecution, the accused and his co-accused disguised themselves in army uniforms, stopped a car at gunpoint, shot and killed two people, injured three others, and abducted two more victims who were later found murdered in nearby mountains. Ahmed was specifically accused of firing on the victims.

Having already been denied bail once by the trial court, Ahmed applied to the Balochistan High Court, arguing only that he was entitled to bail because his trial had been delayed for over a year without conclusion, which under the law can sometimes justify bail on statutory grounds.

The High Court rejected this argument. It found that the delays were mostly due to legitimate reasons: the Covid-19 pandemic, the case being transferred due to threats against witnesses, security concerns because Ahmed was considered a dangerous criminal, and defense lawyers repeatedly seeking adjournments during cross-examination. Only a few delays were attributable to absent prosecution witnesses. The court held that since most witness testimony had already been recorded, the trial was likely to conclude soon, and that bail on delay grounds isn't available to someone considered a hardened, dangerous criminal accused of premeditated, serious crimes. Bail was therefore refused.

title: Muhammad Ismail and 3 others V. Cantonment Executive Office, Quetta Cantt and others,
explainer:
This case is about a family dispute over inheritance after the death of Faqeer Hussain, a Shia Muslim man who died childless in 2020, leaving behind property and bank accounts. His cousins (the petitioners) claimed they were entitled to a share of his estate, while a nephew (Respondent No. 4, through Respondent No. 1) had already obtained a succession certificate and letter of administration recognizing his right to inherit. Both sides had earlier filed competing succession certificates in court, and the nephew's claim was accepted while the cousins' was rejected. The cousins then filed a separate civil suit for a declaration of shares, but the trial court rejected their plaint outright, and an appellate court upheld that decision. They then brought this revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined Shia inheritance law, which divides heirs into three classes, with each class excluding the next from inheritance. Parents and children form the first class, grandparents and siblings the second, and uncles, aunts and their descendants the third. Since the nephew fell into the second class and the cousins fell into the third class, the nephew's claim took priority and the cousins were excluded entirely. Because both lower courts had already reached the same factual and legal conclusions, the High Court found no error and dismissed the cousins' revision petition, confirming the nephew as the rightful heir. This case clarifies how Shia inheritance rules determine priority among distant relatives.

title: Muhammad Musa and 2 others V. National Bank of Pakistan through Branch Manager,
explainer:
This case involved a bank recovery suit under Pakistan's banking finance laws. National Bank of Pakistan sued Muhammad Musa and two others to recover about 1.4 million rupees on an agricultural loan that had gone unpaid. When the borrower failed to appear in the Banking Court at Quetta, the court proceeded against him ex-parte (without his participation) and eventually decreed the suit in the bank's favor.

The borrower appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing he was never properly served with notice of the case and so never got a chance to defend himself, violating his constitutional right to a fair hearing.

The High Court agreed. It examined the trial court's record and found that the reports from the bailiff (court officer) and courier service about serving notice on the borrower were missing or silent on whether service had actually happened. Under the relevant law, the Banking Court is required to ensure proper service through specific methods like bailiff delivery, registered post, courier, or newspaper publication before proceeding against a defendant. Since none of this was properly documented, the court held that the borrower had been "condemned unheard," meaning judgment was passed against him without he ever getting a fair chance to respond.

As a result, the High Court set aside the original judgment and sent the case back to the Banking Court for a fresh trial, directing that the borrower be given the opportunity to file his defense. This case reinforces that courts must strictly verify proper service of notice before deciding a case against an absent party.

title: Munir Ahmed V. Ali Raza and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court, Sibi Bench, deciding a civil revision petition. Munir Ahmed had filed a lawsuit seeking declaration, possession and a permanent injunction over land he claimed to own, alleging that Ali Raza was unlawfully interfering with his possession. The trial court rejected his plaint outright under Order VII, Rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code, without going to trial, and the appellate court upheld that rejection. Munir Ahmed then challenged this in the High Court.

The High Court found that the lower courts had acted wrongly. It noted that the plaint did disclose a cause of action, and that revenue records attached to the plaint showed Munir Ahmed as the recorded owner of the land, a fact the government respondents did not dispute. The court held that whether he could actually prove his ownership and rights was a factual matter to be tested through evidence at trial, not something that could be decided by simply throwing out the case at the outset. It also found that the trial court had failed to follow proper procedure by not first framing the legal and factual issues in the case as required by law.

As a result, the High Court set aside the rejection of the plaint and sent the case back to the trial court, treating the application for rejection as still pending, so proper procedure could be followed. This matters because it reinforces that courts cannot dismiss lawsuits prematurely without following due process and giving parties a chance to present evidence.

However, the investigating officer later received affidavits from three people supporting the accused's claim that they were elsewhere when the crime happened (a plea of alibi), and based solely on these affidavits, discharged the accused from the case without doing proper investigation or verifying the affidavits.

Habib Barkat challenged this discharge in the Balochistan High Court, arguing it was done improperly and without following proper police procedures. The court agreed, ruling that the investigating officer acted illegally and arbitrarily. It held that a plea of alibi is a matter to be examined through evidence during trial, not something police can use to close a case when there is already credible evidence linking the accused to the crime. The court noted that one of the stolen trucks had since been recovered from a driver, reinforcing suspicion against the accused.

The court set aside the discharge order, allowing the case to proceed. This ruling reinforces that police cannot use flimsy alibi evidence to shut down investigations prematurely, and that determining guilt or innocence based on alibi is the court's job, not the police's.

title: Bibi Khadija V. Pir Muhammad and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the estate of a government employee, Ali Muhammad, who died during his service in Balochistan's Education Department. He left behind his widow, Bibi Khadija, and his nephews and niece, but no children. Various death-related dues were at stake, including pension, provident fund, group insurance, financial assistance, leave encashment, gratuity, benevolent fund, and bank savings.

The trial court had ruled that the widow alone was entitled to the monthly pension, group insurance, financial assistance, and benevolent fund, while the remaining benefits, including gratuity, leave encashment, and bank deposits, should be split between the widow and the nephews/niece according to Islamic inheritance shares. The widow appealed, arguing that gratuity and leave encashment were not part of the inheritable estate (Tarka) but were grants or concessions from the employer, meaning she alone should receive them.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with her. It held that benefits like gratuity, benevolent fund, group insurance, financial assistance, and pension are not part of the deceased's inheritable estate because such benefits can only be claimed by the employee during their lifetime, not automatically passed on as inheritance. Since Ali Muhammad died in service, the lower courts erred by including gratuity within the inheritable Tarka. The court partly allowed the widow's petition, correcting this legal error. This case matters because it clarifies which employment-related benefits go directly to a spouse versus which are shared among all legal heirs under Islamic law.

title: Ejaz V. The State,
explainer:
Ejaz was convicted separately in four different criminal cases arising from incidents in 2013 and 2014, including murder, attempted murder, rioting, obstructing a public servant, mischief, and illegal arms possession. The trial court and later the High Court (on earlier appeals) had already reduced some of his sentences, but overall he was sentenced to a combined total of 37 years imprisonment plus fines, with his life sentence for murder being the most serious.

In this appeal, filed through the jail superintendent since Ejaz was too poor to hire counsel himself, he asked that all his sentences from the four cases be served concurrently (at the same time) rather than one after another. The prosecution did not oppose this request.

The High Court examined the law under Section 397 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which gives courts discretion to order multiple sentences to run together. Noting that Ejaz had already served 10 years, earned significant remission for good behavior, and still had about 18 years left to serve, the court found this to be a genuine case of hardship. It emphasized that punishment should aim to reform a person so they can return to society, not just punish indefinitely.

The court allowed the appeal, ordering all sentences from the four cases to run concurrently, with credit for time already served. This means Ejaz's total remaining prison time is significantly reduced.

title: M/s Nasar Enterprises through attorney V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Services and General Administration Department, Government of Balochistan and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a government tender for supplying uniforms to staff of Balochistan's Services and General Administration Department. Six companies bid for the contract, including the petitioner, Nasar Enterprises. During technical evaluation, three firms, including the petitioner, were disqualified as "non-responsive" because of issues with their sales tax registration status. Among the remaining qualified bidders, another firm, NFK Traders, offered the lowest price and was awarded the contract. That firm then supplied the uniforms, which were inspected, approved, and distributed to staff, completing the process.

Nasar Enterprises challenged this outcome in court, arguing that the evaluation criteria used to disqualify it were not properly disclosed in the original tender notice and that its complaints to the Grievance Redressal Committee were never properly addressed, amounting to unlawful procurement.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It found that the entire procurement process was already complete, a "past and closed transaction" that could not be reopened through a constitutional petition. It also noted that the petitioner never asked for clarification about the bidding criteria within the five-day window required by procurement rules, and filed its grievance complaint 56 days late, well beyond the allowed period, so the complaint was never properly considered.

This case highlights that bidders must raise objections to tender terms and file complaints promptly, and that courts are reluctant to unwind already-completed government procurement contracts.

title: Safina and another V. Jawahir Begum and 6 others,
explainer:
This case is about who is entitled to inherit the property of a deceased man, Muhammad Afzal, who left behind a widow and a daughter but no son. His brother, Muhammad Aslam, claimed he too was entitled to a share of the estate as a surviving heir. The widow and daughter had gotten the property mutated (transferred) into their names based on a religious ruling (fatwa) they claimed justified excluding the brother, and they later sold part of the property to a third party.

The trial court dismissed the brother's suit, but the appellate court reversed this and ruled in his favor. The petitioners (widow and daughter) then challenged that appellate decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court applied established Islamic inheritance law (citing Mulla's principles of Mohammadan Law) and held that the widow was entitled to one-eighth of the estate, and the daughter to one-half, as "sharers." The brother, as a "residuary" heir, was entitled to whatever remained after these shares were allocated. The court upheld the appellate court's determination of shares but disagreed with its decision to cancel the registered sale deed to the third party, since that sale did not affect the brother's rightful share. The revision petition was dismissed.

The case matters because it clarifies how Islamic inheritance shares are calculated when a deceased person leaves a wife, daughter, and brother, but no son, and confirms that a brother can inherit as a residuary heir even when direct female heirs exist.

title: Imran Taj Gichki V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved corruption charges under Pakistan's National Accountability Ordinance. The accused, including a former Secretary to the Chief Minister, were alleged to have accumulated assets disproportionate to their known income, causing a loss of over Rs. 184 million to the government through corrupt practices. The trial court had convicted one accused (ITG) while acquitting another (SI). Both the conviction and acquittal were challenged before the Balochistan High Court.

The prosecution's case relied heavily on the statement of an approver recorded under Section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The court found this testimony unreliable because the approver had been in NAB custody for over a month without proper documentation of court appearances, raising concerns about coercion. The judicial magistrate had also failed to follow mandatory procedures when recording the confession. Additionally, the prosecution failed to produce five material witnesses regarding property transactions, and documents showed the disputed house actually belonged to other individuals with UK citizenship, not the appellant. The court also found no evidence that the appellant misused his official authority for illegal gains, a necessary element for the corruption charge.

Because the prosecution failed to provide credible, corroborated evidence, the court dismissed the appeal against the acquittal (upholding it) and allowed the appeal against the conviction, meaning the convicted person was cleared too. This case highlights the importance of proper evidence-gathering procedures and corroboration in corruption prosecutions, and safeguards against unreliable approver testimony.

title: Bangul Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a kidnapping FIR registered under sections 365, 147, 148 and 149 of the Pakistan Penal Code, alleging that the accused abducted two men, demanded money ("Batta"), tortured them, and made objectionable videos when they refused to pay. While the trial was underway before the Sessions Judge, the complainant asked that the case be shifted to the Anti-Terrorism Court, arguing the facts amounted to terrorism-related offences. The accused, on the other hand, wanted the case sent to a Magistrate's court. The Sessions Judge accepted the complainant's request and transferred the case to the Anti-Terrorism Court, prompting the accused to challenge this transfer before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court held that an ordinary Sessions Court has no authority to directly transfer a case to the Anti-Terrorism Court on its own. Instead, the law requires that if it appears during trial that the case involves offences meant for the Anti-Terrorism Court, the Sessions Court must send a formal reference to the High Court under Section 526(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code, and only the Chief Justice can then decide the matter after hearing all sides. Since the Sessions Judge bypassed this proper legal procedure, the High Court set aside the transfer order and sent the matter back for fresh decision according to law. This ruling clarifies the correct legal process for shifting terrorism-related cases between courts, ensuring procedural fairness.

title: Ghulam Qadir V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves Ghulam Qadir, who was arrested and charged under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, after police allegedly recovered 1130 grams of charas (cannabis) from him near Uthal, Balochistan. He applied for post-arrest bail after the trial court had already rejected his request.

His lawyer argued that he had no prior criminal record, that the investigation was complete, and that he was no longer needed for further inquiry. The State opposed bail, arguing he had been caught red-handed with the narcotics.

The Balochistan High Court examined the First Information Report (FIR) and found a significant flaw: no sealed parcel of the recovered narcotics had been prepared at the scene, and the FIR did not even mention whether a sample was taken from the alleged drugs for testing. The court held that this omission created doubt about the prosecution's case, and such doubt, even at the bail stage, should benefit the accused. It relied on a Supreme Court precedent confirming that benefit of doubt can be extended at the bail stage.

Concluding that this amounted to a case requiring further inquiry under Section 497(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, the court granted Ghulam Qadir bail, subject to sureties totaling Rs. 200,000. The court clarified its observations were tentative and would not affect the trial's outcome.

This case highlights how procedural lapses in evidence handling, like failing to secure and sample seized narcotics, can be crucial in securing bail even in serious drug cases.

title: Muhammad Anwar V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves Muhammad Anwar, who was arrested in Balochistan on 29 May 2022 after police received information that terrorists belonging to a banned organization intended to carry out bomb attacks during election days. According to the police report, the Counter Terrorism Department recovered 1260 grams of explosive material and 6 meters of prima wire from his possession. He was charged under the Explosive Substances Act and the Anti-Terrorism Act.

Anwar sought bail, arguing that nothing was actually recovered from him and that the prosecution had not obtained the mandatory legal sanction required under the Explosive Substances Act. The trial court had already refused him bail, so he approached the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court reviewed the case only at a preliminary, tentative level, as is standard at the bail stage, without deeply analyzing the evidence. It found that explosive material and wire had indeed apparently been recovered from Anwar, and that he had not shown any hostility or grudge by the police that might suggest he was falsely implicated. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent involving similar circumstances, the court held that such recoveries constitute reasonable grounds to deny bail in cases involving serious explosives and terrorism charges.

The court therefore dismissed his bail application, while noting he could still raise new grounds later during his actual trial. This case illustrates how courts treat bail requests cautiously in terrorism and explosives cases, especially where physical evidence was recovered directly from the accused.

title: Farooq Ahmed and 2 others V. Muhammad Aqib Javed and 2 others,
explainer:
This case was about a custody dispute over a young girl named Minsha, following her mother's death. Her real father applied to the Family Court to get custody of his daughter, but the child's maternal grandmother and other relatives resisted, delaying the proceedings repeatedly. The Family Court eventually granted custody to the father, and this decision was upheld on appeal by the District Judge. The grandmother then challenged both rulings before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that under Islamic law she should have priority to raise the child, and that she and other petitioners were not given a fair chance to be heard.

The High Court rejected these arguments and dismissed the petition. It found nothing against the father that would disqualify him from having custody of his own daughter—he was educated, had no legal disqualification, and had been actively pursuing custody since the start. The court also clarified that Family Courts are not bound by the technical procedures of the Civil Procedure Code or Evidence Act, since they are meant to resolve family matters quickly rather than get bogged down in lengthy litigation.

The judgment reinforces the principle that in custody cases, the welfare of the child is the most important factor, and that a fit, willing father generally has a strong claim to his child's custody over other relatives, absent proof of misconduct or unsuitability.

title: Khalid Mehboob V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary, Government of Balochistan, Civil Secretariat, Quetta and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved Khalid Mehboob, a civil servant (BPS-19 officer) in Balochistan's Irrigation Department, who was serving as Project Director of the Awaran Dam Project. His services in that role were suspended through an official notification citing weak administration, lack of interest in the procurement process, negligence and inefficiency, which allegedly led to delays in executing the dam project. He challenged this suspension order before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that a junior officer had been wrongly appointed in his place and that the government's action was tainted by mala fide intent.

The High Court dismissed the petition without going into these merits, holding that it did not have jurisdiction to hear the case. Since the petitioner was a civil servant and the dispute concerned his terms and conditions of service, Article 212 of the Constitution required such matters to be taken to the Service Tribunal rather than the High Court. The court relied on a Supreme Court precedent confirming that service-related disputes fall under the exclusive domain of tribunals, and that High Courts can only intervene under Article 199 in extraordinary situations of significant public importance, which was not the case here.

This judgment matters because it reinforces the principle that civil servants must generally pursue service-related grievances, including allegations of unfair treatment or mala fide action, through specialized Service Tribunals rather than through constitutional petitions in High Courts.

title: Noor Khan V. Sher Khan and 11 others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court concerned a dispute over a 22-year-old court decree. In 1999, a suit was filed by members of certain tribes against members of other tribes, in a representative capacity under Order I, Rule 8 of the Civil Procedure Code, meaning a few individuals sued on behalf of larger groups sharing the same interest. The suit was decided in 2000. Many years later, in 2017, the petitioner, Noor Khan, claimed he only then learned of this old judgment and decree. He filed an application under Section 12(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, alleging the decree had been obtained through fraud and misrepresentation, and that he lacked earlier knowledge of it. Both the trial court and the appellate court rejected his application, so he approached the High Court.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It held that anyone alleging fraud under Section 12(2) bears the full burden of proving it with specific details, which Noor Khan failed to provide. The court also found that proper public notice had been given when the original suit was filed, satisfying legal requirements for representative suits. Crucially, his own uncle had been a party to the original case, undermining his claim of ignorance, and he provided no documents establishing his right to challenge the decree. The ruling reinforces that vague fraud allegations and unexplained decades-long delays cannot be used to reopen settled judgments.

title: Collector Model Customs Collectorate of Gawadar V. Syed Shabbir Ahmed Shah and another,
explainer:
This case involved a truck that was stopped by customs officials in Pakistan on suspicion of smuggling. When inspected, the vehicle was found to contain hidden compartments filled with over 13,000 liters of Iranian diesel. Customs authorities also had the vehicle's chassis chemically tested, and the report showed that its chassis number had been tampered with, self-punched with fake digits to hide the vehicle's true identity, with the original number becoming visible after chemical treatment. Based on this, the Additional Collector of Customs ordered the vehicle permanently confiscated.

The vehicle's owner appealed, and the Customs Appellate Tribunal reversed the confiscation, allowing the vehicle to be released if the owner paid a fine equal to 20 percent of its customs value. The customs department then challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court ruled in favor of the customs department, finding that the Tribunal had made a serious error by ignoring the unchallenged forensic report proving the chassis number was fake. The Court held that a vehicle with a tampered chassis number was rightly subject to outright confiscation, not just a fine, citing Supreme Court precedents that such forensic findings deserve strong weight unless properly challenged. The Tribunal's order was set aside, and the original confiscation order was restored. This case reinforces that vehicles used in smuggling with falsified identification cannot simply be bought back through fines.

title: Ajab Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved four men accused of carjacking and extortion in Loralai, Balochistan. According to the complainant, on 13 January 2022, Ajab Khan and Behram Khan, along with two unidentified armed men, stopped his vehicle and robbed him of his car and mobile phone, and separately demanded 20 million rupees in extortion money. A First Information Report was registered under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code covering robbery, criminal intimidation, and common intention, along with a terrorism-related provision. All four accused sought bail after their earlier bail request was rejected by the trial court.

The Balochistan High Court treated the applicants differently based on the evidence against each. Ajab Khan and Behram Khan were specifically named in the original complaint, and the stolen vehicle was allegedly recovered from them, so the court denied them bail. However, the other two applicants, Amanullah and Naseebullah, were not named in the original complaint; they were only implicated later through a supplementary statement based on an affidavit, and no formal identification parade had been conducted to confirm their involvement. Because the evidence against these two was weaker and required further investigation, the court granted them bail on surety bonds of Rs. 500,000 each.

This case illustrates how courts assess bail differently depending on the strength and timing of evidence against each accused person, and highlights the importance of identification procedures in criminal cases.

title: Faqir Muhammad V. Muhammad Younas and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over ownership and possession of a piece of land in Quetta. Faqir Muhammad filed a civil suit seeking declaration of ownership along with mandatory and permanent injunctions, and also asked the court for a temporary (interim) injunction to stop the other party, Muhammad Younas, from interfering with, trespassing on, constructing on, or creating third-party rights over the disputed land while the main case was pending. He claimed the land was inherited property recorded in his name, supported by revenue records and a site map showing specific boundaries.

The trial court rejected his request for interim injunction, and an appellate court upheld that rejection. Faqir Muhammad then challenged both decisions before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court noted that an official inquiry conducted by revenue authorities into the ownership dispute appeared to support Faqir Muhammad's claim, and this finding had not been challenged by the opposing party through any formal appeal. Based on this, the court found that Faqir Muhammad had established a prima facie case in his favor, and that the lower courts had no valid reason to deny him interim protection.

The High Court set aside both earlier orders and granted the interim injunction, while directing the trial court to proceed quickly and decide the actual case on its own merits, independent of these preliminary observations. This case illustrates how courts assess requests for temporary protection in property disputes—weighing prima facie evidence—without deciding the final outcome of the underlying ownership question.

title: Syed Ali Akhtar V. Syed Murtaza and another,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal shooting incident and whether the accused should get bail before arrest. The complainant, a first-year student, alleged that Syed Murtaza shot him in the leg with a pistol during an altercation in Quetta, causing a fracture. Murtaza was booked under Section 324 of the Pakistan Penal Code, which covers attempted murder. A trial court had granted him pre-arrest bail, and the complainant asked the Balochistan High Court to cancel that bail.

The High Court found that medical evidence (an injury certificate) and CCTV footage supported the complainant's version of events, showing the accused had pointed a pistol at the complainant and fired. The court held that whether the accused actually intended to kill the complainant was a matter for the trial court to decide later, but on the face of it, a serious act causing a homicidal-type injury had occurred. Given this, the court ruled that the trial court had wrongly granted anticipatory bail, since such extraordinary protection is meant only for cases where an accused can show he is being falsely implicated out of malice, not as a routine option in serious crimes. The High Court therefore canceled the bail and ordered it recalled.

This case matters because it reinforces that pre-arrest bail is a special, limited protection, not something granted automatically, especially when strong evidence points to serious violent crime.

title: Commissioner Inland Revenue Zone-I, Regional Tax Office, Quetta V. Messrs Balochistan Onyx Development Corporation Ltd.,
explainer:
This case is about a tax dispute between the Commissioner Inland Revenue and Balochistan Onyx Development Corporation, a company that mines and sells marble. For the 2009 tax year, the company declared a net income of about Rs. 726,812. The Commissioner selected the company's case for audit and later, using powers under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, raised its assessed income to over Rs. 63 million, creating an additional tax demand of about Rs. 22 million. The company challenged this, and both the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals) and the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue ruled in the company's favor, cancelling the tax authority's order. The tax department then appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The Court examined whether the Commissioner had proper legal authority to select the case for audit and whether the increased tax liability was validly created. It held that under the law, tax authorities can only revise an assessment upward if they have definite, concrete information justifying the change - not mere guesswork or assumptions. In this case, the increased income figure was based on presumptions rather than solid evidence, which violated the legal requirement. The High Court therefore upheld the earlier rulings favoring the company and dismissed the tax department's appeal.

This case matters because it reinforces that tax authorities cannot arbitrarily inflate a taxpayer's declared income without solid justification, protecting businesses from speculative tax demands.

title: Muhammad Tahir V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by Muhammad Tahir against his conviction for murder under the Pakistan Penal Code, following the death of the complainant's brother, allegedly stabbed with a knife during a group clash. The prosecution's case rested mainly on eyewitness testimony from relatives of the deceased and on recovery of a knife said to be the murder weapon.

The Balochistan High Court found serious problems with this evidence. The eyewitnesses were closely related to the complainant and were themselves accused by the defense side, meaning they had strong motive to shift blame rather than tell an impartial story. Despite the incident happening in a crowded area, no independent or neutral witnesses were examined, even though some bystanders had reportedly wanted to give statements. The witnesses' accounts also contradicted each other and contradicted medical records, particularly about who brought the deceased to hospital and when the initial quarrel occurred. Notably, co-accused had already been acquitted on the very same evidence, and that acquittal was never challenged. Additionally, the recovered knife was never sent for forensic testing to confirm the blood matched the victim, undermining its evidentiary value.

The court concluded the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, noting the incident appeared to be a sudden mutual brawl rather than a planned murder, with both sides making accusations against each other. The appeal was allowed and the conviction set aside. The case highlights the importance of independent witnesses and forensic verification in securing safe convictions.

title: Saifullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Saifullah who was convicted by a trial court in Quetta for transporting 8 kilograms of charas (cannabis) on his motorcycle, under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. He was sentenced to 10 years in prison and a fine.

Saifullah appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the prosecution had not properly proven how the narcotics samples were handled and sent for laboratory testing, meaning the chain of custody was broken.

The High Court agreed with him. It found that the investigating officer claimed he sent the drug samples to the Forensic Laboratory through a courier or "docket," but the laboratory's own report showed the samples were received directly from the investigating officer himself, contradicting his statement. No special messenger was ever produced or questioned to confirm delivery, and there was no proof the samples were sent through insured post, as required by law. This violated mandatory rules meant to ensure the integrity of drug evidence.

Because this crucial link in the chain of custody was missing or contradicted, the court ruled that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. As a result, Saifullah's conviction was overturned and he was acquitted.

This case highlights how important proper procedure and documentation are in narcotics cases—if the handling of evidence cannot be reliably verified from recovery to lab testing, a conviction cannot stand, even if drugs were allegedly found.

title: Sardar Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Sardar Muhammad, who was caught by police on a motorcycle carrying a sack containing 15,000 grams of charas (hashish). He was tried by a Special Judge for Narcotics in Loralai, convicted, and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine.

On appeal to the Balochistan High Court, his lawyers argued several points: that the safe custody of the seized narcotics was not properly proven, that the forensic laboratory report did not follow proper testing protocols, that there were contradictions in the prosecution's evidence, and that police had failed to comply with mandatory requirements under Section 21 of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, since the raid was based on prior spy information.

The High Court rejected these arguments. It found that the forensic report actually did comply with the required rules and Supreme Court guidelines, and that the defense had never objected to the report during the trial itself or invoked the relevant procedural provision to challenge it. The court also held that compliance with Section 21 of the Act is not mandatory but merely directory, meaning that any lapse by police in following it could lead to disciplinary action against the officer, but would not make the recovered narcotics inadmissible as evidence or invalidate the case. Since the prosecution's witnesses remained consistent even under lengthy cross-examination, the court found no fault in the trial court's judgment and dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and life sentence. This case clarifies how much procedural strictness courts expect in narcotics cases.

title: Murtaza V. State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Murtaza who was accused of shooting a person, Syed Akhtar Hussain, in the leg during a street altercation in Quetta in May 2022. He was initially charged under Section 324 of the Pakistan Penal Code, which covers attempted murder. Murtaza had first obtained pre-arrest bail, but the High Court later cancelled it after the complainant challenged it, on the grounds that investigation was still ongoing. After his arrest, Murtaza applied for post-arrest bail, which the trial court rejected. He then approached the Balochistan High Court again.

The complainant's lawyer argued that since pre-arrest bail had already been cancelled once, and the evidence suggested intent to kill, bail should not be granted again, especially since the offence fell under a category where bail is normally restricted.

The High Court, however, granted bail. It reasoned that only one shot had been fired, hitting a non-vital part of the body, raising questions about whether there was real intent to kill or just a spontaneous reaction during a heated argument. The court said such questions needed further examination during trial, not at the bail stage. It also noted that the trial had not even begun, the applicant had already spent over a month in custody, and the trial court had used language in its earlier order that seemed to judge the case's merits prematurely, rather than making the required tentative assessment appropriate at the bail stage. This case illustrates how courts weigh doubt and incomplete evidence in bail decisions, even for serious charges.

This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with a complaint filed under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005 against members of the Christian Community of Quetta, accusing them of illegally occupying land claimed by a complainant who wanted to build a housing society there. The complainant's son, acting under a power of attorney, had initiated the case, and a lower court had taken up the complaint, ordered a police inquiry, and issued notices to community elders. Those accused sought acquittal, arguing there was no evidence they had illegally dispossessed anyone or belonged to any land-grabbing group, but the trial court refused to acquit them, prompting this petition to the High Court.

The High Court found serious problems with the case. The complainant himself was unsure of his property's boundaries and had only recently attempted to demarcate it, without properly following the Land Revenue Act's rules for such demarcation. His allegations were inconsistent, and the report used against the accused was self-contradictory. The court held that both the wrongful act and criminal intent required under the law were missing, and that courts should not mechanically order police investigations on every complaint without solid evidence.

The High Court quashed the complaint, criticizing the trial court for entertaining it against an entire community without any specific allegation against any individual, especially given the Christian Community's reputation as law-abiding. The court noted this was really a property demarcation dispute, for which proper civil forums exist, not a criminal matter.

title: Rehmdil V. Mst. Bibi and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a husband, Rehmdil, challenging a family court's decision ordering him to pay dower (250 mitcal of gold) and maintenance to his wife and children. The wife had filed a suit for recovery of dower and maintenance, and although the husband initially appeared in court and even hired a lawyer, he later stopped attending proceedings. As a result, the trial court decided the case ex-parte (in his absence) and ruled against him.

The husband appealed, but his appeal was rejected because it was filed too late, and he failed to provide a valid reason for the delay. He then approached the Balochistan High Court, arguing he hadn't gotten a fair chance to present his case and that the decision was based only on the wife's witnesses.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It noted that the husband had voluntarily disappeared from proceedings despite engaging a lawyer, so he could not later complain about the ex-parte decision. The court also observed that he never actually disputed owing the dower amount. Importantly, the court reaffirmed that Family Courts operate under their own procedures and are not bound by the Civil Procedure Code, a deliberate legislative choice meant to ensure quick resolution of family disputes and spare litigants from prolonged litigation.

This case matters because it reinforces that family court litigants must actively pursue their cases, and it highlights the special, simplified procedural rules governing family law disputes in Pakistan.

title: Hameeda V. Khan Muhammad and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a widow, Hameeda, who sued her father-in-law seeking two things after her husband died of cancer in 2017: her unpaid dower (40 gold Misqals and Rs. 200,000 cash), and a share in property she claimed her husband owned, including plots in Karachi and other belongings. Her husband's family denied he owned such property and argued her claims were invalid.

Both the trial court and the appellate court dismissed her suit, and she then approached the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal on two grounds. First, her dower claim was filed about four years after her husband's death, but the law (Article 104 of the Limitation Act, 1908) only allows three years to claim dower after a marriage ends through death or divorce. Since she filed late, the claim was time-barred. Second, her claim to a share of her husband's property was not something a Family Court could even hear, since inheritance and property-share disputes fall outside the specific list of matters (like dower, maintenance, custody, etc.) that Family Courts are authorized to decide under the Family Courts Act, 1964. She also hadn't provided any documents proving her husband owned the claimed property.

The court dismissed her petition but noted she could still pursue her property claim before the proper forum. The case illustrates the importance of filing dower claims within the legal time limit and shows that inheritance disputes must go to civil courts, not Family Courts.

title: Riaz Ahmed V. The Government of Balochistan through Secretary Food Balochistan Civil Secretariat, Zarghoon Road, Quetta and others,
explainer:
Riaz Ahmed worked as an Assistant Food Controller for the Balochistan Food Directorate. In 2015, he faced allegations that he sold thousands of bags of government wheat to flour mills on credit, in violation of departmental rules. An inquiry was opened but dragged on for years. He was formally issued a show-cause notice in 2017, and he retired from service in 2019 while the inquiry was still unresolved, with the retirement notification itself referencing the unproven allegations. His pension and gratuity were withheld pending the outcome. After court intervention, the department finally imposed penalties on him in 2022, ordering recovery of the alleged embezzled amount and deduction of his pension and gratuity.

Ahmed challenged this, arguing the penalties came far too late. The Balochistan High Court agreed. Under the Balochistan Employees' Efficiency and Discipline Act, 2011, disciplinary proceedings against a retired employee must be finalized within two years of retirement. Since Ahmed retired in 2019 and the penalties were only imposed in 2022, well beyond that two-year limit, the court ruled the punishment order was issued without legal authority and was null and void. It set aside the penalties and ordered the government to pay his retirement benefits.

The case matters because it reinforces that retired government employees cannot be kept in indefinite limbo by delayed departmental inquiries, and agencies must act within the legally prescribed time limits.

title: Abdul Ghaffar V. The State,
explainer:
This case is a criminal appeal decided by the Balochistan High Court involving Abdul Ghaffar, who was tried and convicted under laws relating to abduction for ransom, dacoity, attempted murder, and obstruction of public servants. The allegations stemmed from three connected FIRs involving the kidnapping of a diesel businessman's clerk and brother, theft of cash and records, and a later armed encounter with police in which two accused persons died.

The High Court found serious flaws in the prosecution's case. The appellant was not named in any of the three FIRs, and no weapons were recovered from him despite claims he was arrested after the encounter. The two abduction victims gave contradictory testimony - one did not implicate the appellant at all, while the other identified him in court despite no formal identification parade ever being conducted, making that identification unreliable. Their witness statements across the three cases were also found to be suspiciously identical, violating procedural rules requiring statements to be recorded separately. Medical evidence further contradicted the police account of when and how the appellant was injured and arrested, and investigators failed to collect blood samples from the alleged crime scene, casting doubt on where the encounter even took place.

Given these inconsistencies, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted the appellant, allowing all three appeals. The case highlights the importance of proper identification procedures, consistent witness testimony, and physical evidence in securing safe convictions.

title: Abdul Rehman and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Abdul Rehman and Naseebullah, convicted of rape under Section 376 of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced to fourteen years in prison each, plus fines. The complainant, a young woman without a permanent home, told police that three men had forcibly taken her near a drainage area and raped her. A police patrol found her crying shortly after the incident, and she immediately identified two of the attackers, who were arrested on the spot; the third fled. She was medically examined, and samples were sent for forensic DNA testing, but the DNA report did not link the accused to the samples collected.

On appeal, the defense argued that contradictions existed in the victim's statement and that the negative DNA result entitled the men to benefit of the doubt. The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments, holding that a prompt, detailed FIR, consistent testimony from the victim confirmed by independent police witnesses, and the absence of any ill will between the accused and police strongly supported the prosecution's case. The court also explained that a negative DNA finding does not automatically clear an accused, since many factors, including handling errors, can affect such results. Citing precedent, the court held that a victim's credible, truthful testimony alone can support a conviction even without corroborating forensic evidence. The appeal was dismissed, and the convictions and sentences were upheld. This case reinforces that courts can rely on a survivor's reliable testimony despite inconclusive forensic evidence.

title: Allahi Dad and 4 others V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 5 others,
explainer:
This case involved fishermen and businessmen in Pasni, Balochistan, who filed a constitutional petition claiming that a local political activist was pressuring authorities to expel non-local fishermen, most of whom came from Sindh. The petitioners said the activist had organized a sit-in (Dharna) blocking the Coastal Highway to force this expulsion, and that the local administration had caved in, allegedly agreeing to remove the Sindhi laborers within 15 days. They also claimed that after the protest, threats were made against them and other businessmen, and although FIRs were filed against the activist, police were not arresting anyone or pursuing the cases in court. The petitioners asked the High Court to direct the government to protect their constitutional rights.

The Balochistan High Court held that while peaceful protest to raise genuine grievances is healthy for society, such protests cannot be allowed to violate the fundamental rights of others who did not consent to the disruption. The court emphasized that no one is above the law, and if government officials secretly agreed to any arrangement violating citizens' constitutional rights, such an agreement would be illegal and those officials would face consequences. The court relied on the Supreme Court's Faizabad Dharna judgment, which held that the right to assembly is not absolute and must not be used to threaten public order or unlawfully restrict others' rights, including free movement.

title: Mihral and another V. Mst. Zargul and another,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute between a husband and wife in Balochistan over dower payment and maintenance allowance. The wife had filed a suit claiming that although 100 Misqal of gold was fixed as dower (Haq Meher) at the time of marriage, only 15 Misqal had been paid, leaving 85 Misqal outstanding. She also sought dissolution of marriage and maintenance for herself and her daughter, claiming her husband, who she said was mentally unsound, had stopped supporting them.

The trial court and the first appellate court both ruled in the wife's favor, ordering payment of the remaining 85 Misqal of gold and awarding maintenance covering roughly seventeen years of separation. The husband and his father (who had been directed to pay on the husband's behalf due to the husband's alleged mental incapacity) challenged these decisions before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the dower award, finding the husband failed to prove he had paid more than 15 Misqal. It also upheld the maintenance order in principle, agreeing that the husband's father, as grandfather of the children, could be held responsible for payment. However, the court found that awarding maintenance for a full seventeen years was legally incorrect, since the law (Limitation Act, Article 120) only allows recovery of past maintenance for six years before filing suit. The court therefore modified the decision, limiting past maintenance to six years, while otherwise upholding the lower courts

title: Mir Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
Mir Ahmed was accused of murdering Abdul Hameed by shooting him outside his home in Quetta in the early morning hours of 22 July 2012, shortly after Sehri. The prosecution's case was that Mir Ahmed came to the house, called out to be let in, and opened fire as the family came to the door, killing Abdul Hameed while threatening the other family members before fleeing on a motorcycle. The alleged motive was a rejected marriage proposal. Five eyewitnesses, including the victim's father, brothers, and a neighbor, testified against him. His father and brothers were also initially charged with conspiracy but were acquitted at trial, while Mir Ahmed himself evaded arrest for about seven years before being caught.

The Balochistan High Court upheld his conviction, rejecting arguments that the witnesses were unreliable simply because they were relatives, since there was no proof of enmity or motive to falsely implicate him, and he was already known to them so misidentification was unlikely. Minor inconsistencies in testimony were considered natural given the long passage of time. The court also treated his lengthy absconsion as strong supporting evidence of guilt, alongside medical evidence matching the witnesses' account. Finding the prosecution had proven the case beyond doubt, the court dismissed his appeal and confirmed the murder conviction. The case illustrates how courts evaluate eyewitness credibility, family relationships, and flight from justice in serious criminal trials.

title: Rehman V. Dur Muhammad and 3 others,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court, dealt with a dispute over local government election eligibility. Rehman challenged Dur Muhammad's candidacy for a reserved "Peasant" seat in Union Council elections in Kohlu district, arguing that Dur Muhammad could not run because he served as Chairman of the Zakat Committee, a government-appointed position. The Returning Officer and an Appellate Authority had both rejected this objection and allowed Dur Muhammad to contest.

The core legal question was whether the Balochistan Local Government Act, 2010 (Section 24(1)(f)) bars government servants and officials of state-controlled bodies from contesting local elections, and whether a Zakat Committee Chairman falls into that category. Looking at the Balochistan Zakat and Ushr Act, 2012, the Court found that the Chairman of a Tehsil Zakat Committee is effectively a public servant, since the position involves service in a statutory body controlled by the provincial government. The Court also reasoned that someone with discretionary power to distribute Zakat funds to poor voters could unfairly influence or "hijack" elections in his constituency, undermining fairness and transparency.

The Court accepted the petition, ruling that Dur Muhammad was disqualified, and directed the Returning Officer to remove his name from the list of validly nominated candidates. The judgment matters because it reinforces safeguards against conflicts of interest and potential vote manipulation by officials who control distribution of public welfare funds.

title: Muhammad Hassan Kakar and others V. Vice-Chancellor University of Balochistan, Quetta and others,
explainer:
This case involved employees of the University of Balochistan who worked in non-teaching positions and sought promotions or upgradation of their posts based on a 2013 notification issued by the university's Human Resource Director. That notification set out a policy allowing staff to move up pay scales simply after completing a fixed number of years in their current post, without reference to qualifications, skills, or performance. The employees argued the university had applied this policy inconsistently, upgrading some staff while denying the same benefit to others, amounting to discrimination.

The university countered that an audit had found the underlying notification itself was flawed, since past promotions had been granted purely on length of service while ignoring qualifications, skills, training, and proper procedure. Committees, including one formed by the Higher Education Commission, had investigated these irregularities.

The Balochistan High Court held that promotion and upgradation are legally distinct: promotion means advancement in rank and must be based on merit and fitness, not just seniority, while upgradation is a monetary benefit granted under policy to address pay stagnation, not a right. The court found the 2013 notification illegal and void from the start, set it aside, and directed the university to review all promotions and upgradations made under it, undoing any that weren't merit-based, while ordering that the petitioners' promotion claims be reconsidered strictly on merit without delay.

title: Rehmatullah and 2 others V. The State,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court and concerns a bail application by three men, Rehmatullah and two others, accused of murdering their complainant's nephew and injuring his son. The dispute stemmed from allegations that the accused were involved in an illegal drugs business, and after the complainant reported this, one accused's brother was dismissed from the police force, allegedly prompting revenge attacks in February 2020 that left one victim dead.

The trial court had earlier convicted the applicants and sentenced them to life imprisonment, but the High Court set that conviction aside and sent the case back for retrial because a procedural requirement (Section 353 of the Criminal Procedure Code) had not been properly followed. While the retrial was pending, the accused sought bail, arguing they had already been detained for more than two years without their trial concluding, which normally entitles an accused to bail under Section 497 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The court rejected this argument. It explained that the law denies this benefit to accused persons who are considered hardened, desperate, or dangerous criminals, and this restriction is not limited to people with prior convictions. Given the serious and repeated nature of the attacks and the drug-related allegations, the court found the applicants fell into this excluded category. The bail application was therefore dismissed, though the court clarified its comments were tentative and would not affect the actual trial's outcome.

title: Ghulam Dastagir and another V. Allah Baksh,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Kuchlak, Balochistan, over a piece of land measuring 5,000 square feet that included a house, a shop used as a medical store, and a storage area. The petitioners claimed they had built and possessed this property, but while one of them was away in Karachi seeking medical treatment for the other, the respondent allegedly broke the locks and forcibly took over most of the property, except the medical store. The petitioners sued under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, a special law that allows someone dispossessed of property to quickly recover it without the case turning into a dispute over ownership or title, provided the suit is filed within six months of the dispossession.

Both the trial court and the appellate court had dismissed the petitioners' suit, ruling against them. The petitioners then approached the Balochistan High Court through a civil revision petition, arguing that the lower courts had ignored strong documentary evidence, such as utility records from gas, electricity, and telephone companies, showing the property was in their name and possession.

The High Court agreed with the petitioners, finding that the lower courts had misread or ignored important evidence. Even though courts are usually reluctant to interfere with matching factual findings of two lower courts, the High Court held that such interference is justified when evidence has been clearly misread or misunderstood. It set aside the earlier decisions and ruled in favor of the petitioners, restoring their possession.

title: Najeebullah and others V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and others,
explainer:
The Balochistan High Court decided who has the power to transfer and post officers in the province's Prosecution Service, particularly those at grade 17 and above. The dispute arose after a letter from the Government of Balochistan declared that the Prosecutor General had no authority to issue transfer or posting orders for senior prosecution officers, insisting that this power belonged exclusively to the Secretary of the Prosecution Department and other senior government officials, based on delegation-of-powers rules. Several prosecution officers, whose transfers had been cancelled through this letter, challenged it in court, arguing that the law creating the Prosecution Service gave full administrative control, including transfers, to the Prosecutor General.

The court examined the Balochistan Prosecution Service Act of 2003, which defines the Prosecutor General's role as managing and controlling prosecutors, and vests administration of the service in that office. The judges held that the law's intent was to create an independent, impartial prosecution system free from executive interference, similar to how the Constitution separates the judiciary from the executive. They reasoned that fair prosecution requires similar independence from government control.

As a result, the court ruled that the Prosecutor General, not the Secretary of the Prosecution Department, holds the authority over transfers and postings, and it struck down the impugned letter. This ruling matters because it reinforces the independence of the prosecution service from executive interference, which the court considered essential for a fair criminal justice system.

title: Abdul Jabbar V. Government of Balochistan, Forests and Wildlife Department, Quetta, through Secretary and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved a resident of Ziarat district whose tribe, the Panezai Tribe, had reportedly given land free of cost to the Forest Department decades earlier, based on an alleged 2000 agreement promising that tribe members would be given preference in future job appointments within the department. When the Forest Department advertised various posts (such as tube well operator, driver, security guard, and gardener) and did not give priority to Panezai Tribe candidates, the petitioner asked the Balochistan High Court to enforce the old agreement and direct the department to favor his tribe's applicants.

The court dismissed the petition. It found that the agreement itself did not actually contain any clause guaranteeing preferential appointments. More importantly, the court ruled that any agreement essentially trading land for public jobs is illegal and void, since public offices cannot be bought or sold, and appointments must be based on merit. It cited the Contract Act, which voids agreements with unlawful objects, and the Specific Relief Act, which bars enforcement of contracts requiring continuous performance beyond three years. The court also noted the petitioner's claim that the arrangement was meant to last "for all generations" made it inherently unenforceable.

The ruling reaffirms that public sector jobs in Pakistan must be awarded on merit, and that promises exchanging land or favors for guaranteed government employment have no legal standing, regardless of how longstanding or informally accepted such arrangements might be.

title: Abdul Ghaffar V. Muhammad Ayub and another,
explainer:
Abdul Ghaffar sued Muhammad Ayub and another person to recover Rs.10 million, claiming he had arranged this loan for them and that they had signed a guarantee agreement and promissory notes promising repayment. He said part of the money was paid in cash and part through bank cheques belonging to third parties. The defendants denied ever signing these documents, calling them forged, and had them examined by the Forensic Science Laboratory. The lab's expert found that the signatures on the documents did not match the defendants' actual signatures. The trial court dismissed Ghaffar's suit, finding he had failed to prove that the documents were genuinely executed by the defendants.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court upheld this decision. It explained that while the law normally presumes a promissory note was made for real consideration, this presumption can be challenged, and once the defendants flatly denied signing the documents, the burden shifted to Ghaffar to prove genuine execution. He could not do so: the forensic report cast serious doubt on the signatures, the claim of paying millions of rupees in cash at court premises seemed implausible, the agreement was not properly notarized, the oath commissioner who supposedly witnessed the notes was never produced, and Ghaffar failed to show he had the financial capacity to lend such a large sum. Because of these gaps, the court found no error in the trial court's judgment and dismissed the appeal, meaning Ghaffar could not recover the money.

title: Ahmedullah and another V. Province of Balochistan through Addl. Chief Secretary (Dev) and others,
explainer:
This case is about whether shipbreakers at Gaddani, Balochistan, had to pay a tonnage fee to the government for dismantling imported ships, or whether they could avoid this charge by claiming they worked on privately owned plots rather than land controlled by the Balochistan Development Authority (BDA).

The petitioners, who run shipbreaking businesses, argued they beached and scrapped vessels on private plots, so the tonnage fee under the Balochistan Development Authority Act and related rules should not apply to them. They also argued the fee was unlawful because the government was not providing them any service in return, and that a fee (as opposed to a tax) legally requires such reciprocal benefit. They further challenged how the fee had been increased.

The court rejected these arguments. It explained that under a Martial Law Order later incorporated into the Constitution as Article 270-A, shipbreaking in Balochistan's coastal area can legally happen only on plots officially allotted by the BDA; doing it anywhere else without BDA permission is prohibited. So claiming to operate on private land didn't help the petitioners, since such activity was unlawful regardless. The court also noted the plots in question actually belonged to the government, not private owners. As a result, all three petitions were dismissed.

The case matters because it confirms that shipbreaking in Gaddani is tightly regulated, that operators cannot escape regulatory fees by claiming private land ownership, and it reaffirms constitutional backing for government control over this industry.

title: Abdul Rasheed V. the Secretary Local Government Civil Secretariat, Quetta and 4 others,
explainer:
This case was about a resident of the Sariab area in Quetta who repeatedly asked the courts to ensure a promised football ground and sports facilities were actually built for his community. Years earlier, authorities including the Commissioner Quetta and the Administrator of Metropolitan Corporation Quetta had identified a specific piece of land for this purpose and formally told the High Court, on record, that they had no objection to using it for a football ground. This project was even included in the government's official development budget (PSDP) for 2021-2022. Despite these clear commitments, the Corporation kept delaying, tried to get its earlier "no objection" statement erased from the court record, and later attempted a review of the court's order, all of which failed. The petitioner even filed a contempt case before bringing this fresh constitutional petition.

The High Court held that the constitutional right to "life" under Article 9 is not limited to bare survival but includes amenities and facilities that allow people to live with dignity, which can include recreational and sports facilities. Since the Corporation had already agreed to the project and it was budgeted for, the court ruled that its later excuses were an attempt to frustrate its own earlier commitments and the court's orders. The petition was allowed, and authorities were directed to hand over the land for the football ground as originally approved. This case matters because it shows courts can enforce promises made by public authorities and treat public infrastructure like sports facilities as part of citizens' fundamental rights.

title: Mst. Aziza Khanum alias Shah Pari and another V. Member-II, Board of Revenue, Government of Balochistan, Civil Secretariat, Zargoon Road, Quetta and 5 others,
explainer:
This case involved a woman and her husband who claimed ownership of land and buildings in Quetta, saying they had bought various pieces of property, built a double-story structure with shops and flats on it, and had rented these out to tenants. The wife also claimed her husband had gifted part of the property to her, though this gift was later disputed between them before being resolved through a compromise. When the wife discovered that some of the land was officially recorded in the government's revenue records under different people's names (linked to an old 1961 auction), she sued to have the records corrected in her favor and to stop any changes to the property.

Both the trial court and the first appeal court rejected her entire claim. She then took the matter to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found that the lower courts had misread the evidence. While the wife's claim to one portion of the property lacked proof, she had a valid claim to the other half, since she and her husband had actually built the structure on it. The High Court partially reversed the lower courts' decisions, declaring the couple owners of half the disputed property and ordering revenue authorities to update records accordingly. For the remaining portion, if authorities ever decided to sell or lease it, the court ruled the couple would have the right of first refusal at the highest bid price, since they had built the structure there.

This case matters because it shows courts correcting errors where lower courts wrongly dismissed an entire claim instead of recognizing the valid parts supported by evidence.
