title: Noor Ul Haq V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary Civil Secretariat, Quetta and 4 others,
explainer:
This case is about how the government picks and advertises small-scale water projects for farmers in Ziarat, Balochistan. Noor Ul Haq, the petitioner, challenged tenders issued for drilling and installing agricultural bores under a public-sector development project. He argued the tender notices were vague and improperly issued to avoid competitive e-tendering, and that the sites for the bores were never properly identified through the beneficiary-selection process required by law. He pointed to earlier Supreme Court and High Court rulings on the same problem.

The government's lawyers said the e-tendering issue had already been fixed and that site and beneficiary selection would happen after the bidding process, following criteria approved by the Provincial Cabinet in 2018.

The High Court disagreed with the government's approach. It found that the tender notices only vaguely mentioned villages without proper feasibility studies, surveys, or exact locations, violating the Planning Commission of Pakistan's guidelines for including projects in development programs. The court noted that a proper scrutiny committee and criteria existed for selecting beneficiaries and sites, but these were not followed before advertising the tenders.

As a result, the court set aside the entire procurement process and directed authorities to stop including vague, poorly planned projects in development programs, in line with existing rules and prior court rulings. The petition was allowed, reinforcing accountability and transparency in how public development funds are spent.

title: Sher Afghan Khan Zarkoon V. Government of Balochistan, Local Government, Rural Development and Agrovilles Department, Quetta through Secretary and 6 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over local body elections in Kohlu for the seat of Chairman, Municipal Committee. Twelve councillors voted; the petitioner received six votes, and his rival, respondent No.7, received five votes, with one vote cast for respondent No.7 being rejected due to alleged double marking on the ballot, which the petitioner argued compromised the secrecy of the vote. The petitioner was declared the winner. Respondent No.7 challenged the rejection before the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP), which ruled in his favour, ordering that the rejected vote be counted and that a lot be drawn since the count would then be tied at six votes each. The petitioner challenged this ECP order before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court held that it could not resolve the factual dispute over whether the vote was validly rejected, since that required an inquiry into facts, which is not normally done in constitutional petitions. However, it found that the Presiding Officer had failed to conduct a mandatory on-the-spot summary inquiry into the disputed ballot, as required under the local government election rules, especially since extra marks appeared on the ballot that a voter could not have made himself. Because this procedural failure could have affected the outcome, the Court declared the entire election for Chairman void and directed the Election Commission to hold fresh elections. The case highlights the importance of proper verification procedures to ensure fair and transparent local elections.

title: Dr. Musadiq aziz and 6 others V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Health Department Civil Secretariat, Quetta and another,
explainer:
The case concerned seven doctors who applied for advertised health department posts requiring a Master's Degree in Public Health, among other qualifications. The application deadline set by the Balochistan Public Service Commission was 30 December 2022, but the petitioners had not yet received their final semester results at that time; their degrees were only completed after their results came out in February 2023. Although they sat and reportedly passed the written test, the Commission disqualified them from interviews because they lacked the required degree by the cutoff date.

The petitioners argued that since they eventually obtained the degree and had passed the written exam, they had earned a vested right to be considered, and pointed to a precedent where nurses were given relaxation for submitting documents late.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition, ruling that candidates must possess the required qualifications before applying, not obtain them afterward. The court rejected the idea of relying on "hope certificates" suggesting a candidate would eventually pass, calling the concept illogical. It held that passing a written test does not create a vested right if the applicant was ineligible from the start, and that advertised eligibility criteria cannot be altered or relaxed once the application deadline has passed. This case reinforces that strict compliance with eligibility deadlines is required in public service recruitment.

title: Messrs Kurdish Mining Enterprises through Adnan Aziz Kurd and others V. Secretary Mines and Mineral, Government of Balochistan, Quetta and 12 others,
explainer:
This case involved a decades-long dispute over mining leases for marble and onyx in Chagai district, Balochistan. Originally, three mining leases belonged to companies linked to the family of the late Malik Mir Hassan Khan. In 2009, the government's Director General of Mines and Minerals cancelled these leases under Rule 90 of the Balochistan Mineral Rules, 2002, which allows cancellation of leases that are left unworked or idle. The leases were then given to new parties, the Kurdish Mining Enterprises petitioners, who developed the mines and began paying royalties.

However, the original family challenged the cancellation, arguing they were never given a chance to explain themselves before their leases were taken away, and pointed out that records actually showed substantial extraction from the mines during the relevant period, contradicting the claim that the leases were idle. After lengthy litigation, including an earlier remand by the High Court, the Provincial Government's appellate authority eventually set aside the 2009 cancellation and restored the leases to the original family.

The petitioners then challenged this restoration before the Balochistan High Court. The Court held that Rule 90 requires giving the lease holder an opportunity to be heard before cancellation, which had not happened. Since the original cancellation was procedurally unfair and possibly based on incorrect facts, the Court refused to interfere with the government's decision restoring the leases, and dismissed the petitioners' case. This shows the importance of due process and fair hearing before cancelling legal rights like mining leases.

title: Ali Nawaz V. Election Commission of Pakistan, Islamabad and others,
explainer:
This case involved an election dispute for the seat of Vice Chairman, District Council, Usta Muhammad. The appellant, Ali Nawaz, and the other candidate had both received equal votes, but the Returning Officer declared two of the appellant's votes as spoilt without conducting any inquiry, resulting in the other candidate being declared the winner. Nawaz challenged this before the Election Tribunal, but his petition was dismissed on technical grounds, specifically that it was not properly verified as required under Rule 74 of the Balochistan Local Government (Election) Rules, 2013, which requires verification similar to Order VI Rule 15 of the Civil Procedure Code.

The Balochistan High Court found that the Election Tribunal had wrongly focused on procedural technicalities instead of examining the real dispute, which was whether the two votes were correctly declared spoilt. The Court held that there had been substantial compliance with the verification requirements, and that election petitions should not be dismissed on hyper-technical grounds when a genuine controversy exists between the parties. It ruled that such matters should be decided on their merits rather than technicalities.

As a result, the High Court allowed the appeal, set aside the Election Tribunal's order, and effectively required that the real question, whether the appellant's votes were validly rejected, be properly examined. This case matters because it reinforces the principle that election disputes should be resolved based on substance and fairness rather than being thrown out due to minor procedural defects.

title: Wahid Bakhsh and others V. Balochistan Awami Party through Representative Secretary Coordination and others,
explainer:
This case involved local government representatives (councillors) from Tump Municipal Committee who had been elected on tickets of the Balochistan Awami Party (BAP). BAP accused them of defection, claiming they had switched allegiance to the National Party, and sought their disqualification under the Balochistan Local Government Act, 2010, as amended in 2023. The Secretary of the Local Government Department accepted the complaint, declared the councillors defectors, disqualified them, and vacated their seats. They challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The law requires that any declaration of defection must be made in writing by the "Party Head" specifically, who must also give the accused member a chance to explain before making such a declaration. In this case, however, the complaint was actually filed by someone called the "Secretary Coordination" of BAP, a position not even recognized in the party's own constitution, while the underlying declaration was made by the party's Secretary General - not the Party Head as the law requires.

The High Court ruled that when a law specifies a particular manner or particular authority for taking an action, it must be done exactly that way or not at all. Since the mandatory requirement of a declaration by the Party Head was not fulfilled, the entire complaint and subsequent disqualification proceedings were legally invalid. The Court therefore allowed the appeal, protecting the councillors from disqualification due to this procedural defect, and reinforcing that technical legal requirements safeguarding elected representatives must be strictly followed.

title: Jamshaid Hussain and 3 others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved four men convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Quetta for allegedly possessing pistols, live rounds, detonators, explosive substances, and prima cord under suspicious circumstances. Police claimed they acted on a tip that the accused were linked to a proscribed organization and were bringing weapons and explosives from Afghanistan. They were sentenced to rigorous imprisonment under the Explosive Substances Act and the Pakistan Arms Ordinance.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found the prosecution's case riddled with serious contradictions. Witnesses gave conflicting accounts about whether a Bomb Disposal Team or the Counter Terrorism Department first arrived at the scene, who actually separated and packaged the explosive samples, and how the initial report reached the police station located over 80 kilometers away. The officer in charge of the Bomb Disposal Team could not even identify the accused despite claiming to have witnessed their arrest. Additionally, the prosecution failed to prove the safe custody of the recovered explosives from the time of seizure until they reached the forensic laboratory, since the relevant police register entry was never produced.

Given these unexplained inconsistencies and gaps in evidence, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, meaning the convictions were overturned. This case underscores how courts require reliable, consistent evidence and proper chain-of-custody documentation before upholding serious criminal convict

title: Akhtar Hussain Langove Member Provincial Assembly and 5 others V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary, Quetta and 3 others,
explainer:
This case concerns hiring practices at the Quetta Water and Sanitation Authority (Q-WASA). Petitioners, who belonged to Quetta District, challenged the appointment of employees from other districts of Balochistan, arguing that since the Quetta Water and Sanitation Authority Act, 2004 applied only to Quetta District, only residents of Quetta should be eligible for jobs there. They asked the court to declare these appointments illegal and order that only Quetta domicile holders be hired.

The court examined the relevant law and found that the 2004 Act empowered the authority to make service regulations, and under Regulation 13 of the 2011 Employees' Service Regulations, any applicant with a domicile or local certificate from anywhere in Balochistan—not just Quetta—was eligible to apply. The job advertisement itself reflected this broader eligibility, consistent with the regulations.

Crucially, the court noted that the petitioners had participated in the recruitment process without objecting to either the regulations or the advertisement, and only challenged the process after failing to get selected. Since the regulations had been in force since 2011 without challenge, the petition was also barred by delay (laches).

For these reasons, the Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition, upholding the appointments and confirming that Q-WASA jobs were open to eligible candidates from across Balochistan, not restricted to Quetta residents.

title: Ghulam Yaseen and another V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Home and Tribal Affairs and 7 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a challenge to how recruitment was conducted for 34 Inspector posts (BPS-16) in Balochistan Police through the Balochistan Public Service Commission. Candidates were required to meet a minimum physical standard, including a height of 5 feet 7 inches, as set out in the Police Rules, 1934. Two petitioners who took part in the recruitment process claimed that although they performed well, they were overlooked because the Chief Minister (first the Caretaker Chief Minister, and later the elected Chief Minister) had granted relaxations in the physical standard to certain other candidates who did not meet the height and chest measurement requirements, without proper justification or the required opinion from the competent authority.

The Balochistan High Court found that these relaxations were granted without transparency or valid reasoning, especially since many other candidates may not have even applied believing themselves ineligible under the stated criteria. The court held that fair and merit-based recruitment is essential to maintaining discipline in a uniformed force like the police, and that allowing exceptions without justification undermines that integrity.

The court declared all such relaxations granted by both the Caretaker and the elected government as illegal and void, and set aside the related recommendations. The petition was allowed. This ruling reinforces the principle that recruitment rules, especially objective physical standards, must be applied uniformly and cannot be bypassed through unexplained executive discretion.

title: Muhammad Ilyas V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 2 others,
explainer:
Muhammad Ilyas was a government employee who was dismissed in 2010 over allegations of forging exam results and involvement in exam malpractice. He challenged his dismissal, and the Supreme Court ordered a fresh, proper inquiry, leaving the question of reinstatement and back-benefits to the authorities. This fresh inquiry cleared him of all charges, and he was reinstated in 2019.

After reinstatement, Ilyas sought his back benefits, arrears, seniority and promotion. While officials were sorting this out, the Chief Secretary formed a committee to examine his back-benefits claim in light of a Supreme Court ruling. However, the S&GAD Secretary misunderstood this direction and instead started a whole new disciplinary inquiry against Ilyas on the very same allegations he had already been cleared of.

The Balochistan High Court ruled that this second inquiry was illegal and void, because it violated the constitutional principle against double jeopardy (Article 13) - meaning a person cannot be punished or tried twice for the same offence. The court rejected the government's argument that the petition wasn't allowed to be filed in the High Court, since no final decision on his service terms had yet been made. It set aside the fresh inquiry and directed the authorities to only determine, through proper process, whether Ilyas is entitled to back benefits - not to reopen the settled misconduct charges.

title: Muhammad Afzal Jami V. Province of Balochistan through Senior Member, Board of Revenue, Balochistan and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a lawyer, Muhammad Afzal Jami, who had represented several clients in civil suits before the Qazi Gwadar between 2004 and 2008. He claimed he had struck a deal with his clients: if they won their land cases, they would transfer 200 acres of land to him as his legal fee. The suits were later decided by compromise, and land was reportedly mutated in his name. However, in 2015, the Board of Revenue Balochistan declared the entire land settlement of that area null and void and ordered it to be redone. When the new settlement proceedings took place, the lawyer's name was not included as an owner, despite his participation. He then went to the High Court asking for the land record (Fard) to be issued in his name and for the 2015 notification to be set aside.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed his petition. It held that receiving land as payment for legal services violates Rule 149 of the Pakistan Legal Practitioners and Bar Councils Rules, 1976, which prohibits lawyers from taking such fees, and also breaches constitutional principles under Articles 29 and 30. Because the arrangement had an unlawful basis, it was void under Section 23 of the Contract Act, 1872. The court also noted the petitioner failed to prove the original landowners' status and had delayed challenging the notification for years, making his claim barred by laches. This judgment reinforces that lawyers cannot legally accept land or property as fees, and reaffirms limits on delayed legal challenges.

title: Malik Muhammad Naseem Khan (Now late through legal herirs) and 2 others V. Mst. Bibi Zahra and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over inherited land in Quetta. Bibi Zahra claimed her brothers had denied her rightful Islamic inheritance share in properties left by their late father, Malik Sher Muhammad. She applied to revenue authorities to have her name included as a co-sharer in the official land records.

Her brothers (the petitioners) opposed this, arguing that their father had already gifted part of the properties to his sons during his lifetime, and that Bibi Zahra had already received her share in cash under a 2008 agreement.

The revenue authorities, at multiple levels including the Deputy Commissioner, the Commissioner, and the Senior Member Board of Revenue, all ruled in favor of Bibi Zahra and ordered her name entered in the land records as a rightful co-sharer. The brothers then challenged these decisions in the High Court.

The High Court dismissed their petition. It noted the contradiction in the brothers' case: if their sister truly had no share in the gifted property, why did they claim to have paid her cash in 2008 for her share? The court also found the 2008 agreement legally void because it was never registered and did not even specify the amount supposedly paid. Additionally, the brothers had suspiciously left her name out of other inheritance mutations over the years.

This case matters because it reinforces women's inheritance rights in Pakistan and shows courts will look past technical or informal family arrangements designed to deny women their rightful share of ancestral property.

title: Hamdullah V. Faizullah and 9 others,
explainer:
Hamdullah, the elected Chairman of a Union Council in Killa Saifullah, faced a no-confidence motion moved by two council members. The motion failed to get the required votes. Hamdullah argued that under Section 33 of the Balochistan Local Government Act, 2010, once a no-confidence motion fails, the proposer and seconder automatically lose their council membership. When the Election Commission did not remove them, he approached the Election Tribunal, which rejected his appeal. He then challenged that rejection before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed his appeal too. It found a basic flaw in his approach: the law he relied on (Section 37) allows election results to be challenged only through an election petition filed by an actual candidate in that election. Hamdullah was not contesting an election, so this route did not apply to him. His real complaint was about a no-confidence vote, governed by a different provision (Section 33), not an election dispute.

The court also noted that the letter Hamdullah relied on to prove the motion had failed did not meet the legal requirements for officially declaring such a result, since it lacked key details, such as who presided over the proceedings and why proper notifications were not sent to authorities as required by law.

The case clarifies that no-confidence disputes and election disputes follow different legal procedures, and one cannot be used to resolve the other.

title: Mushtaq Hussain Khan V. Mir Khan Khetran and another,
explainer:
This case involved a request to move a criminal trial from one district to another due to safety concerns. The applicant, Mushtaq Hussain Khan, was facing trial under a cheque-fraud provision (Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code) in an FIR filed at a police station in Barkhan, Balochistan. He asked the High Court to transfer the case to Quetta, arguing that he lived in Punjab and feared for his life if he had to travel to Barkhan to attend court due to the local law and order situation. He also pointed out that the complainant, though originally from the Barkhan area, actually lived in Islamabad and had filed three other similar complaints there, raising questions about why this particular case was filed in Barkhan.

The complainant and the state opposed the transfer, saying the fear of danger was unproven and speculative.

The High Court sided with the applicant. It held that when deciding transfer requests, courts must take genuine safety concerns seriously rather than dismiss them, especially since the right to a fair trial is protected under Article 10-A of the Constitution. Since the applicant could show real apprehension about attending proceedings in Barkhan, and questions existed about why the case was filed there, the court transferred the trial to a Magistrate's court in Quetta.

This case matters because it reinforces that personal safety concerns and fairness can justify moving a trial to a different location, protecting a person's constitutional right to a fair trial.

title: Sohail Mirza and others V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 7 others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved three employees of the University of Balochistan who were terminated from service in 2015 over alleged irregularities involving examination forms and bank fee challans for a 2014 exam. An inquiry committee had found their explanations unsatisfactory and recommended termination, which the university's Syndicate approved, though the Senate later reduced the punishment to compulsory retirement. The employees challenged this action, arguing they were never properly informed of the specific charges against them, were not issued a final show-cause notice, and were denied the chance to see the evidence or cross-examine witnesses. They also pointed out that no inquiry officer had been formally appointed, and that the affected students had already passed their exams without complaint.

The court agreed with the employees. It held that a fair hearing, including proper notice, access to evidence, and the right to cross-examination, is a basic requirement of due process. Since the university failed to follow its own disciplinary rules in conducting the inquiry, the entire proceeding was flawed and could not justify such a severe punishment. The court ordered the employees reinstated, though they would remain suspended until a fresh, properly conducted inquiry is completed.

This ruling reinforces that public institutions must strictly follow their own disciplinary procedures and give employees genuine opportunities to defend themselves before imposing serious penalties like termination.

The defendants argued that an old, unregistered 1971 family settlement had already resolved ownership, excluding the daughters' claim. The alleged 1971 settlement was unregistered (a legal defect), inconsistent with later revenue entries, and only raised after mutation records were formally updated in the daughters' favor—suggesting it was a fabricated, contradictory defense. The court emphasized that women's inheritance rights are legally protected and cannot be defeated through unsubstantiated or technical claims. The revision petition was dismissed, and the petitioners

title: Divisional Superintendent Pakistan Railways, through Authority/Authorized Officer V. Taj Muhammad Khan,
explainer:
This case involved a legal dispute between Pakistan Railways and a customer, Taj Muhammad Khan, whose silk seed consignment was destroyed in a train fire in 2013. Khan sued for compensation of over six hundred thousand rupees for his lost goods, and both the trial court and the appellate court in Quetta ruled in his favor, ordering Railways to pay.

Pakistan Railways challenged these rulings before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the lawsuit was legally flawed from the start because the Federal Government of Pakistan had not been made a party to the case, as required by law. Under Section 79 of the Civil Procedure Code and Article 174 of the Constitution, suits against the government must formally name the Federation of Pakistan itself, not just a local department or officer.

The High Court agreed with Railways. It found that this was a fundamental legal requirement, not a mere technicality, and that both lower courts had wrongly ignored this defect even though it had been raised. Since a purely legal question like this can be raised at any stage, the High Court set aside both previous judgments and sent the case back to the trial court to be heard afresh, this time with the Federal Government properly included as a party.

This case matters because it reinforces the rule that lawsuits against the government must follow strict procedural requirements, ensuring proper legal representation and preventing decisions made without the right party being involved.

title: Zafar Ali V. Province of Balochistan through Secretary Food and another,
explainer:
This case involved Zafar Ali, who had been appointed as an Assistant Food Controller in 2009. His appointment, along with two others, was challenged in an earlier case, and the Balochistan High Court ruled in 2017 that the appointments were illegal, having resulted from malafide conduct and not genuine test results. Zafar Ali's services were terminated following that ruling. He appealed to the Supreme Court, which dismissed his appeal, and a subsequent review petition was also rejected, making that decision final.

Ali later filed this new petition asking the High Court to order his reinstatement with back pay, arguing he deserved this based on a separate Supreme Court order in an unrelated case. The High Court rejected his request, holding that the matter was already finally decided by both the High Court and the Supreme Court in the earlier litigation. Since his appointment had been conclusively declared illegal, the court had no authority to reach a different conclusion. The petition was barred by the legal principle of res judicata, meaning the same issue between the same parties cannot be relitigated once finally decided. The court also noted that one bench of a High Court cannot overturn or contradict another bench's ruling, and civil proceedings in the High Court follow the Civil Procedure Code's rules, including finality of judgments. The petition was dismissed, reaffirming that courts cannot reopen settled matters.

title: Ghulam Hussain V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Ghulam Hussain, who was stopped at a police checkpoint in Kohlu, Balochistan, while driving a car in which police allegedly found 28 kilograms of charas (hashish) hidden in secret cavities. He was tried under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, convicted, and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine by the trial court. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him. The judges found serious flaws in how the prosecution handled the evidence. Only one gram of sample was taken from each of the 28 packets, and all these tiny samples were then sealed together in a single parcel rather than kept separate—something the court said was not a reliable method for testing. The prosecution also failed to prove who actually carried the sample to the chemical laboratory, could not produce the police storage register (Malkhana), and gave contradictory accounts from different witnesses about who recovered the drugs, where exactly they were found, and who took custody of the evidence.

The court held that when the safe custody and secure transmission of narcotics evidence cannot be proven, that evidence cannot be used to convict someone. Because the prosecution's case was riddled with contradictions and failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, the appeal was allowed and Ghulam Hussain was acquitted. The case highlights how procedural lapses in handling drug evidence can undermine even serious narcotics prosecutions.

title: Project Director University of Loralai and another V. Zarif Khan Hussainzai and Brothers through Managing Director,

Their contracts contained an arbitration clause naming the Vice Chancellor of the University as the sole arbitrator to resolve disputes. When the contractor sought to have the arbitration agreement filed in court, the trial court referred the matter to that named arbitrator. On appeal, the contractor argued the Vice Chancellor was biased against it, citing the termination of its contract and other conduct, and the appellate court agreed, replacing the Vice Chancellor with a different arbitrator, a Technical Advisor from the C&W Department.

The University challenged this substitution before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court held that under the Arbitration Act, 1940, a court cannot simply substitute an arbitrator who was validly named by the parties in their contract. Such a change is only permitted if the arbitrator's authority is formally revoked with the court's permission under Section 5, or if the arbitrator is removed under Section 12 for reasons like failing to act, incapacity, or death. Since none of these formal steps had been taken, and mere apprehension of bias was not sufficient legal ground, the appellate court had no power to replace the named arbitrator on its own.

This case matters because it clarifies that parties' choice of arbitrator in a contract must be respected unless proper legal procedures for removal are followed, reinforcing predictability and party autonomy in arbitration agreements.

title: Imam Bakhsh and 6 others V. Muhammad Siddique,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over land in Balochistan. In 1991, an elderly woman agreed to sell her land to a man for a price that included cash, a tractor, and livestock. He took possession, but a dispute arose because she claimed she never received the promised animals and the tractor was defective. This led to years of proceedings before revenue authorities, and eventually the Supreme Court allowed the buyer to pursue the matter through a civil suit.

The buyer then sued for declaration and specific performance of the sale agreement. Both the trial court and the appellate court ruled in his favor. The sellers appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing the suit was filed too late, well beyond the normal limitation period, and that the time spent in revenue proceedings should not count toward excusing the delay.

The High Court agreed with the sellers. It held that time spent pursuing remedies before revenue authorities does not count as time spent in "another civil proceeding" under the Limitation Act, since revenue authorities are not courts. It also found the buyer failed to prove he actually paid the agreed price, and noted he delayed suing for over four years while the seller was an elderly, illiterate woman out of possession. Since specific performance is an equitable remedy, the court ruled the buyer did not deserve it. The High Court therefore overturned the lower courts' decisions and dismissed the buyer's case, emphasizing that unreasonable delay and unclean hands defeat claims for equitable relief.

title: Faiz Muhammad V. Province of Balochisan through Chief Secretary, Civil Secretariat, Quetta and others,
explainer:
Faiz Muhammad joined the Social Welfare Department in 1992 and was later promoted to Deputy Director (B-18) in 2016. The department planned to upgrade his specific post to Director (B-19), and an Up-gradation Committee recommended this. However, the Provincial Cabinet deferred the decision in October 2020. He filed a petition asking the court to overturn that deferral, and also challenged a 2019 notification that had posted another official (respondent No. 5) to a different Director-level post, alleging that official had interfered with his case.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition on two grounds. First, it held that up-gradation of a post is legally different from promotion of a person—up-gradation is meant to address structural issues like restructuring a department or relieving stagnation in an isolated post, not to benefit one specific individual. Since the petitioner's case was personal to him rather than part of a broader policy applied across a category of employees, it did not meet the legal requirements for up-gradation, regardless of the committee's recommendation. Second, regarding the challenge to the 2019 posting notification, the court found the petitioner had waited three to four years to contest it without any explanation, so the claim was barred by unreasonable delay (laches).

This case reaffirms that government employees cannot demand upgrading of their posts as a personal right and must challenge administrative decisions promptly.

title: Fehmida Kiran V. Chairman House Allotment Committee/ Secretary S&GAD and 2 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over a government house in Quetta. Fehmida Kiran had been allotted a house that respondent No. 3 claimed had already been allotted to him earlier by the Chairman of the House Allotment Committee. He filed a civil suit seeking a declaration that he was the lawful allottee, along with an injunction against his eviction.

During the trial, evidence was recorded from multiple witnesses. However, midway through the proceedings, Fehmida Kiran asked the court to first decide whether the suit was even legally maintainable, arguing that the respondent should have used an appeal process available under special housing allotment rules instead of going to civil court. The trial court agreed and dismissed the suit for this reason, even though it had already recorded substantial evidence and had earlier twice refused to reject the case on similar grounds.

The respondent appealed, and the appellate court sent the case back for a full decision on its merits. Fehmida Kiran then challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision. It held that once a court starts recording evidence, it should not switch back to deciding technical questions about maintainability, since factual and mixed legal-factual questions require evidence to be properly examined. It also reaffirmed that civil courts retain jurisdiction to hear cases where a public authority's action is alleged to be illegal, mala fide, or without jurisdiction, despite the existence of alternate remedies. The revision petition was dismissed, meaning the case will now proceed to a full trial on its merits

title: Zakaullah and 6 others V. Ghazi Khan and 3 others,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court, dealt with two related civil revision petitions.

The first involved a father who sued his in-laws' family for return of Rs. 1,800,000, claiming he had paid this amount as dowry-related expenses when his three sons married three sisters from the defendants' family. The marriages (Nikah) were performed, but the "Rukhsati" (formal sending of the brides to their husbands' home) never took place, and years later the plaintiff demanded his money back when the marriage did not proceed. The trial court had ruled in his favor, but the appellate court reversed this decision and dismissed the suit. The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision, noting that earlier Family Court judgments showed no money had actually been paid for dower, maintenance, or dowry articles. The High Court found the plaintiff had pursued a false and vexatious claim in bad faith, dragging the defendants through unnecessary litigation, and imposed Rs. 200,000 in special compensatory costs against him under Section 35-A of the Civil Procedure Code.

The second case concerned a separate dispute over an arbitration award involving immovable property. The High Court ruled that since the award was never registered as legally required, it could not be enforced as a court order, and set aside the lower appellate court's decision confirming it, since that court had exceeded its jurisdiction.

The judgment highlights that courts can penalize litigants who bring bad-faith claims, and that unregistered arbitration awards involving property cannot be legally enforced.

title: Bibi Ayesha V. Muhammad Akbar and others,
explainer:
This case is about what happens when a party fails to appear or submit required documents in court, and how that failure should be legally treated. Bibi Ayesha's civil suit was dismissed by the trial court because she repeatedly failed to submit her list of witnesses on the scheduled dates. The trial court dismissed the case citing Order XVII, Rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code, a provision meant for situations where a party fails to produce evidence and the court decides the case on its merits. This dismissal was upheld on appeal.

The High Court found this was legally wrong. Since no evidence had actually been presented or examined, the trial court could not have decided the case "on merits" under Rule 3. Instead, the situation should have been treated as a simple failure to prosecute the case, governed by different provisions (Order XVII, Rule 2 and Order IX, Rule 8), which are not appealable but can be remedied by applying to restore the suit. The court also ruled that the date fixed only for filing a witness list was not a "hearing," making the dismissal void, and that the appellate court had wrongly exercised jurisdiction over a non-appealable order.

The High Court partly allowed the revision petition, set aside the appellate court's decision, and gave Bibi Ayesha the opportunity to apply for restoration of her original suit. The case clarifies the correct legal category for such dismissals and protects litigants from losing cases on technical, non-merits grounds.

title: Javed Iqbal V. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary Communication, Civil Secretariat, Islamabad and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved Javed Iqbal, an employee of the National Highway Authority (NHA), who challenged his transfer order in the Balochistan High Court. He had been posted as Deputy Director (Maintenance) at Ormara in September 2021, but just eight months later, in May 2022, he was transferred again to a different post in Karachi. He argued this violated NHA's own service regulations, particularly one requiring officers to normally serve three years at a post, and another requiring employees aged 57 or above to be posted near their hometown rather than being frequently transferred.

The NHA argued that transfers were purely administrative matters and that the petitioner had actually committed misconduct by not handing over charge promptly.

The court ruled in favor of the petitioner. It found that the transfer order gave no special reasons justifying why the normal rules were bypassed, and that under the General Clauses Act, government orders must be reasoned, not arbitrary. The judges held that moving an officer after only eight months, without justification, effectively amounted to punishment, wasted public resources, and reflected poor governance. Since the petitioner was 57 and nearing retirement, the transfer also violated the rule protecting older employees from frequent relocation. The court declared the transfer notification illegal and of no legal effect, allowing the petition. This case reinforces that transfer powers, even discretionary ones, must be exercised reasonably and with recorded justification.

title: Shahzad Khan and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Shahzad Khan and Muhammad Ali, who were caught allegedly transporting 170 kilograms of charas (cannabis resin) in a car. A trial court in Sibi convicted them under narcotics law and sentenced them to life imprisonment plus fines. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted both men, finding serious flaws in how the prosecution handled the case. Key problems included: the investigating officer never actually visited the recovery site or prepared the sealed evidence packets himself; the official in charge of storing the evidence gave his statement 21 days late with no explanation; witnesses gave contradictory accounts about who received custody of the drugs and when; there was an unexplained gap of several days where nobody could say who held the drugs before they were sent for testing; and the case papers never even specified which of the two accused was actually driving the car, making it impossible to prove either man knowingly possessed the drugs. The court also noted the chemical report described the substance as raw cannabis resin, not the smokable "baked" form, and that a government official present during the arrest was never called as a witness.

The court emphasized that prosecutors must prove an unbroken, secure chain of custody for narcotics evidence from seizure to laboratory testing. Because that chain was broken here, and the investigation was conducted unprofessionally, the evidence could not support a conviction, so the appeal was allowed and the men were acquitted.

title: Abdul Khaliq V. The State,
explainer:
Abdul Khaliq was arrested after a vehicle he was driving overturned and levies personnel allegedly found 70 packets of Charas (a narcotic) hidden beneath the seats. He was charged under section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, which covers large-quantity narcotics offences carrying punishment ranging from 14 years to death. The trial court had refused him bail. He approached the Balochistan High Court seeking bail, arguing that laboratory reports from the Forensic Science Laboratory had found that the seized substance did not actually contain any narcotic or psychotropic drug.

The High Court first clarified the law on bail in narcotics cases: bail is completely barred only when an offence is exclusively punishable by death. Since section 9(c) allows punishment ranging from 14 years' imprisonment up to death, bail is not automatically barred, though it remains difficult to obtain. Turning to the facts, the court noted that seven forensic reports consistently found the seized material was not identified as hashish and contained no narcotic substance at all. Given this scientific evidence undermining the core allegation, and the principle that bail should not be used as punishment and that benefit of doubt can be extended even at the bail stage, the court found grounds to grant bail. This case illustrates how forensic evidence contradicting the prosecution's narcotics allegation can be decisive in securing bail, even in serious drug cases.

title: Ali Haider and another V. The State,
explainer:
Ali Haider and Fateh Muhammad were convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Sibi for the murder of a coal mine worker, Noor Ali, who was shot during an incident in November 2018. They were sentenced to life imprisonment and fined. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the convictions and acquitted both men, finding the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The court identified several serious flaws in the evidence. The accused were strangers to the complainant and witnesses, yet no physical description of them was given in the initial police report, making the later identification parade unreliable. There was also an unexplained one-month delay between the accused's arrest and the identification parade, and the accused and witnesses were kept at the same police station beforehand, meaning witnesses may have seen the accused before the formal identification. The magistrate conducting the identification parade also failed to follow proper procedure, such as recording details of everyone in the lineup. Additionally, recovered weapons and bullet casings were not sent separately for forensic testing, the weapon was found in a public flood channel rather than somewhere exclusively controlled by the accused, and its recovery came over two months after the crime, further undermining its reliability.

This case matters because it reinforces strict standards for identification evidence and physical evidence in serious criminal cases, showing that convictions cannot stand on procedurally flawed or unreliable evidence, even in terrorism-related murder cases.

title: Messrs Sabir Traders Sole Proprietorship and another V. National Bank of Pakistan through Manager,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between borrowers, Sabir Traders and its owner, and the National Bank of Pakistan over an unpaid loan. The bank had sued the borrowers for recovery of over 73 lakh rupees, and the Banking Court at Dera Allah Yar ruled in the bank's favor, ordering repayment. The borrowers appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing they were never properly heard before the decision was made against them and that they only later learned about the case.

However, the High Court found that the appeal itself was filed too late. Under the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001, appeals must be filed within 30 days, but the borrowers filed theirs 12 days after this deadline. They asked the court to excuse the delay under the general Limitation Act, claiming they hadn't known about the judgment, but the court found this claim false, since records showed they had received a certified copy of the judgment well within the appeal period.

The court also ruled that the general Limitation Act's provision allowing delay to be excused does not apply here, because the special law governing bank recovery cases has its own strict, independent timeline. Additionally, the borrowers failed to give the bank advance notice of their appeal, another mandatory legal requirement they ignored.

Because of these failures, the High Court dismissed the appeal without examining its merits. This case illustrates how strict deadlines under special banking recovery laws override the more flexible general limitation rules, and how failing to meet procedural requirements can prevent a case from even being heard

title: Muhibullah and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against convictions for murder and robbery. The accused were charged with shooting the complainant's brother during a robbery and were convicted under Pakistan's Penal Code. The Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence and found serious flaws in the prosecution's case.

The court identified multiple problems: the identification parade of the accused was held eight days after their arrest, an unexplained delay that undermined its reliability, especially since it took place at the police station where the accused were already in custody. The witnesses had not described distinguishing physical features of the accused beforehand, further weakening this evidence. A recovered mobile phone allegedly belonging to the victim was never properly identified by witnesses, and its unique identification number was not verified. A pistol recovered from the accused did not match forensic tests with the bullet casing found at the scene, and even where a later match was claimed, there was an unexplained seven-day delay in sending items for forensic analysis. A recovered motorcycle was based on an inadmissible confession made to police. The prosecution also withheld a witness whose earlier statement suggested the actual shooter's face was muffled, which the court said implied unfavorable evidence was being concealed.

Given these cumulative weaknesses, the court ruled the prosecution had failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It allowed the appeals and acquitted the accused, reinforcing the principle that identification parades are weak evidence and convictions cannot rest on unreliable recoveries or delayed forensic procedures.

title: Aftab Ashraf V. Khursheed Ashraf and others,
explainer:
This case involved a decades-long family property dispute in Quetta, going back to 1993, between siblings over a jointly owned piece of land. Earlier litigation had already established, all the way up to the Supreme Court, that the property was jointly owned and had to be divided according to specific shares. Despite this, the case kept returning to court because the losing party resisted implementing the partition and later filed a fresh suit, which was also fought over technicalities like res judicata (whether the matter had already been legally settled).

In the present round, the defendant (petitioner) was accused of deliberately delaying proceedings, particularly by refusing to cross-examine the plaintiff, who had to travel from abroad to testify. When the trial court restored his right to cross-examine on condition he pay the plaintiff's travel expenses, he still failed to do so, and also failed to present his remaining evidence despite many adjournments. Both the trial court and the first appellate court ruled against him, ordering partition of the property.

The High Court, reviewing the case, refused to interfere with these decisions, finding them well-reasoned. It held that the property was jointly owned and each party was entitled to their share through formal partition. The court dismissed the petitioner's revision.

This case highlights how courts handle deliberate delay tactics in litigation and reaffirms that previously settled ownership issues cannot be endlessly relitigated.

title: Jameel Ahmed V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary C&W Department Civil Secretariat, Quetta and 6 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a government job reserved for persons with disabilities. Two posts of Sub-Divisional Officer/Assistant Director in Balochistan's Communication and Works Department were advertised under the disabled persons' quota. The petitioner, who had a disability, applied and placed third on the merit list, but the Balochistan Public Service Commission recommended another candidate (respondent No. 7) for the post instead.

The petitioner argued that respondent No. 7 was not actually disabled and had previously declared himself medically fit when applying for a different job, as an Assistant Sub-Inspector in the Police Department, a post he now held after training. The petitioner claimed the disability certificate used to get the quota job was fraudulent.

The Balochistan High Court held that since respondent No. 7 had earlier declared himself medically fit for another job, the legal principle of estoppel prevented him from later claiming disability status to secure the quota post. A person cannot take contradictory positions to suit different situations. The court also ruled that the petitioner, having placed third for two available quota seats, had sufficient standing to challenge the appointment as an "aggrieved person" under Article 199 of the Constitution.

The court allowed the petition, effectively siding with the petitioner. The case matters because it protects the integrity of disability quotas in public employment, preventing able-bodied individuals from wrongly claiming such benefits through inconsistent representations.

title: Abdul Sattar and others V. Abdullah and others,
explainer:
Two sets of buyers claimed rights over the same land in Musakhail, and their competing lawsuits ended up before the Balochistan High Court on appeal.

Group one, Abdul Sattar and another man, said they bought the land from two brothers (the recognized owners) in 2009, paid the full price, took possession, and later got a written contract signed in 2010. A third party, Buzdar, disputed this and claimed the same land through his own separate deal.

Buzdar's claim was that he agreed to buy a half-share in the same property from the same brothers plus other family members, paying part of the price with more due later, and had also taken possession.

The trial court had partly ruled in Buzdar's favor and dismissed Abdul Sattar's suit. Both sides appealed.

The High Court examined the evidence, including how many witnesses signed each contract, as required by law for such documents. It found Abdul Sattar's sale agreement was properly witnessed and proven, and rightly enforceable only against the two brothers who actually owned and had authority to sell their shares - not against female family members who never agreed to the sale.

Crucially, the court found that Buzdar's agreement involved paying partly with money and partly by promising his daughter in marriage - an arrangement it ruled immoral, against public policy, and legally void under the Contract Act. Since the deal illegally mixed lawful and unlawful terms, the whole agreement failed.

Both appeals were dismissed, with Abdul Sattar's original limited victory over the two brothers standing.

title: Naimatullah and others V. Mir Jamal and others,
explainer:
Naimatullah and others v. Mir Jamal and others is a Balochistan High Court civil revision decided in 2022 concerning a dispute over agricultural land in Kharan. The respondents claimed their predecessor had bought the land in 2002 from a woman named Ameer Bibi for Rs.100,000 under a sale contract, and that after her death her son signed a confirmation deed in 2011 acknowledging the sale. When they tried to get the land transferred in revenue records, other family members (the petitioners) objected, claiming ownership through separate mutation entries and documents from 2009. The trial court dismissed the respondents' suit, but the appellate court reversed this and decreed in their favor.

The High Court, however, sided with the petitioners and restored the trial court's dismissal. It held that under the Qanun-e-Shahadat (Pakistan's evidence law), a contract of sale must be proved through two attesting witnesses who confirm they saw the document being signed. Here, the respondents only produced the scribe and one witness, and neither actually testified to witnessing the signing. Since the sale contract was not properly proved, the confirmation deed built on it also failed. The court also noted that a mere sale contract does not itself transfer ownership rights, so a declaratory suit based on it was not even legally maintainable.

This case matters because it reinforces strict evidentiary requirements for proving property sale documents in court, and clarifies that unregistered sale agreements alone cannot establish ownership.

title: Mado Khan V. Talib Jan and another,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Mado Khan, who had lodged a criminal case against Talib Jan and another person after being injured by them. During the criminal proceedings, Mado Khan appeared before the Magistrate and formally stated, under oath, that he had forgiven the accused in the name of Allah, without receiving any compensation. Based on this statement, the accused were acquitted under a compromise provision of criminal law.

Later, Mado Khan filed a separate civil suit claiming that there had actually been an arbitration award requiring the respondents to pay him Rs. 400,000 as compensation and to leave the area, and that they had failed to pay the remaining Rs. 300,000. He sought recovery of this money and their expulsion from the village.

Both the trial court and the appellate court dismissed his suit, and he approached the Balochistan High Court in revision.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It held that Mado Khan's earlier sworn statement before the criminal court, that he had forgiven the respondents unconditionally, was binding on him under the law of evidence (Qanun-e-Shahadat Order). By later claiming compensation was owed, he was contradicting his own prior statement, and the law does not allow such contradiction, a principle known as estoppel. The court also confirmed that findings and statements from criminal proceedings can be legally relevant in civil cases. Since he failed to rebut the presumption of truth attached to his earlier statement, his civil claim could not succeed. The revision petition was dismissed.

title: Mst. Khan Bibi (widow) and 4 others V. Bibi Rahima and 5 others,
explainer:
Mst. Khan Bibi and 4 others V. Bibi Rahima and 5 others, PLD 2023 Balochistan 40, decided by the Balochistan High Court, dealt with a family property dispute after the death of one Pir Muhammad. His legal heirs, including daughters, sought their rightful shares in his estate. While some properties had already been divided among heirs through inheritance mutations, one property was registered only in the names of male heirs (the appellants), excluding the female heirs. The plaintiff, one of the daughters, sued for a declaration of her share, correction of revenue records, partition, possession, and an injunction.

The appellants argued that the female heirs had already been compensated during the father's lifetime through cash and jewelry, and that the father had made an oral will excluding them from that particular property. The trial court rejected this defense and ruled in favor of the plaintiff.

On appeal, the High Court upheld the trial court's decision. It found the oral will unproven because the witnesses' testimony was hearsay and one witness was biased due to personal disputes with the plaintiff's family. The court also held that even if the father had given gifts to his daughters during his lifetime, this did not extinguish their legal right to inherit their share after his death, since inheritance rights arise only upon death, not before.

This case reaffirms that oral wills must be proven through direct, credible evidence, and that lifetime gifts to heirs cannot be used to deny them their rightful inheritance shares.

title: Abdul Ghaffar V. The State,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and involves Abdul Ghaffar, who was convicted by a trial court for possessing 1000 grams of charas (hashish) under Pakistan's narcotics law, and sentenced to ten months in prison plus a fine. He appealed his conviction.

The police claimed they found him walking suspiciously near a road, searched him, and recovered the drugs from his trousers. A sample was sent for chemical testing, and the prosecution presented several witnesses, including the officer in charge of the police station's storeroom where the seized drugs were kept before being sent for testing.

The defense argued two main points: that there was an unexplained delay in sending the sample to the lab, and that the prosecution failed to prove the drugs were safely and reliably stored throughout the process. The court rejected the delay argument, ruling that the 72-hour rule for sending samples for testing is a guideline, not a strict requirement, and any delay here was reasonably explained by holidays.

However, the court agreed with the second argument. The storeroom officer testified he logged the evidence in a register, but the prosecution never actually produced that register in court, nor did the investigating officer collect a copy of it. This gap meant there was no solid proof the drugs were properly secured and not tampered with between seizure and testing.

Because this broke the "chain of custody," the court found reasonable doubt in the case and overturned the conviction, acquitting the appellant. The case highlights how gaps in evidence handling can undermine even seemingly strong prosecution cases.

title: Mir Hammal V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Mir Hammal who was convicted by a special narcotics court in Turbat for transporting four kilograms of charas (hashish), allegedly found in a bag on his motorcycle during a police checkpoint stop. He was sentenced to four years in prison and a fine, and the trial court also denied him credit for time already spent in custody, citing a prior conviction.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction. It found serious flaws in how the prosecution handled evidence. First, the police failed to produce the official Store Room Register that would have proven the seized drugs were kept safely and without tampering, even though a witness referred to such an entry. Courts require the actual document, not just verbal claims about it. Second, there were unexplained contradictions and a 23-day delay in recording witness statements, plus an unexplained change in testimony about which sealed parcel was handed over, raising doubts about the evidence's reliability. Third, the trial court wrongly used the appellant's alleged bad character (a previous conviction) against him, even though he hadn't presented any evidence of good character, which the law says is required before bad character can even be considered.

Because of these lapses in following proper evidence and procedure rules, the High Court ruled the conviction unsafe and acquitted the appellant, highlighting how strict evidentiary standards protect the accused from wrongful convictions in narcotics cases.

title: Muhammad Alam V. Malik Zahoor Ahmed and another,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running property dispute in Quetta between Muhammad Alam and Malik Zahoor Ahmed. Zahoor Ahmed had sued Alam for encroaching on his land, and Alam claimed the mutation document supporting the claim was forged. Over the years, Alam repeatedly sought transfer of both the main civil suit and a related revision petition from one court to another, alleging bias against the judges handling his case. The District Judge, Quetta rejected his transfer applications, and Alam challenged those rejections before the Balochistan High Court through two civil revision petitions.

The High Court dismissed both petitions, finding that Alam had acted in bad faith. It noted that he had repeatedly changed lawyers, delayed proceedings, and made unfounded, baseless allegations against judicial officers without genuine justification. The court held that transferring a case away from a competent court is only warranted where there is a real and reasonable apprehension of bias, not merely dissatisfaction with how proceedings are going. It emphasized that courts have a duty to discourage litigants from misusing transfer applications, adjournment requests, and frequent changes of counsel as delaying tactics, since allowing such practices undermines the justice system's ability to function.

This judgment matters because it reinforces an important principle: parties cannot manipulate the legal process through repeated, meritless transfer applications and baseless accusations against judges to stall proceedings, and courts must be vigilant in preventing such abuse to ensure timely justice.

title: Muhammad Alam V. Malik Zahoor Ahmed and another,
explainer:
This case is about a long-running property dispute in Quetta where a tenant/defendant, Muhammad Alam, repeatedly tried to have his case moved between different courts. The original suit, filed in 2012 by Malik Zahoor Ahmed, concerned an alleged encroachment on land, with Alam claiming the mutation document supporting the claim was forged.

Over eleven years, Alam filed numerous applications, including requests to transfer the case away from certain judges, arguing bias and procedural unfairness. Alam challenged these rejections before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the record and found that Alam had used delaying tactics for over a decade, including repeated adjournment requests, transfer applications, and frequent changes of lawyers, all while the case remained stuck at the trial stage. The court found no genuine bias by the trial judge and noted that the case had already been shifted between multiple courts at Alam's own request in the past.

The High Court refused to interfere with the lower court's decision, dismissed both revision petitions, and imposed exemplary costs on Alam. The judgment emphasizes that courts must guard against litigants misusing procedural applications to stall justice, since such practices undermine the judiciary's constitutional duty to deliver timely justice.

title: Abdul Aziz V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about the murder of Muhammad Kareem, who was shot on 11 May 2022 in Sanni, Balochistan. His brother, Abdul Aziz, filed a police report naming Abdul Aziz (the appellant, a different person with the same name) and several others as the assailants, alleging the killing was linked to a family feud (siahkari). The trial court convicted the appellant and sentenced him to life imprisonment plus a fine, based on the testimony of the complainant and other witnesses along with medical and circumstantial evidence.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction. The judges found serious problems with the prosecution's case: the complainant admitted he did not actually see the appellant firing at his brother, only saw him holding a weapon after hearing shots. The medical report showed a single bullet wound, contradicting the claim that six armed men had fired repeatedly. The complainant's conduct was also suspicious, he claimed to have taken his dying brother to the hospital, yet his name was missing from hospital records, and he wasn't seen there by any witness. The court concluded the complainant likely wasn't present at the actual shooting and had exaggerated his account.

Applying the principle that any reasonable doubt must benefit the accused, and citing the maxim that it is better to acquit ten guilty people than convict one innocent person, the court acquitted the appellant. This case highlights how courts scrutinize eyewitness credibility and forensic consistency before upholding serious convictions.

title: Shabbir Ahmad V. The State,
explainer:
Shabbir Ahmad was convicted by a trial court in Sibi for the murder of two people, Gul Muhammad and his son Mazar Khan, who were shot while riding motorcycles. He was sentenced to life imprisonment on two counts, running consecutively, and ordered to pay compensation. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction. It found major flaws in the prosecution's case. The pistol allegedly used was not actually recovered from the appellant's possession, and no one established who it really belonged to. A key prosecution witness admitted police had never recorded his statement, so that evidence was discarded. The trial court had relied heavily on a video where the appellant supposedly confessed to police, but confessions made to police are not admissible as evidence under the law. Simply being arrested at the crime scene while injured did not prove guilt, especially since the shooting happened in a crowded, open market where anyone could have been present. The court also noted the FIR was filed nearly 14 and a half hours after the incident, with no explanation for the delay, and the investigation had actually started before the FIR was even lodged, raising serious doubts about the case's credibility.

Because the prosecution failed to prove the appellant's involvement beyond reasonable doubt, the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction. This case underscores that confessions to police cannot be used against an accused, and unexplained delays in filing a criminal complaint can seriously undermine a prosecution's credibility.

title: Naveed Ahmed V. Family Judge, Panjgur and another,
explainer:
This case involved a family court dispute in Panjgur, Balochistan. A woman had earlier won a court case against her husband for recovery of dower and maintenance allowance, and this decision was upheld through the courts. When she sought to enforce the decree, the Family Court ordered the husband to pay the market value of gold, past and future maintenance in monthly installments, and a share of fruit trees as dower.

The husband did not appeal this enforcement order through the normal legal channel. Instead, he went straight to the High Court, arguing that the payment installments set by the court were too high given his limited income and family responsibilities.

The High Court refused to hear the case on its merits. It ruled that the order being challenged was a final decision under the Family Courts Act, 1964, not a temporary or interim order, and that the law provides a specific right of appeal to the District Court for such decisions. Since this alternate remedy existed and was adequate, the husband was legally required to use it before approaching the High Court under its special constitutional powers.

The court emphasized that constitutional jurisdiction should not be used as a shortcut when a proper legal forum, created specifically to handle such disputes, is available. Bypassing that process undermines the purpose of specialized courts and overburdens the High Court. The petition was dismissed, meaning the husband must pursue his appeal before the District Court instead.

title: Ghulam Nabi V. The State,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and involves a bail application by Ghulam Nabi, who was accused in a criminal case arising from a violent incident in which his father was killed and he himself was injured. The incident led to two competing versions of events, a cross-version FIR, meaning both sides accused each other of starting the violence. Ghulam Nabi was named in a case filed by the family of the men who died on the other side, while he and his family had filed their own case against that same complainant for killing his father.

The court noted that the investigation concluded both parties should face trial, and that key facts, such as how the accused's father died and how the accused was injured, remained unexplained by the complainant. The judge found that it was not possible, at this early stage, to determine who was the real aggressor without a full trial and detailed evidence. Since no specific role or weapon was attributed to Ghulam Nabi, and nothing was recovered from him, the court held that keeping him in custody served no purpose.

The court granted him bail, relying on the legal principle that in cross-version cases, where both sides blame each other for the same incident, bail can be granted on the ground of further inquiry, since deciding who is truly at fault requires deeper examination of evidence that only a full trial can provide.

title: Bismillah and 2 others V. Naik Muhammad through Legal Heirs,
explainer:
This case is about a civil dispute over land in Quetta, where Naik Muhammad and others (later represented by their legal heirs) sued Bismillah and two others, claiming ownership and possession of certain property and asking the court to stop the defendants from interfering with it.

During the case, after their witnesses had already testified and an attempt to amend their claim was rejected, the plaintiffs asked the trial court for permission to withdraw the suit conditionally, meaning they wanted the right to file a fresh case later. Their stated reason was that they lacked certain documents relating to the property. Both the trial court and the appellate court allowed this withdrawal.

The defendants challenged this before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that simply lacking documents does not qualify as a formal defect or sufficient ground under the law (Order XXIII, Rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Code) required to permit conditional withdrawal with the right to sue again. They also argued that missing documents could have been produced later under other procedural rules, and that both lower courts had given only brief, unreasoned orders without properly examining the law.

The High Court agreed with the defendants. It held that the lower courts failed to apply their minds to the facts and law, and that this amounted to a jurisdictional error, not just a technical mistake. As a result, the High Court set aside both orders and rejected the plaintiffs' application for withdrawal, allowing the original suit to continue. This case highlights that courts must give proper legal reasoning before permitting withdrawal of a suit with the right to refile.

title: Mst. Malala Bibi V. Inspector General of Police, Balochistan, Quetta and another,
explainer:
This case is about whether a widow could claim compensation under a government policy that came into effect after her husband had already died. Malala Bibi's husband, a Deputy Superintendent of Police, died on 2 June 2020 from Covid-19 while in service. The Balochistan government later introduced the Civil Servants' and Employees' Benefits and Death Compensation Policy on 11 August 2020, offering financial packages to families of employees who died in service. The petitioner argued she was entitled to Rs. 10 million under this policy and that a later letter cutting her compensation to Rs. 1 million was illegal and discriminatory, since another officer's widow had received the full Rs. 10 million.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed her petition. It held that the policy was prospective, meaning it only applied to deaths occurring after it was issued on 11 August 2020. Since her husband died before that date, no right to compensation had accrued to her under the policy, and she could not be treated as an "aggrieved person" entitled to constitutional relief. The court relied on Supreme Court precedents establishing that government notifications and policies generally operate forward in time unless clearly stated otherwise.

This case matters because it clarifies that welfare or compensation policies cannot automatically be applied retroactively to benefit people whose claims arose before the policy existed, even in sympathetic circumstances like a Covid-19 death during government service.

title: Babar Ali and another V. Muhammad Iqbal and 2 others,
explainer:
Two people, Babar Ali and Ahmed, filed an appeal after the men accused of shooting at them and their relatives were acquitted by a trial court. The original case involved allegations that four men on motorcycles opened fire on the complainant's car, injuring the complainant's brother and cousin, leading to charges under sections dealing with attempted murder and property damage.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the acquittal, dismissing the appeal. The court found several serious flaws in the prosecution's case. First, there was an unexplained delay of more than 48 hours in registering the police report (FIR), which raised doubts about the reliability of the allegations. Second, the accused were only identified by the complainant and witnesses at the police station, eleven days after the incident, without a proper identification parade, and there was no claim that the accused were previously known to the witnesses, making this identification legally worthless. Third, police investigators had begun investigating and collecting evidence before the FIR was even officially registered, which the court called a material illegality. Finally, there was an unexplained 18-day delay in sending the weapon and bullet casings for forensic testing, and they were sent together in a way that undermined their reliability as evidence.

Given all these lapses, the court ruled the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The judgment reinforces the principle that acquitted persons enjoy a "double presumption of innocence," making it harder to overturn such acquittals on appeal.

title: Ali Murad Pirkani and others V. Abdul Malik and others,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute between landlords and the family of a deceased tenant over agricultural land in Balochistan. The tenant's heirs claimed they had inherited his tenancy, continued farming the land and sharing crops with the landlords, but were forcibly and unlawfully dispossessed. They sued in a civil court seeking declaration of their tenancy rights, restoration of possession, and an injunction. The landlords argued that civil courts had no power to hear such a case, since the Balochistan Tenancy Ordinance, 1978 gives Revenue Courts exclusive jurisdiction over disputes about tenants being wrongfully dispossessed. The trial court agreed and rejected the plaint, but the appellate court reversed this, reasoning that since the landlords denied any landlord-tenant relationship, an ordinary civil court could hear the matter.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed with the appellate court. It held that the law clearly and expressly bars civil courts from hearing suits by tenants seeking restoration of possession; such matters must go to the Revenue Court, regardless of whether the landlord disputes the tenancy relationship. However, the court found the trial court used the wrong procedural route by rejecting the plaint outright; instead, it should have simply returned the plaint so it could be refiled in the correct forum, the Revenue Court.

The ruling clarifies that tenancy possession disputes under this law must go through Revenue Courts, not civil courts, ensuring cases are decided in the proper legal forum.
