title: State through Prosecutor General Accountability, NAB V. Nisar Hussain Shah and another,
explainer:
This case involved a former government official, Nisar Hussain Shah, who served as Director General Livestock and had earlier worked as a superintendent at a sheep farm. The National Accountability Bureau (NAB) accused him of amassing extensive properties in Lahore, Quetta, Loralai and Ziarat, plus large unexplained bank deposits, all allegedly beyond what his known income could support, and of using his family members and son to hold some of these assets. The Accountability Court in Quetta tried him under the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999, but acquitted him after hearing seventeen prosecution witnesses and four defense witnesses. NAB then appealed the acquittal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the acquittal. It reasoned that while owning unexplained assets shifts some burden onto the accused to explain them, the prosecution still bears responsibility for proving that the explanations given were false or inconsistent with the properties. The court found that NAB's investigators had failed to properly investigate the accused's defense and had not adequately established that his claimed sources of income were illegitimate. The court also emphasized that appellate courts should be very cautious about overturning acquittals, since an acquitted person enjoys a doubled presumption of innocence. Because the investigation was flawed and the prosecution had not discharged its burden, the High Court dismissed the appeal, meaning the acquittal stood. This case highlights how weak investigation can undermine even serious corruption cases.

title: Naimatullah and 11 others V. Faizullah and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute between two families in Zhob, Balochistan. The respondents claimed a piece of land was their ancestral property based on old land records from 1952, and alleged the petitioners were trying to forcibly take possession. They sued for declaration and permanent injunction in the Qazi's Court, a special court set up under the Balochistan Civil Disputes (Shariat Application) Regulation, 1976, which applied to tribal areas. The trial court ruled in favor of the respondents, and an appellate body called the Majlis-e-Shoora upheld that decision.

The petitioners challenged this in the Balochistan High Court, arguing the appellate court's judgment was flawed because it failed to properly identify and address the key legal points in dispute, as required under procedural law, and did not give clear reasons for its decision despite receiving a detailed site inspection report.

The High Court agreed that the appellate judgment was legally defective for not following proper procedure. More importantly, it found a bigger problem: the Regulation under which these special courts operated was created using constitutional powers tied to Pakistan's tribal areas. Since the 25th Constitutional Amendment abolished that tribal status, those courts no longer had legal authority to exist. The High Court had already ordered that pending cases from such courts be transferred to ordinary civil courts. Therefore, it set aside the appellate judgment and sent the case back for fresh decision by the proper ordinary court.

title: Muhammad Ismail Muhammad Shai V. Hon'ble Chief Justice Balochistan, through Registrar and others,
explainer:
This case involved a judicial officer who claimed he was unfairly passed over for promotion in 2011 and 2014, while junior colleagues were promoted ahead of him. He argued he was never told why he was superseded and that there was nothing against him in his service record.

He first challenged this before the Balochistan Subordinate Judiciary Service Tribunal, which dismissed his appeals. He then went to the Supreme Court, which also dismissed his case but noted that if his promotion claim had merit and hadn't been properly examined, he could try filing a constitutional petition in the High Court.

He then filed these constitutional petitions before the Balochistan High Court, asking the court to grant him promotion and seniority retroactively, ahead of the colleagues who had been promoted instead of him.

The High Court dismissed the petitions. It held that administrative decisions of the Chief Justice or the High Court, such as promotion matters, are not fully shielded from constitutional review, but disputes about seniority and antedated promotion cannot be resolved through a writ petition under Article 199 of the Constitution. It also noted that the High Court had already expressed its view on the matter earlier and could not revisit it in a fresh petition.

The case matters because it clarifies the limits of constitutional court intervention in internal promotion and seniority disputes within the judiciary, reinforcing that such administrative matters are not ordinarily subject to writ jurisdiction.

title: Saira Atta V. The Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and others,
explainer:
This case was about whether the Balochistan government could re-employ retired officers, including one particular officer, on contract or ad hoc basis against government posts. The petitioner, a qualified civil servant, argued that such re-employment was illegal because it blocked promotion opportunities for serving officers, violated Supreme Court guidelines set out in a 2013 judgment, and did not follow proper procedure or rules under the Balochistan Civil Servants Act, 1974.

By the time the case was heard, the government explained that the contract of the retired officer in question had already expired, and the post created for him had been abolished, so that specific grievance became moot.

However, the High Court still addressed the broader legal question. It held that re-employing retired civil servants must strictly follow Section 14 of the Balochistan Civil Servants Act, 1974, and related official instructions, which carry the force of law. The court emphasized that re-employment against sanctioned posts is problematic because it blocks junior officers waiting for promotion and disturbs their seniority. Such re-employment should only occur in the public interest and in exceptional cases, without blocking promotion rights. The court directed the government to avoid such appointments going forward and, where genuinely necessary, to follow the Supreme Court's guidelines carefully. The petition was disposed of with these directions, reinforcing protections for serving civil servants' promotion rights.

title: Messrs S.Q. Corporation through Proprietor and others V. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary Internal Affairs, Government of Pakistan, Islamabad and others,
explainer:
This case involved a business, S.Q. Corporation, that had taken finance facilities from a bank and fell into default on a large outstanding amount. The bank filed a recovery suit in court and also lodged a complaint with the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) alleging wilful default, a criminal offence under the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001. The FIA began an inquiry and issued notices to the petitioners even while the civil recovery suit was still pending before the High Court.

The petitioners argued that criminal proceedings for wilful default cannot begin until a civil court has actually determined the amount of default and fixed liability. They said the FIA's inquiry was premature and illegal, especially since an earlier, related inquiry had already been closed and was allegedly being revived through a renumbered "corrigendum."

The Balochistan High Court agreed that while the FIA does have legal power to investigate complaints of wilful default under the 2018 Rules, such a complaint can only be filed after civil liability has been properly established through the pending recovery suit. Since the bank's complaint was filed before that liability was fixed, it was premature. The court quashed the complaint and notices, but clarified the bank could file a fresh complaint once the civil suit is decided and default liability is confirmed. This ruling reinforces that criminal wilful-default proceedings must follow, not precede, civil determination of debt liability.

title: Muhammad Sajid Tareen V The Govt. of Balochistan through Chief Secretary Balochistan & others,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court in 2021, dealt with the systematic exclusion of women from inheriting property during land settlement and mutation processes across the province. The petitioner brought to the court's attention that when land records were being settled, properties were often mutated only in the names of male family members, while female heirs' names were left out because revenue authorities were not making efforts to identify or include them.

The government's own response confirmed there was no proper mechanism to ensure women's inclusion before settlement. The court found that simply publishing notices in newspapers was inadequate, especially in remote areas where women often lack access to newspapers or cannot read them.

The court ruled that women's inheritance rights are protected under Islamic law and cannot be denied. It declared that any mutation or settlement excluding female heirs would be null and void, even without going to civil court. Women also could not be deprived of their share through gift deeds, relinquishments, or other pressures.

To fix this, the court ordered concrete measures: using NADRA records to verify family trees, distributing information through schools, hospitals, mosques, and loudspeaker announcements, setting up complaint cells, registering criminal cases against violators, and setting strict deadlines for deciding inheritance-related court cases. This judgment matters because it created enforceable safeguards to protect women's legal inheritance rights, which had long been ignored in practice despite existing law.

title: Saif Ud Din V. Muhi Ud Din and another,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with when police can be directed to register a criminal case (FIR) through an "ex-officio Justice of Peace" -- a role performed by a Sessions Judge under section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The petitioner, Saif Ud Din, challenged an order by the Sessions Judge/Justice of Peace directing police to register an FIR against him based on a complaint by Muhi Ud Din. The petitioner argued that the alleged incident, supported by a medical certificate showing only minor bruises and scratches, did not amount to a cognizable offence (one serious enough for police to investigate and arrest without court permission).

The High Court agreed. It clarified that a Justice of Peace can only order registration of an FIR when the complaint discloses a cognizable offence. For non-cognizable offences, the complainant instead has two other legal routes: asking police to record the matter in the daily diary and seek a magistrate's permission to investigate, or filing a private complaint directly before a magistrate. Since no cognizable offence was made out here, the court quashed both the Justice of Peace's order and the FIR that police had registered.

Separately, the judgment also addressed police delay and confusion in complying with the court's earlier orders, with senior police officials appearing and apologizing for the lapse. The ruling is significant for clarifying the limited powers of a Justice of Peace and protecting individuals from FIRs registered without proper legal basis.

title: Taj-Ud-Din and another V. The State,
explainer:
Two men, Taj-ud-Din and Syed Muhammad, were tried for allegedly abducting a young man, Olas Khan, near Pishin and committing sodomy with him. According to the complainant, Taj-ud-Din offered him a lift, drove him away at gunpoint, and assaulted him; he was then taken back and a second assault allegedly occurred, this time involving the second accused, Syed Muhammad. The trial court convicted both men under section 364-A of the Pakistan Penal Code (kidnapping/abduction) and sentenced them to life imprisonment.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence, including the victim's testimony, medical evidence, and recovered items such as clothing, a pistol, a mobile SIM, and cash. The court found that while the medical and circumstantial evidence supported that sodomy had occurred, the facts did not properly fit the offence of abduction under section 364-A. The court also rejected one accused's police confession as inadmissible, noting that such statements must be accepted entirely or not at all, and could not be selectively relied upon.

The High Court altered the conviction from section 364-A to section 377 (unnatural offence/sodomy) and reduced the sentence from life imprisonment to ten years for both men, while dismissing the appeal otherwise.

This case matters because it clarifies how courts must correctly match proven facts to the appropriate criminal charge, and reinforces that confessions to police cannot be used selectively as evidence.

title: Sui Southern Gas Company Ltd., Regional office and others V. Muhammad Rahim and others,
explainer:
This case involved gas theft allegations against several people accused of illegally tapping Sui Southern Gas Company (SSGC) connections in Quetta. FIRs were registered by the police against the accused under the Gas (Theft Control and Recovery) Act, 2016. However, earlier the Balochistan High Court had quashed these FIRs, holding that offences under this special law are non-cognizable, meaning police cannot register an FIR for them. Instead, the law requires that a complaint be filed directly before the special Gas Utility Court. Following the quashment, the trial court acquitted the accused persons, and SSGC challenged these acquittals through multiple appeals, which were heard together since they raised the same legal question.

The High Court upheld the earlier reasoning: because the Act contains a specific procedure (an overriding "notwithstanding" clause) requiring complaints to go before the Gas Utility Court rather than through police FIRs, registering an FIR under this Act was improper and appeared driven by ulterior motives. The court emphasized that when law prescribes a particular procedure, that procedure must be strictly followed, and citizens have a fundamental right to be treated according to law. Where authorities bypass mandated procedures, the High Court can intervene under its constitutional powers to protect citizens' rights.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that special economic offences like gas theft must follow the specific legal procedure created for them, preventing misuse of ordinary criminal process (FIRs) in matters governed by special statutes.

title: The State through Deputy Attorney General V. Zahid Khan and others,
explainer:
Four people accused of running illegal Hawala/Hundi currency exchange operations, in violation of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947, were acquitted by trial courts in Quetta before their trials were even completed, using an early-acquittal provision (section 265-K, Cr.P.C.). The State, through the Federal Investigation Agency, appealed these acquittals to the Balochistan High Court.

The key issue was that FIRs against the accused were registered by FIA officials based on complaints from State Bank of Pakistan officers, but without the mandatory prior authorization from the Federal Government or the State Bank of Pakistan required under the law before such cases can be initiated. This is not a minor technicality - the law specifically requires this authorization as a safeguard before criminal proceedings can begin.

The High Court held that when a law prescribes a specific mandatory procedure, bypassing it constitutes a serious illegality that violates a citizen's fundamental rights. Since the FIA had not followed the proper legal procedure in lodging these cases, the court ruled that justice demanded the acquittals be upheld, regardless of other considerations. The court cited the principle "justice should prevail no matter if the heaven falls."

As a result, the High Court dismissed the State's appeals and upheld the acquittals in all four cases. The judgment underscores that procedural safeguards built into laws exist to protect citizens' rights, and authorities cannot ignore them even while pursuing valid investigations.

title: Hafiz Zubair and another V. Mst. Hazar Naz (Widow) and 13 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a Hajj and Umrah travel business set up as private limited companies. The original plaintiff, whose heirs later continued the case, claimed he was wrongly removed as a director and denied his 25% share and profits in one of the companies, allegedly through fake documents. He sued for a court declaration recognizing his directorship and share, cancellation of the fraudulent paperwork, and recovery of money owed to him. The trial court ruled in his favor, and an appellate court upheld that decision.

The company directors who lost then challenged the case before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that civil courts had no authority to hear the matter at all. They pointed to the Companies Ordinance, 1984, which states that only the High Court, not ordinary civil courts, can decide disputes about title or shares in a company. They argued the lower courts' judgments were void for lacking proper jurisdiction.

The High Court agreed that this was a serious problem: although the defendants had raised the jurisdiction objection early on, the trial court never formally framed it as a legal issue or decided it before proceeding to judge the rest of the case. Because determining jurisdiction first is essential, the High Court sent the case back to the trial court, directing it to specifically decide the jurisdiction question first, gathering additional evidence on that point if necessary, before proceeding further. This ensures cases are heard by the properly authorized court from the outset.

title: Ajmal and 2 others V. Additional Sessions Judge-IV, Quetta and 4 others,
explainer:
This case is about three men accused of murder and abduction who had been formally discharged from the case by the investigating officer for lack of evidence. Later, after the complainant complained about the investigation and a court ordered the case transferred to the Crimes Branch for fresh investigation, a Judicial Magistrate issued new arrest warrants for the same men and then remanded them to police custody.

The petitioners challenged this, arguing that once a charge sheet (challan) against other accused persons in the same case had already been submitted to the Trial Court (Additional Sessions Judge, Khanozai), that court alone had jurisdiction over the matter. They argued the Judicial Magistrate had no authority to issue fresh warrants or grant remand, since the case was already pending before the Trial Court.

The Balochistan High Court agreed. It held that the discharge order could only be reviewed by the Trial Court that had taken cognizance of the case after the challan was filed. The Judicial Magistrate had no jurisdiction to issue warrants or grant remand because the matter was already sub judice (pending) before the Trial Court. The Court therefore set aside the Magistrate's warrants and remand orders, and allowed the petition.

This matters because it reinforces the principle that once a case is properly before a trial court, other magistrates cannot interfere or issue conflicting orders, protecting the integrity of judicial process and jurisdictional boundaries.

title: Muhammad Saleem and others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved three men convicted by a trial court for the murder and robbery of a person, allegedly acting together to snatch money from the victim, who was then shot dead when he resisted. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court against their convictions and sentences under sections dealing with murder, robbery, and common intention.

The High Court overturned the convictions and acquitted the accused, finding the prosecution's case riddled with serious doubts. First, the sole eyewitness only gave his statement to police 24 days after the incident, with no credible explanation for the delay, making his account unreliable. Second, the witness appeared to have been introduced by the complainant rather than coming forward independently. Third, the police claimed the accused were traced through "spy information" and technology, but provided no actual evidence supporting this claim. Fourth, the identification parade meant to confirm the accused's identity was conducted improperly - inside jail premises while the accused was already under police investigation, and the witness actually failed to identify them correctly. Fifth, the weapon and bullet casing were sent for forensic testing 72 days after the crime, an unexplained delay that undermined the lab report's reliability. Finally, medical evidence wasn't properly corroborated.

The court held that these combined weaknesses meant the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. This case matters because it demonstrates how courts scrutinize procedural lapses - delayed statements, flawed identification parades, and forensic delays - to protect the fundamental principle that guilt must be proven conclusively

title: Ramzan and others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved the murder of the complainant's son, who was allegedly slaughtered with a sharp weapon by several accused acting together. The First Information Report initially named unknown persons, but the complainant later named the accused in a supplementary statement. The prosecution's case largely relied on a confession one accused reportedly made before a jirga (a traditional community assembly), which was video recorded on a mobile phone by the deceased's brother and later handed over as evidence.

The Balochistan High Court found serious problems with how this evidence was handled. The video recording was never actually played in court, the accused were never given a copy or a chance to admit or challenge it, and none of the roughly 200 jirga members who witnessed the alleged confession were called as witnesses to confirm what happened. The court also noted that the investigation was mishandled twice, first by levies and then by the Crimes Branch, causing damaging delays and raising doubts about the evidence collected.

Rather than deciding guilt or innocence, the High Court sent the case back to the trial court with clear instructions: the investigating officer must prepare and provide the accused with a copy of the video, at least two jirga witnesses must be summoned, and the video must be played in court with the accused given a fair chance to cross-examine witnesses. This ruling emphasizes that confessions, even before informal community bodies, must be properly verified and tested in court before being used as evidence of guilt.

title: Muhammad Hassan V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man, Muhammad Hassan, who was convicted of murdering his wife by stabbing her and strangling her with a dupatta. A trial court in Dalbandin sentenced him to life imprisonment, and he appealed to the Balochistan High Court arguing there was no direct evidence against him apart from a confession recorded after his police remand period had ended, which he later retracted.

The High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction. It found that Hassan himself walked into the police station the morning after the killing and voluntarily reported what he had done, even producing the blood-stained knife. The court treated this spontaneous, unprompted statement as reliable because it was made naturally, before any formal investigation began. His guilt was further confirmed by a judicial confession recorded later by a magistrate, who followed proper legal safeguards to ensure it was voluntary. The court explained that even a delayed or later-retracted confession can still support a conviction if it is shown to be true and voluntary. Additionally, medical evidence, including injuries on the body, and forensic recovery of blood-stained items matched the confession and witness accounts.

This case matters because it clarifies how Pakistani courts assess confessions and circumstantial evidence in murder cases, showing that a voluntary, corroborated confession, even if later retracted, can be sufficient to sustain a conviction.

title: Messrs Sara Enterprises Government Contractors through Proprietor V. Secretary Finance, Government of Balochistan, Quetta and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a government contractor who completed an irrigation construction project in 1998 under a work order from a Balochistan government department. Payment was delayed for years, leading the contractor to seek arbitration, which eventually resulted in a court decree in 2018 ordering payment. When the money was finally released in 2019, the government deducted 15 percent as tax under the Balochistan Revenue Authority Act, 2015. The contractor challenged this deduction, arguing that the tax law came into effect in 2015, long after the work was done in 1998, and therefore could not be applied to this old, completed transaction.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the contractor. It held that new laws are generally meant to apply going forward, not backward, unless the law specifically says otherwise. Since the 2015 Act did not state that it applied retrospectively, it could not be used to tax a transaction that had already been completed in 1998. The court emphasized that tax laws, which impose financial burdens, must be interpreted strictly and narrowly, and a taxpayer cannot be made liable unless they clearly fall within the law's scope.

As a result, the court declared the tax deduction illegal and void, and ordered the government to refund the deducted amount to the contractor. This case highlights the important legal principle that laws imposing taxes or liabilities cannot be applied to past events unless clearly intended by lawmakers.

title: Palwasha Sherani and others V. Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC) and others,
explainer:
This case involved medical and dental school hopefuls who failed the 2023 MDCAT (Medical and Dental College Admission Test), which is required for admission to MBBS and BDS programs. The petitioners argued the test was flawed, claiming it was conducted by an unauthorized body instead of the proper provincial authority, that the questions were too difficult and outside the syllabus, and that cheating using electronic devices had occurred during the exam. They asked the Balochistan High Court to cancel the test entirely and order a fresh one, or alternatively let them be admitted using vacant seats.

The respondents, including PMDC and the medical university, countered that the allegations were unsupported by evidence, that a committee had investigated cheating claims but found only a minor leak involving a few questions, and that thousands of students had passed the test fairly. They noted no petitioner had raised objections before taking the exam or used available complaint procedures afterward.

The court dismissed the petitions. It found the petitioners had no real evidence backing their claims, had not objected to the test's difficulty or content beforehand, and had failed to use available remedies before rushing to court. The court also noted that any seats left unfilled would simply carry forward to the next year's admissions based on province-wide merit. This ruling reinforces that courts will not interfere with academic admission processes based on unproven allegations, especially when proper procedural channels were bypassed.

title: Balochistan Bar Council through Vice-Chairman V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary Balochistan, Civil Secretariat and 2 others,
explainer:
This case was about whether a government official's tenure as Member of the Balochistan Environmental Protection Tribunal could legally be extended a second time. The Balochistan Bar Council challenged a notification dated 30 December 2022 that extended the term of respondent No. 3, arguing this violated the Balochistan Environmental Protection Act, 2012 and the Balochistan Environmental Protection Tribunal Rules, 2017, which allow a member's tenure to be extended only once, for three years.

The respondent had originally been appointed Member in 2016, then given what was labeled a fresh "appointment" in 2019 (which the court treated as actually being his one permitted extension), and then extended again in 2022. The Balochistan High Court held that neither the law nor the rules permitted a second extension or any re-appointment beyond the single allowed extension. It found the 2022 extension to be an unlawful, "colourful" exercise of power by the Chief Minister, made by overlooking the relevant law, rules, and official summary. The court declared the second extension null and void from the start, set aside the notification, and ordered the government to formally remove the official from his position.

This matters because it reinforces that government appointments to statutory tribunals must strictly follow the specific rules governing tenure limits, and courts can strike down appointments made in disregard of those legal limits, even when framed as routine extensions.

title: Muhammad Ishaq and others V. Government of Balochistan and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a government employee's transfer on deputation. The petitioners were regular employees of the Metropolitan Corporation Quetta (MCQ), appointed in 2007, working in BPS-17 and BPS-18 positions. They challenged a September 2024 notification that placed Respondent No. 6 on deputation to MCQ for three years, along with a related order assigning him specific zones as an architect/in-charge. The petitioners argued this was done without proper procedure, without consulting the right authorities (claiming only the Chief Secretary or S&GAD could approve such a transfer), and that it disrupted their existing work and violated government policy, alleging Respondent No. 6 was pursuing the post for personal gain.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It held that postings are the exclusive prerogative of the concerned department, and employees cannot demand postings based on personal preference. The court found the petitioners failed to show any actual prejudice caused to them, or any vested or fundamental legal right that was violated. It also held that the deputation order for Respondent No. 6 was passed reasonably, following proper procedure, for a fixed three-year term, and could not be overturned merely on allegations of personal motive.

This ruling reinforces that administrative transfer and deputation decisions largely fall within a department's discretion, and courts will not interfere unless a clear legal right or fundamental right is shown to be violated.

title: Justice of Peace can agree or disagree with Police Report
explainer:
This case involved a woman who alleged that a shopkeeper and others committed rape against her, and when police refused to register a case, she approached an Ex-Officio Justice of Peace (an additional sessions judge acting in that capacity) seeking a direction for registration of an FIR. The Justice of Peace ordered the police station to record her statement and proceed if a cognizable offence was made out. The shopkeeper challenged this order before the Lahore High Court.

The High Court noted that before passing this order, the Justice of Peace had actually called for a police report, which found no occurrence had taken place, raised questions about the woman's character, and suggested the complaint was made with malicious intent, possibly for blackmail, and linked to a property dispute. However, the Justice of Peace ignored this report entirely without giving any reasons for rejecting it.

The court held that while a Justice of Peace is not obligated to seek a police report before deciding such applications, once a report is called for and obtained, it cannot simply be ignored. If the Justice of Peace disagrees with the police findings, reasons must be recorded explaining why. Passing an order contrary to an obtained report without any justification is not acceptable.

The court therefore set aside the order and dismissed the application, though it left open the possibility for the woman to pursue other legal remedies. This ruling clarifies the proper procedure Justices of Peace must follow when police reports are part of the record.

Ghazala Ali, the appellant, accused her brother and sister-in-law of forging documents to fraudulently transfer ownership of her late father's house, thereby depriving her and other family members of their rightful inheritance share. She filed an FIR in 2018 alleging that fake signatures of her deceased father had been used, along with a forged succession certificate, to transfer the property.

The trial court acquitted the accused before full trial, using Section 249-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows early acquittal when there is no reasonable chance of conviction. Ghazala Ali appealed this decision to the Islamabad High Court.

The High Court upheld the acquittal. It found that the family's inheritance dispute had already been resolved through a signed family settlement agreement in 1998, which the appellant herself had signed and never got legally cancelled. The court also noted that the FIR was filed roughly 27 years after the original property transfer and about 20 years after the settlement agreement, an unexplained and lengthy delay. Crucially, a handwriting expert's report, verified by senior FIA officials, found that the father's signatures matched his usual signatures, contradicting the forgery claim. The court concluded there was no credible evidence implicating the respondents in fraud or forgery, and dismissed the appeal.

This case highlights how long delays in reporting alleged crimes, combined with prior settlements and expert evidence, can undermine criminal allegations, especially in family property disputes.

title: Father's right to custody after mother's death
explainer:
This case, decided by the Supreme Court of Pakistan, dealt with a dispute over custody of four children after their mother's death. The father, Nasir Raza, and the children's maternal grandmother, Walayet Begum, both sought custody. The grandmother had initially been granted custody by the Guardian Judge, but an appellate court later awarded custody to the father. The High Court then reversed that decision and restored custody to the grandmother, allowing the father only scheduled visits. The father challenged this High Court ruling before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court ruled in the father's favor. It held that as the natural guardian, and given the children's ages, the grandmother's right of custody (hizanat) no longer applied. The Court found the father willing, financially capable, and available to raise his children, noting he had neither remarried nor returned to work abroad in order to care for them, and that his own mother could help in the household. Since there was no evidence he was unfit or unwilling to be a guardian, the Court held it would be unjust to deny the children their father's care. It set aside the High Court's judgment and restored custody to the father, while directing that the children continue spending weekends with their grandmother to preserve their emotional bond with her.

This case matters because it reaffirms that a father's right to custody, as natural guardian, generally takes precedence when he is fit and willing, while still recognizing the importance of maintaining children's emotional ties to other close family members.

title: Custodial Rights of Maternal Grandparents
explainer:
This case involved a custody dispute over a young girl, Rukhsar Bano, aged about two and a half years, who had lived with her maternal grandmother since birth. Her father, a Pakistan Army officer, sought her custody, and the lower courts (the Guardian Judge and the Additional District Judge) had ruled in his favor. The maternal grandmother challenged these decisions before the Lahore High Court, arguing that the father had made no effort to build a relationship with the child and that the case had been filed to hand her over to her paternal grandparents rather than for her genuine welfare.

The High Court reaffirmed the general principle that a father, as natural guardian, is normally entitled to custody unless disqualified, but custody decisions must ultimately serve the child's welfare. Since the child had never developed an emotional bond with her father and had only ever known her maternal grandmother's care, the court found that abruptly removing her would be traumatic. It also noted that new evidence about the father's job retirement and his son's school admission had emerged after the original trial, and had not been properly considered.

Rather than deciding custody outright, the High Court sent the case back to the trial court to hear fresh evidence, while allowing the father supervised visitation twice a month to build a bond with his daughter. This case highlights how Pakistani courts prioritize a child's emotional stability and actual welfare over rigid legal entitlements of parents.

title: PLJ 2010 Lahore 338
explainer:
This case involved a husband and wife from Rawalpindi who both went to court over issues arising from their divorce. The wife, Mst. Shehnaz Bano, had filed a family court suit seeking dissolution of her marriage, return of her dowry articles, and maintenance. The marriage was dissolved, and later the family court also awarded her maintenance but rejected her claim for dowry articles. On appeal, the appellate judge (Additional District Judge) sided with her on the dowry issue, ordering the husband to return the articles, but kept the maintenance amounts unchanged. Both parties were unhappy and separately challenged this appellate decision before the High Court.

The wife argued her husband hadn't personally appeared in the original proceedings and that her dowry claim was valid. The husband argued the maintenance amount was too high. The High Court found the wife's evidence about the dowry articles unconvincing, noting inconsistencies such as purchase receipts dated before the marriage, and ruled that the family court had not properly examined the evidence when it first ruled on this point. The court also rejected the husband's complaint about maintenance, noting he was well-off and working in Dubai.

The court did make one change: it increased the child's maintenance allowance by ordering an automatic 10% annual increase, reasoning that rising costs mean children's needs grow over time, and building in automatic increases would reduce the need for future court cases. Both petitions were otherwise dismissed.

title: Re-examination without cross examination is not possible
explainer:
This case comes from a murder trial in Attock district, where an FIR had been registered under sections dealing with murder. During the trial, a doctor testifying as a prosecution witness gave his main statement (examination-in-chief) in court, but his cross-examination by the defence was postponed to a later date. Before that cross-examination could happen, the prosecution asked the trial court to let it re-examine the doctor first, because it wanted to bring on record a statement the deceased had allegedly made to police in the hospital, which the doctor had signed. The trial court agreed and allowed this re-examination to happen before the defence had cross-examined the witness.

The accused challenged this order in the Lahore High Court. The court held that while the law does allow a witness to be re-examined if the court thinks it necessary for a fair decision, this must follow the proper sequence: examination-in-chief first, then cross-examination by the opposing side, and only after that re-examination. Re-examination cannot jump ahead of cross-examination.

The High Court therefore allowed the revision petition, ruling that the doctor must first be cross-examined by the defence, and only afterward should the re-examination take place, with a further chance for the defence to re-cross-examine if new matters come up. This case matters because it clarifies the correct order in which witnesses must be examined during criminal trials, protecting the defence's right to fair cross-examination.

title: Mistake in Evidence can be ractified
explainer:
This case is about a land dispute in Punjab. Abdul Majeed sued the sons of a deceased man named Hamza, claiming that Hamza had orally agreed to sell him about 44 kanals of land for Rs. 3,00,000, that Rs. 50,000 had already been paid as advance, and that after Hamza's death his sons refused to complete the sale. The sons denied any such agreement, saying the land actually belonged to their mother, the respondent's own sister, and that he was simply trying to grab her inheritance.

The trial court and the first appellate court both ruled in favor of Abdul Majeed, ordering specific performance of the alleged sale agreement. The Lahore High Court, however, examined the actual oral evidence given by the plaintiff's witnesses and found serious inconsistencies: the witnesses contradicted each other on who was present, none of them specified when the alleged agreement was made, and the plaintiff's own testimony did not clearly establish that the sons had agreed to sell or that they had received the advance payment. The court held that under the law of evidence, the burden of proving such an oral agreement was heavy, and the plaintiff failed to meet it through reliable testimony.

The judgment emphasizes that courts must decide cases based on evidence actually on record, and that a decision built on misreading or ignoring evidence amounts to a legal error correctable by higher courts. This case highlights how appellate courts can step in to fix mistakes when lower courts overlook contradictions in evidence.

title: Article 140- Cross Examination of a Witness
explainer:
This case concerns a criminal revision from the Sindh High Court about how witnesses can be cross-examined, arising from proceedings under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005. During cross-examination, defence counsel tried to confront a witness with a document (an application filed in other proceedings) to challenge his credibility. The trial court refused to allow this, saying the document could not be shown or its contents put to the witness because it had not been formally exhibited in the case.

The High Court found this approach wrong. It examined Article 140 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, which allows a witness to be cross-examined about previous statements in writing without first showing or proving the document, as long as it is relevant. Only if the cross-examiner intends to contradict the witness using that writing must the witness's attention specifically be drawn to the relevant parts, and the document produced at that stage. The court held that merely referring to a document to test a witness's credibility does not require it to already be exhibited. The trial judge had wrongly blocked a relevant question altogether, which was against the law.

The court set aside the trial court's order and allowed the revision. This matters because it clarifies the balance between defence and prosecution rights during trials, ensuring witnesses can be properly and fairly cross-examined without unnecessary technical obstacles, while preserving rules for when documents must be produced to contradict testimony.

title: Open Merit & Transparency in Educational Institutions
explainer:
This case, decided by the Peshawar High Court, concerned a student, Ahmad Danyal, who was denied admission to F.Sc Pre-Medical and Pre-Engineering programs at Islamia College and University College for Boys, Peshawar. He challenged the admission system, arguing that only 150 seats were available on open merit, while 250 seats were reserved for self-finance students and about 120 seats were set aside for various special quotas, including seats for children of college employees and teachers. He argued this arrangement violated the constitutional right to equal treatment and non-discrimination under Articles 25 and 27, and undermined the newly recognized fundamental right to education under Article 25-A.

The Provincial Government itself agreed that reserving so many seats for special quotas, particularly for employees' and teachers' children, was disproportionate and unfair to deserving students who competed on merit.

The Court held that public educational institutions belong to the public, not to their staff or administration, and that giving preferential quotas to employees' children was arbitrary and unlawful. However, it distinguished this from quotas for disabled students or students from backward and underdeveloped regions, including FATA, which the Constitution specifically permits to promote social and educational upliftment.

The Court allowed the petition, declaring the self-finance and special quotas (other than those constitutionally justified) illegal and without lawful authority. The ruling reinforces the principle that admission to public educational institutions should primarily be based on open merit and transparency, protecting equal educational opportunity for all students.

title: No case if EOI is not submitted on time
explainer:
This case involved a company, Premier Battery Industries, that challenged a public notice issued by the Karachi Water & Sewerage Board (KW&SB) inviting expression of interest for building a power project on a build-operate-own basis. The company claimed the notice violated public procurement rules because it did not give enough time or sufficient details for parties to submit bids.

The Sindh High Court had already dismissed the company's petition, mainly because it found the company had no legal standing to challenge the process. The Supreme Court agreed and refused to grant leave to appeal.

The Court found that the company never actually submitted an expression of interest by the deadline, did not meet the technical or financial qualifications required (such as experience in power projects or the required financial turnover), and had made no documented attempt to form a consortium with an eligible partner. It also waited about a month after the deadline before going to court, undermining any claim of urgency.

The Court further held that this was not genuine public interest litigation, since such litigation must clearly show good faith and a real concern for public welfare, not personal gain. Here, the company was found to be pursuing its own economic interest, essentially trying to reopen a process it had missed. The petition was dismissed, reinforcing that only genuinely affected or public-spirited parties can challenge government procurement notices in court.

title: Non Payment of Surety makes the bail inoperative
explainer:
This case involved five petitioners who were accused of forgery, cheating, and related offenses under the Pakistan Penal Code. They had applied to the Islamabad High Court for pre-arrest bail, which was granted on an interim basis, but on the condition that they submit bail bonds of Rs. 20,000 each along with sureties of equal amount within a set time.

The petitioners repeatedly sought adjournments but never actually furnished the required bail bonds or sureties, despite nearly two weeks passing. Because they failed to comply, the police went ahead and arrested them, reasoning that since the conditions for bail were never fulfilled, the bail order had never actually taken effect.

The High Court agreed with this reasoning. It held that a grant of bail is not automatically effective the moment it is announced; it only becomes operative once the accused actually furnishes the required bail bonds and sureties, since it is the surety who takes on the responsibility of producing the accused before the court. Since no such bonds or sureties were submitted here, the bail order never came into force, and the arrest was lawful. As a result, the petitioners could no longer seek pre-arrest bail, since they were already in custody; instead, they would need to apply for post-arrest bail through the normal process.

This case matters because it clarifies that courts treat compliance with bail conditions, not just the announcement of bail, as the real trigger for release, reinforcing accountability in the bail process.

title: Right of Custody of Minor is not an absolute right
explainer:
This case involved a father, Muhammad Afzal, who sought legal guardianship and custody of his three children from their mother, Parveen Bibi, after the couple separated and she filed for divorce. He argued that as the natural guardian under Islamic law, and since the sons were over seven years old and the daughter had reached puberty, he should be granted custody. The trial court rejected his application, and he appealed to the Azad Jammu and Kashmir High Court.

The High Court upheld the trial court's decision and dismissed the father's appeal. It ruled that a father's right to custody is not automatic or absolute, even under the general rule of Muslim law that gives fathers guardianship rights once children pass certain ages. The paramount consideration in any custody matter is always the welfare of the child. The court noted the children had lived with their mother for a long time, had grown closer to her, and were old enough to express a preference, which the law allows courts to consider. The father failed to prove any specific harm or misconduct by the mother that would disqualify her from custody, such as remarriage to an unrelated person, immoral conduct, or neglect. The court suggested the appeal may have been filed mainly to avoid paying child maintenance. This case reinforces the principle that in custody disputes, courts prioritize children's best interests and emotional bonds over rigid application of traditional guardianship rules.

The case was restored, but the Rent Controller then struck off the tenant's right to defend itself for having missed a rent deposit during the period the case stood dismissed, and ordered eviction. The petition was allowed, meaning the matter was sent back for proper determination.

title: Importance of 342 Statement in a Criminal Trial
explainer:
This Supreme Court judgment concerns Muhammad Saddique, who was convicted of murder and other offences and sentenced to death by a trial court in Balochistan, with the High Court upholding the conviction. He was accused of shooting his brother's two sons and injuring his own father during a family dispute. He had initially been tried and convicted in absentia under special terrorism laws, but that conviction was later set aside and a fresh trial ordered after his arrest.

The key problem was that the only direct eyewitness to the shooting, an injured witness named Jumma Khan, and another witness had died before the fresh trial could record their testimony. Instead of properly bringing their earlier statements on record according to law, the trial court simply accepted a death certificate and relied on the witness's old statement from the earlier in-absentia trial, then convicted the appellant based on that evidence. The High Court upheld this approach.

The Supreme Court explained that dead witnesses' prior statements can only be used as evidence if properly introduced under the law, and clarified the legal distinction between recording evidence when an accused is a proclaimed absconder versus conducting a full trial in absentia under special terrorism legislation. The judgment also reaffirms that any incriminating evidence must be specifically put to the accused during his Section 342 examination, or it cannot be used against him. This case highlights how procedural fairness and proper evidentiary rules must be followed even in serious criminal cases involving the death penalty.

title: PLJ 2018 Islamabad 276
explainer:
This case involved a landlord-tenant dispute over commercial premises in Islamabad, leased under a five-year agreement. The landlord filed an eviction petition alleging rent default and breach of lease terms. During proceedings, the Rent Controller ordered the tenant to deposit monthly rent in court pending final decision. The eviction case was later dismissed for non-prosecution, but the landlord applied to have it restored, and it was restored. The Rent Controller then struck off the tenant's right to defend itself because it had failed to deposit rent for a certain period, and ordered eviction. The tenant's appeal to the Additional District Judge was also dismissed, prompting this petition before the Islamabad High Court.

The tenant argued it should not have been penalized for not depositing rent while the case was dismissed and no longer pending, and that it deposited rent promptly once it learned of the restoration application. It also claimed it had tried to pay advance rent as required by the lease, which the landlord refused to accept.

The High Court held that when a case dismissed for non-prosecution is restored, earlier interim orders (like the rent deposit order) are revived, but disputed factual questions—whether the tenant actually tried to pay the required advance rent and whether it breached the lease—must be properly examined through an inquiry by the Rent Controller. The Court allowed the petition, sending the matter back for proper determination rather than upholding automatic eviction.

explainer:
This case involves a legal challenge over how the Chairman of the Capital Development Authority (CDA) and its Board members were appointed. The petitioner questioned the Federal Government's actions in nominating the elected Mayor of Islamabad as an ex-officio member of the CDA Board, and then separately directing him to perform the additional duties of Chairman on a part-time basis.

The Islamabad High Court ruled that this arrangement was illegal. Under the CDA Ordinance of 1960, members and the Chairman must be formally appointed for fixed terms (four years for members, five years for the Chairman), following specific qualifications and procedures set out in the law. title: Three months delay in FIR
explainer:
This case from the Lahore High Court involved two brothers, Zubair Ashraf and Qais Ashraf, who sought pre-arrest bail after being named in an FIR accusing them of armed robbery. The complainant, a widow, alleged that on 29 April 2014 the petitioners and others broke into her house with firearms and stole gold ornaments and cash. However, the FIR was not registered until 2 August 2014, more than three months later.

The defense argued the case was false and motivated by personal grudge, since Zubair Ashraf had married the complainant's daughter with her consent, and no stolen property was recovered from either petitioner.

The court treated the two petitioners differently. For Zubair Ashraf, the court found he had used his family connection to gain access to the complainant's home and, in the process, caused serious harm to two families, including allegedly pressuring the daughter into supporting him. The court refused him bail, saying such conduct deserved firm treatment despite the lack of recovered property.

For Qais Ashraf, the brother, the court found there was reasonable doubt about his involvement, and since such doubt can be given the benefit of the accused even at the bail stage, it confirmed his pre-arrest bail on furnishing bonds.

The case illustrates how courts assess bail applications individually based on each accused's specific role and circumstances, even when they are co-accused in the same case, and how the benefit of doubt can apply differently to different defendants.

title: Provisions of 367 CRPC are mandatory for conviction
explainer:
This case involved six petitioners, Ali Muhammad and others, who were accused of demolishing two walls of a house belonging to Feroze Khan and encroaching on his property in 1986. They were tried and convicted under multiple sections of the Pakistan Penal Code relating to criminal trespass and unlawful assembly (Sections 440, 448, 148, and 149). Two of them were sentenced to one year of rigorous imprisonment, while the rest received six months each. Their appeal was dismissed by the Additional Sessions Judge, so they brought the matter before the Lahore High Court.

The High Court did not examine whether the petitioners were actually guilty. Instead, it found a serious legal flaw in how the trial court had handled the conviction. Although the men were charged under four separate legal provisions, the trial court failed to pass a separate sentence for each offense, as required by Section 367(2) and (3) of the Criminal Procedure Code. This provision is mandatory, meaning courts must clearly specify the offense and sentence under each section when someone is convicted of multiple offenses.

Because this mandatory requirement was violated, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence entirely. It then considered whether to send the case back for retrial, but declined to do so, noting that the incident had occurred five years earlier and the petitioners had already endured a long trial process, including being jailed three times. The petition was accepted, and the case was closed without retrial.

title: Objections on Local Commission Report Judgment
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a partnership business between two brothers dealing in iron rods. After one brother died, the surviving brother filed a lawsuit seeking rendition of accounts, arguing he should not be held liable for business losses that occurred after his brother's death, which he claimed were caused by the deceased brother's widow and others who had taken over running the business.

The trial court had earlier ruled there was no actual partnership between the parties and appointed a local commission (an independent investigator) to examine the business accounts. When the commission submitted its report, the appellant initially objected to it, but his lawyer later withdrew those objections in court, leading to a final decree against the appellant's interests. The appellant later argued his lawyer had no authority to withdraw the objections and had done so without his knowledge or consent.

The Lahore High Court found this significant: the appellant was not present in court when his lawyer withdrew the objections, and the lawyer never stated he was acting on his client's instructions. The court held that the lawyer-client relationship is one of trust, and lawyers are legally and morally bound to act only on their client's instructions. Since there was no proof the withdrawal was authorized, the court ruled it was invalid and possibly collusive. The case was sent back to the trial court so the appellant could formally challenge his lawyer's authority to make that statement.

This case matters because it reinforces that lawyers cannot make major decisions, like abandoning objections in a case, without their client's clear consent, and courts must protect clients from unauthorized actions taken in their name.

title: Quashment and Car Custody in one Judgment
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over who should get custody of a car seized by police during a criminal investigation. Police had stopped a Toyota Corolla in 2006 and found fake currency notes and fraudulent identity documents inside, leading to a criminal case against the occupants under charges including forgery and cheating. Since then, the car itself had remained tied up in legal proceedings while various parties tried to claim it.

Orix Leasing Pakistan Limited, a finance company, had originally leased the car to a man named Habibullah Jan under a lease agreement. When Jan failed to make timely payments, the company argued it remained the legal owner and was entitled to get the vehicle back. An earlier claimant, Saif-ur-Rehman, who said he had bought the car from Jan, had already tried to claim the vehicle through the courts but abandoned his case and was later declared a fugitive from the criminal trial.

The Peshawar High Court first rejected a technical objection that this type of petition could not be used to challenge earlier court orders, citing Supreme Court precedent allowing such intervention to prevent injustice. On the main issue, the court found that Orix Leasing was the undisputed owner of the car, no one else had a valid competing claim, and the vehicle was no longer needed for the police investigation. Keeping it parked indefinitely would only cause it to deteriorate. The court therefore ordered the car be returned to the leasing company.

title: Judgment in a Central Excise Act 1944 Case
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over whether customs and excise officers can legally register an FIR (First Information Report) when investigating offences under the Central Excise Act, 1944.

Farman Ali and others had an FIR registered against them under the Central Excise Act. They challenged it in the Peshawar High Court, which ruled the FIR invalid, reasoning that the Act only allows prosecution through a written complaint filed by a Central Excise Officer before a Special Judge, and does not itself provide for registering an FIR like ordinary criminal cases.

The Deputy Director of Customs Intelligence appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court examined Section 13 of the Act in detail, which lays out a complete procedure for excise officers to arrest suspects, record details of the arrest and investigation in a register, and then file a complaint before a Special Judge if there is sufficient evidence. The Court found strong similarities between this recording procedure and the ordinary FIR process under Section 154 of the Criminal Procedure Code, and held that excise officers do have implicit power to register a case in this manner.

However, the Court clarified that even if the FIR format itself was improperly registered, this did not wipe out the entire criminal proceedings, since the officer could still file a formal complaint under Section 13(11), which functions like a police report under Section 173 Cr.P.C. The appeal was therefore partially allowed, meaning the case could proceed based on a validly filed complaint despite the FIR issue.

title: Implementation of Exchange in Revenue Records
explainer:
This case from the Lahore High Court dealt with a property dispute involving two brothers who had each been allotted separate residential plots by the government in Jauharabad, District Khushab. One brother was allotted Plot No. 41 and the other Plot No. 54. The brothers privately agreed to exchange the plots between themselves, and each built houses on the plot the other had originally received, with construction expenses paid accordingly. Years later, the family of one brother sued the Province of Punjab to have the exchange officially recorded in government revenue records, since the government department had never formally updated its records to reflect the swap.

The trial court dismissed the suit, but the appellate court reversed that decision and ruled in favor of the plaintiffs. The Province of Punjab challenged this reversal before the High Court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision. It found that both parties and witnesses had admitted the exchange took place, that construction had been carried out based on it, and that a government official had even acknowledged in court that the department would have no objection to transferring the plots if the parties formally applied, since the land belonged to the Housing Department. Given this clear evidentiary support, the court ruled there was no reason to interfere with the appellate court's judgment favoring the plaintiffs.

The case highlights how courts can order government records to reflect long-standing, mutually accepted private property arrangements when the facts are undisputed.

title: Rent Controller is Bound to Ascertain Relationship at Preliminary Stage
explainer:
This case involved a landlord-tenant rent dispute in Islamabad. A landlady filed an eviction petition against her tenant, and the Rent Controller ordered the tenant to pay monthly rent of Rs. 53,000, both for a past period and going forward, while the case was pending. The tenant challenged this rent order in the Lahore High Court, arguing that the Rent Controller should not have issued such an order without first properly determining, through formal evidence, whether a landlord-tenant relationship actually existed between the parties.

The High Court disagreed. It explained that when a tenant disputes the existence of a landlord-tenant relationship, the law only requires the Rent Controller to make a tentative or preliminary finding based on available material, not a full trial, before issuing an interim rent order. In this case, the tenant had earlier acknowledged the lease agreement and even relied on it himself in his own petition, so the court found no merit in his denial.

The court also held that such interim rent orders are provisional and eventually merge into the final decision of the case, which can be appealed under the law. Since the order was not final, it could not be challenged directly through a constitutional petition in the High Court. The petitioner would have to wait for the final decision and appeal it through the proper forum. The petition was therefore dismissed. This case clarifies the limited scope for challenging interim rent orders in higher courts.

explainer:
This case is about a dispute over an industrial plot of land in Karachi. The plaintiff (respondent No.1) filed a suit in 2005 for specific performance of an agreement to sell against the defendant (respondent No.2). Years later, the appellant, who claimed to have his own separate agreement to purchase the same property from the same seller and to be in possession of it, tried to join that lawsuit as a defendant, arguing that the plaintiff and defendant were colluding to cheat him out of his rights, possibly using a forged agreement. A single judge of the Sindh High Court had refused to let him join the case, and he appealed.

The appellate bench upheld that refusal. It explained that under the law governing civil procedure, a "necessary party" is someone without whom the court cannot make an effective decision, while a "proper party" is someone whose presence helps fully resolve all issues but isn't essential. Deciding whether to add a party is a matter of judicial discretion based on the specific facts, not a rigid rule. The court found the appellant hadn't shown real evidence of collusion between the plaintiff and defendant, and he wasn't actually replacing or standing in for the existing defendant, who was already contesting the case (and had even accused the plaintiff of forgery himself). Since the original judge had properly exercised his discretion, the appeal was dismissed. The case clarifies how courts decide who can be added to ongoing lawsuits.

title: Justice Delayed is Justice Denied
explainer:
This case arose from a civil suit for specific performance pending in a Lahore civil court between Mrs. Fozia Nasir (plaintiff) and Hibbatul Mannan Khalid Omar and others (defendants). The defendants, unhappy with how the trial court was handling the proceedings, filed a revision petition before the Lahore High Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, complaining that the case was being needlessly prolonged.

The Chief Justice noted that by the time the matter came up for hearing, the specific relief originally sought had lost its relevance, since the parties' lawyers agreed that pending miscellaneous applications had already been resolved and both sides wanted the main case decided quickly.

However, the court used the opportunity to make broader observations about delay in litigation. It emphasized that laws like the Code of Civil Procedure and the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order lay down detailed procedures for fair trials, and judges have a serious responsibility to prevent parties from misusing these procedures to stall cases. The court criticized the common practice of courts spending excessive time on miscellaneous and interlocutory applications while neglecting the real dispute, calling this piecemeal approach wasteful and unfair to litigants.

The court disposed of the petition, directing the trial court to decide the suit before the winter vacation of 2008, with cooperation from both parties. The case reinforces the principle that delayed justice amounts to denied justice, urging courts to prioritize timely resolution of the core dispute.

title: Re-employment can be made in Public Interest
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the appointment of the Chairman of AKMIDC (a government-linked mining/industrial development corporation) in Azad Jammu and Kashmir. A retired government officer, who had served as Chief Conservator of Forest, was re-employed on a one-year contract as Chairman of AKMIDC shortly after his retirement. A senior officer of the corporation, who had over 32 years of service and hoped to be considered for promotion to that post, challenged this appointment in the High Court. He argued that the appointment violated government policy on re-employment of retired civil servants and ignored his right to be considered for the position.

The Azad Jammu and Kashmir High Court ruled in favor of the petitioner, declaring the appointment of the retired officer as Chairman AKMIDC to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. The court held that re-employment of retired civil servants should only happen in the public interest and as an exception, not as a routine way to accommodate retired bureaucrats. It should be reserved for highly competent individuals with distinguished expertise, used only when no qualified person is available from existing government cadres. The court also found that the appointment contradicted an earlier cabinet decision and official policy, and that the post in question belonged to a different administrative cadre than the one the retired officer came from.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that government appointments and re-employment decisions must strictly follow established rules and cannot be made arbitrarily or to favor influential retired officials over qualified serving employees.

title: Amicus Curiae Definition as per Judgment
explainer:
This is a decision of the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Supreme Court dealing with a petition asking it to review its own earlier judgment from 1979.

The petitioner had lost an appeal decided by the Court in 1979 and later sought a review of that decision. The Court dismissed the petition for two independent reasons. First, under the Supreme Court Rules, a review petition can only be drawn up and filed by the advocate who represented the party in the original appeal, unless special permission is granted. Here, the review petition was filed by a different lawyer without such permission, which alone was enough to dismiss it. Second, the judgment being challenged was passed in 1979, before the Court was even given the legal power to review its own judgments (that power came only through a 1980 law, which the Court had already ruled applies only to future judgments, not past ones). Since the Court had no review power at the relevant time, it could not now review that old judgment.

The Court also addressed a request by another lawyer to be allowed to argue the case as amicus curiae ("friend of the court") - a neutral legal advisor with no stake in the outcome. The Court explained that only the Court itself can appoint someone as amicus curiae; a lawyer cannot volunteer for that role, especially one who admitted he was acting in the petitioner's interest. This case is significant for clarifying the limited, court-controlled nature of the amicus curiae role and reinforcing procedural rules on who may file review petitions and when review powers apply.

title: Plea of Fraud by Pardanasheen Lady
explainer:
This case involved four illiterate, secluded (pardanasheen) sisters from Okara who claimed they were cheated out of their inherited farmland. Their father had gifted them land, but a local revenue official (Patwari), allegedly working with buyers named as respondents, got two mutations (official land transfer records) attested in 1974 showing the sisters had sold the land for Rs. 32,000 each. The sisters denied ever selling the land, appearing before the revenue officer, or receiving any payment, and sued for a declaration that they remained the rightful owners.

The trial court ruled in their favor, but the appellate court and later the High Court reversed this and sided with the buyers. The Supreme Court took up the case, noting troubling gaps: no male relative was present during the mutation, the women were identified by a lambardar from a different village with no explained connection to them, conflicting testimony about where payment was made, and missing thumb impressions on official records.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the sisters. It held that when illiterate pardanasheen women allege fraud in a property transaction, the burden falls on the party benefiting from the deal to prove it was genuine and fully understood by the women. Since the evidence here was unreliable, the mutations were declared fictitious, illegal, and void. The judgment reinforces important legal protection for vulnerable women against fraudulent property transfers, emphasizing that fraud can invalidate even long-settled transactions.

title: Order passed by Rent Controller under section 44 is not appealable
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over Chouhan Plaza, a building in Mirpur, where two parties each claimed rights to different portions. When tenants vacated the building and deposited its keys with the Rent Controller, one claimant, Malik Abdul Rehman, sought possession of the southern portion he claimed to own, while another party, Ghazala Ajaib, had already received keys to the northern portion. Since ownership of the building was still being litigated in a separate civil court, the Rent Controller handed over the southern portion's keys to Malik Abdul Rehman temporarily, reasoning that leaving the building locked indefinitely would cause it damage, and made this handover conditional on the outcome of the ownership case.

The other party appealed this decision, but the Appellate Authority (District Judge) dismissed the appeal, ruling that the Rent Controller's order was merely an administrative and interlocutory order, not a final decision, and therefore could not be appealed. The appeal was also filed late.

The High Court agreed with this reasoning. It held that under the AJ&K Interim Constitution Act, it does not act as an appellate court over special tribunals like the Rent Controller unless the tribunal exceeded its jurisdiction or acted unlawfully. Since the Rent Controller's order was interlocutory and did not resolve the full ownership dispute, it was not appealable. The court also noted the petition was flawed because the Rent Controller, whose order was being challenged, had not been made a party to the case, which is legally required.

The Federal Shariat Court upheld the conviction, emphasizing that every person is born with inherent human dignity under Islamic principles, regardless of background, and that falsely attacking someone's legitimacy causes real harm to their reputation and feelings. title: Essential Documents for decision can be produced after additional evidence petition acceptance
explainer:
This case arose from a property dispute. The respondents had sued for specific performance of an agreement to sell, claiming the petitioners had failed to complete their end of the deal. The trial court ruled in favor of the respondents and ordered the contract enforced. The petitioners appealed, and during the appeal, they asked the court to allow additional evidence, specifically, records from the stamp vendor and the person who wrote up the document, to prove that what was actually signed was a lease agreement, not a sale contract. The appellate court (District Judge) refused to allow this additional evidence, so the petitioners challenged that refusal in the Lahore High Court.

The High Court sided with the petitioners. It explained that under the law governing additional evidence in appeals, such evidence can be admitted not only when a lower court wrongly refused to admit it, or when it's needed for a just decision, but also whenever there is "any other substantial cause." The court found that the petitioners' claim, that the actual transaction was a lease rather than a sale, had already been raised in their written statement, so they weren't barred from introducing supporting evidence later. It ruled that the District Judge had wrongly refused to exercise this discretion and allowed the additional evidence to be produced.

This case matters because it clarifies that parties aren't automatically barred from introducing important supporting documents on appeal just because they didn't do so at trial, especially when those documents are essential to fairly deciding the true nature of a disputed agreement.

title: Appointment of Arbitrator Judgment
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a construction company, China International Water and Electric Corporation, and the Sarhad Hydel Development Organisation (a government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa entity) over a contract agreement. The company sought recovery of over Rs. 225 million along with markup, and had applied under the Arbitration Act, 1940 for appointment of an arbitrator to resolve the dispute, as provided for in the contract's dispute resolution clause. The trial court dismissed this application, ruling that the claim was barred by limitation and that earlier arbitration decisions covering 2004-2006 had already become final and binding.

The Peshawar High Court disagreed. It found that the trial court had decided the matter hastily, without properly examining the facts, without explaining how the earlier decisions were supposedly final, and without giving the parties a chance to present evidence. The High Court held that questions of limitation in a contract containing an arbitration clause, and disputes over large monetary claims, cannot be resolved summarily; they require proper evidence from both sides. Deciding such matters without a hearing violated basic principles of natural justice.

The High Court therefore set aside the trial court's order and sent the case back for a fresh decision, directing that both parties be given a proper opportunity to present their evidence. This case matters because it reinforces that courts cannot dismiss arbitration-related disputes on technical grounds without a fair, evidence-based hearing, especially in complex commercial contracts.
